item.title: Nearly two thirds of remote First Nations households lack free-to-air TV access
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Authors:

  • Daniel Featherstone, Principal Research Fellow, School of Media and Communication, RMIT University
  • Lyndon Ormond-Parker, Principal Research Fellow, School of Media and Communication, RMIT University; Australian National University
  • Mona Chatskin, Lecturer in Digital Communication, RMIT University
  • Sharon Parkinson, Associate Professor & Associate Investigator ARC Centre of Excellence for Automated Decision Making + Society, Swinburne University of Technology

Nearly two thirds of households in remote First Nations communities do not have access to free-to-air TV, due to issues with the satellite service that delivers television where normal broadcasts are unavailable.

The latest report from the Mapping the Digital Gap project also shows the use of online streaming is on the rise. But here too access can be limited and often unaffordable for First Nations people in remote communities.

Without access to free-to-air TV, spending on pre-paid mobile data may rise, mobile services can become overloaded. People may also depend more on unreliable sources of news and information.

These findings are based on visits we made to 11 remote communities in 2025 and 2026. They build on research conducted since 2022 covering digital access, affordability, digital ability and access to media and information services.

Why free-to-air TV matters

First Nations radio and TV services, such as NITV and Indigenous Community TV, provide trusted, place-based and relevant news, information and language content. Yet access to these services is restricted by issues with VAST, broadcast maintenance, and the changing ways audiences access news.

The Australian government has committed to ensuring Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples achieve equal levels of digital inclusion by 2026. This means they would have access to information and services enabling participation and informed decision-making about their own lives.

The VAST service

In many remote communities, people access free-to-air TV via the federal government’s Viewer Access Satellite Television (VAST) service.

VAST began rolling out in 2010 as analogue TV broadcasts were switched off in favour of digital. Direct-to-home satellite equipment was installed in most remote First Nations households from 2011 to 2013. This replaced community broadcasting in many sites.

However, households now have to maintain this equipment. Failure of set-top boxes is common due to power surges. Smart cards needed for access are also often removed. Satellite dishes and cabling also fail due to damage or deterioration.

Radio and VAST services rely on satellite connectivity. Extreme weather conditions such as cyclones, storms and heavy cloud cover can also affect satellite connections. This can leave households without information services during weather emergencies.

A system breaking down – and it’s hard to repair

In remote communities, technical support typically comes from regional centres which makes maintenance more difficult and costly. A new set-top box typically costs between $400 and $600 in local stores, which can be a significant cost. People also report difficulties with activating smart cards.

We found 63% of our survey respondents had no access to free-to-air TV, up from 50% in 2022. Some remote communities report an even higher than average failure rate of VAST set-top boxes.

In Ampilatwatja, only 24% of VAST TV services were working. Results were similar in Pipalyatjara and Kalka (both 25%), despite satellite dish upgrades on houses in remote South Australia by Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara (APY) Housing. VAST TV rates were also low for Utju (32%), Maningrida (34%) and Woorabinda (38%) in 2026, with Warakurna also on 34% in 2025.

In October, the First Nations Digital Inclusion Advisory Group called for upgrades to VAST services and a return to community broadcasting.

Community-led solutions

To improve free-to-air TV access, two small communities have initiated community-led solutions to reduce set-top box costs and card activation issues.

In Oak Valley, where local staff assist residents to activate set-top boxes, 64% of residents have access to TV services in 2026. In Punmu, the community provides residents set-top boxes with pre-activated smart cards at wholesale prices, and we found 82% of survey respondents have working VAST TV services in 2026, up from 62% in 2025.

Drawing on previous research from the Mapping the Digital Gap project, the NT government recently funded a three-year trial upgrade of TV broadcasting in three Central Australian regional councils. This provides a pilot case study for a potential national upgrade program.

The latest report’s findings also highlight that households are taking up fixed broadband rapidly, up from 8% in 2025 to 32% in 2026, including 24% with Starlink services. This suggests people want to access TV and other digital content on demand, and streaming services are becoming more popular across communities as local media services become more limited.

Overall, there remains a high reliance on prepaid data in remote communities with 93% owning or sharing a mobile phone and 98% of these on pre-paid plans. Despite the high fixed broadband uptake, an average of 88% of communications spending in remote First Nations households goes to prepaid mobile recharges.

A federal government-funded rollout of free community-wide Wi-Fi networks to 23 remote communities across Australia since 2024-25 is helping to address access and affordability challenges in those sites. A second-phase rollout to 52 communities and homelands is also under way.

These and other initiatives led by governments, industry and communities are helping to close the digital gap for remote First Nations communities.

The authors would like to acknowledge co-authors Julian Thomas, Jenny Kennedy, Leah Hawkins, Yee Man Louie, Alison Barton, Shane Bawden and Lauren Ganley for their work on the 2026 Mapping the Digital Gap Outcomes Report.

The Mapping the Digital Gap research project is being undertaken within the ARC Centre of Excellence for Automated Decision-Making and Society, and receives funding from industry partner Telstra and the Australian Research Council. Daniel also co-leads an Australian Government funded national project to measure digital inclusion for First Nations Australians. Daniel is a member of the Expert Panel of the First Nations Digital Inclusion Advisory Board. He is a Director of the Australian Communications Consumer Action Network (ACCAN) and was formerly General Manager of First Nations Media Australia.

Lyndon Ormond-Parker is a Principal Research Fellow on the Mapping the Digital Gap project, which receives funding from Telstra and the Australian Research Council. He also currently holds a part-time ARC Discovery Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Award with the Centre for Heritage and Museum Studies, Australian National University. Lyndon is also co-chair of the First Nations Digital Inclusion Advisory Group.

Sharon Parkinson receives funding from the Australian Research Council, Telstra, the Department of Government Services Victoria, the Commonwealth Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications and the Arts, and The Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute.

item.title: AI is set to change the graduate job market. Here’s how unis can respond
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Armin D Ashenberg, Senior Lecturer in Law and Emerging Technologies, Western Sydney University

Globally, there have been concerns about the likelihood of artificial intelligence (AI) taking people’s jobs and reducing job opportunities for university graduates.

AI software companies, such as OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Anthropic are pursuing AI systems capable of matching or exceeding human performance across a broad range of intellectual tasks.

What does this mean for graduates and universities?

Which jobs are most at risk?

A federal government report, published in July, rated jobs typically involving cognitive tasks as those with the highest exposure to AI automation. This includes accountants, clerks and receptionists.

Jobs that were rated as the lowest exposure to AI automation tended to be those requiring more physical work, such as tradies, carers and truck drivers.

Much of the government narrative has been that jobs will more likely be changed or “augmented” by AI, rather than be cut by the technology.

The report also found that as of February this year, AI had not had significant impacts on the Australian job market. This included job opportunities for graduate students, despite international concerns AI will reduce the number of entry-level roles.

This article is part of a series on how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education.

We take a deeper look into how AI has disrupted degrees, how universities are responding to these new challenges and what the technology means for the sector’s future. You can find more stories here.

However, things might be changing. This month the Reserve Bank of Australia noted there are already some signs younger workers in more AI-exposed industries are struggling to find work in Australia.

The number of graduate jobs in some law firms has been slashed, with low-level tasks passed onto AI. Meanwhile, consulting firms have also cut graduate roles in recent years, but claim its not because of AI.

Just last week, Qantas announced it will outsource 850 jobs to India while investing more in AI.

What does this mean for desk jobs?

AI models have been improving fast and can now automate many tasks in university-qualified jobs.

Still, some experts argue reasoning and critical thinking skills are valuable for graduates in the AI job market.

Research shows AI can still compete.

In a 2024 study, researchers compared the reasoning skills of humans and AI language models (systems programmed to mimic human speech and writing) through a series of tests.

The tests included maths puzzles designed to assess whether people and AI models could recognise that an answer, which seems right at first, is actually wrong. For example, a scarf costs 210€ more than a hat. The scarf and the hat cost 220€ in total. How much does the hat cost? The correct answer is 5€.

People and AI models were then tested on how they reasoned their way to the correct answer.

Researchers found earlier AI systems performed worse than human participants in the study’s reasoning test, while more recent AI models performed better.

If this trend continues, AI could eventually outperform people on a much wider range of reasoning tasks. In one sign of that progress, an OpenAI model recently disproved a longstanding conjecture in geometry dating back to 1946.

My own research reflects similar findings.

We analysed AI’s responses on university criminal law exams in 2023 and 2025. We found its average exam scores improved from 52.5% in 2023 to 76.3% in 2025. The most striking finding was in critical thinking capabilities. Unlike the 2023 study, the 2025 models, on average, performed better than an average university student.

These were specific tests and do not prove AI could displace humans and take over an entire profession. But the results challenge the assumption AI weaknesses will remain unchanged.

What about trades?

Physical work is a challenge for AI. But if a sufficiently capable AI could control reliable, affordable robots then electricians and plumbers could also face competition.

We’re already seeing signs of this shift. Robotaxis carry passengers in a growing number of cities, delivery robots bring meals to customers and autonomous excavators dig on construction sites.

Despite significant progress in robots’ ability to carry out complex physical tasks it’s still unclear how soon they will be able to do more of the work tradies do. For now, students who choose vocational pathways, such as apprenticeships, may face a lower risk of AI-related job disruption.

Working with AI

This doesn’t mean it’s over for white-collar workers.

One likely possibility in an AI job market is that a person working with the technology will achieve a better result than AI alone. This is a form of AI augmentation, which can keep workers relevant and useful.

But research shows collaborating with AI is not an easy skill. Getting useful results takes judgement.

In a 2026 pilot study health-care professionals (mostly nurses) accepted half the deliberately wrong AI recommendations and passed over about one in six correct ones. And in a study looking at how the UK public uses AI for medical advice, researchers found people sometimes left out important details when consulting chatbots. As a result, the chatbots sometimes mixed useful suggestions with misleading ones.

How can unis prepare graduates well?

The possibility of humans working with AI should be central to how universities prepare students for the workforce.

If a worker can’t improve the quality or efficiency of AI’s output, an employer may have little economic reason to involve them.

To add value to the future workforce graduates may need to:

  • understand what a good result looks like when using AI

  • recognise when AI falls short

  • have the knowledge and skills to improve AI’s output.

They also need to learn how to collaborate with AI, how to direct it, question its output and persist until the result is better than what it produced initially.

Universities can’t simply replace disciplinary knowledge with AI skills. Students will need the knowledge and skills their degrees have always required, as well as the ability to collaborate effectively with AI.

The irony is that a technology designed to make our lives easier may actually require us to work harder to stay relevant in the job market.

Armin Ashenberg (formerly published under Armin Alimardani) previously held a part-time contract with OpenAI as a consultant. The organisation had no input into this piece.

item.title: Why the Microsoft 365 outage is different and why it takes so long to restore email services
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Doug Jacobson, University Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Iowa State University

The Microsoft services outage that began on Nov. 12, 2026, is not like other internet outages. The failure affected the Microsoft 365 suite of productivity services, including the video conferencing and collaboration platform Teams, AI assistant Copilot and, significantly, the Outlook email service.

Microsoft reported on Nov. 13 that the company is “continuing to see improvements in service availability” but that “some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery.”

Despite decades of predictions about its decline, email remains a central pillar of how organizations function. Password resets, invoices, legal notices and cybersecurity incident response coordination all depend on it. The Microsoft 365 outage affected businesses, governments and schools around the world.

When most people think about cloud outages, they picture a broken website or a stalled app. When the service going down includes email, however, the mechanics of the failure and how to recover from it are different from those of almost every other cloud service.

Unlike modern web apps or authentication gatekeepers, email wasn’t designed to fail fast, meaning to immediately halt when a problem arises.

Old architecture

When a typical cloud service breaks, it acts like a closed door. If an authentication provider or a cloud application goes down, users are immediately locked out and see an error message. Access stops. When people cannot get into the system, they are not actively generating new work or adding heavy processing loads to the broken servers. Once engineers fix the underlying bug and unlock the door, traffic can resume and the service often recovers fairly quickly.

Email does not have a closed door. It is built on an older, decentralized “store-and-forward” architecture designed to never lose a message, even when the destination is unreachable.

Because email is a network of thousands of independent systems, an outage at one major provider does not stop users on other platforms from hitting “send.” During major email disruptions like the one that hit Microsoft, millions of outside users on Gmail, corporate servers or other platforms could still compose and send emails to affected accounts without seeing an immediate error message.

From the sender’s perspective, everything works normally. Their email provider accepts the message, attempts to hand it off to the downed provider, realizes the destination isn’t answering, and quietly holds onto the message in an outbound queue to try again later.

Major highway crash

One way to think about email traffic in outages is to imagine a multilane interstate highway where an accident blocks two lanes of traffic. Drivers miles away don’t stop leaving their driveways just because there is a wreck up ahead; they keep entering the highway system. Soon, traffic backs up so severely that metered on-ramps have to stop letting new cars merge onto the interstate. Before long, that gridlock spills backward onto local feeder roads and city streets, choking traffic miles away from the actual crash site.

In this analogy, a downed email provider is the crash. Every other email server around the world is an on-ramp or a feeder road. While the outage lasts, millions of messages continue to pile up in queues across the internet, with unaffected servers repeatedly resending email to see whether traffic is moving yet.

When engineers finally fix the root cause of an email outage, it is the equivalent of tow trucks clearing the wreckage from the highway. The road is technically open again, but traffic does not instantly return to normal speed.

First, the massive backlog of vehicles already stuck on the main highway has to start moving. Only after that congestion clears can the on-ramps start letting queued-up cars merge back in, which in turn slowly relieves the gridlock on the surrounding local roads.

Similarly, when a major email provider comes back online, it is immediately hit with a tidal wave of pent-up messages and retry attempts from every other mail server on the internet. Processing those queues without overwhelming the newly restored servers takes time – typically hours to days.

Long, bumpy road to recovery

Because organizations have largely outsourced their email to a small number of global providers, an outage doesn’t just disrupt one company; it can stall entire sectors at once, cutting off the communication tool teams rely on to coordinate their emergency response.

And for everyday users, this unique architecture explains why email failures feel so drawn out: Even hours after a provider officially announces a problem is fixed, messages can still arrive out of order or trickle in slowly as the digital traffic jam finally clears.

item.title: Allegheny County has more license plate readers than any other Pa. county. Here’s what’s at stake
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • TK Vinod Kumar, Faculty in the Law, Criminal Justice and Society Program., University of Pittsburgh

Surveillance is a reality in the modern world. Security cameras record streets, stores, home entrances and even highways – and our phones keep track of where we go. Most of us likely don’t want to live like the characters in George Orwell’s novel “1984,” where an all-seeing government, Big Brother, is always watching. Yet technology used to fight crime has greatly increased the level of surveillance around the world.

In the United States, one technology in particular has become a focus of that debate: automated license plate readers.

These cameras, often mounted on poles at intersections and highway ramps, photograph every passing car. They record its plate, make, color and location, then store that information in searchable databases that police can check against lists of wanted vehicles. Flock Safety, one of the largest vendors, has cameras in thousands of U.S. communities, and their spread has prompted growing concern about privacy.

Allegheny County in southwestern Pennsylvania, home to Pittsburgh, has 827 automated license plate readers, more than any other county in the state.

Critics warn that the cameras can map people’s daily lives with little oversight, while police say they help find stolen cars and missing people. In the borough of Munhall, just outside of Pittsburgh, residents petitioned to remove two Flock cameras on Main Street.

Pennsylvania lawmakers from both parties have proposed at least nine bills, ranging from an outright ban of these devices to warrant requirements. In October the state House passed a bill that would limit their use and how long data is kept.

I study policing and public order in democracies, and I spent more than 30 years in police administration in India and with United Nations missions abroad. I’ve seen firsthand how new technologies can help police and why they need guardrails.

A spectrum of uses

How extensively police use surveillance technologies can fall anywhere across a spectrum. At one end, cameras can be positioned to monitor virtually every vehicle and person within a specified area. At the other, they are deployed sparingly and aimed only at specific vehicles or people, such as stolen cars or past offenders.

Mass surveillance may entail systemic collection of data of large numbers of people in the public space, including those not suspected of any violations. These can include networks of license plate readers that capture all vehicle traveling through an area, or cameras using facial recognition to analyze images of individuals in public spaces against existing databases.

Targeted uses include matching the vehicle numbers or faces of people of interest. These could be past offenders or people whose behavior raises suspicion, such as someone lingering near a bank late at night. Another example is designating certain places, such as airports, military bases, courthouses or power plants, as high-security areas and deploying surveillance technology there, with or without informing the public.

In the middle could be the sweet spot: calibrated use of such technology at an optimum level agreed on through laws or regulations. The level could be measured by the number of cameras in a city, the density of devices per square mile or even the terabytes of data collected.

Risks of mass surveillance

Mass surveillance carries the inherent risk of the state collecting extensive information on its entire population, or on large segments of it, which creates significant potential for misuse. The state could guarantee that the data would be handled responsibly. Even so, the data could be misused on purpose, or accessed by unauthorized persons because of vulnerabilities in data security.

There is also the fear of “surveillance creep.” That is when technologies adopted for one purpose expand into others. License plate readers, for example, are typically sold to communities as a way to find stolen cars, missing children and suspects in serious crimes. But police have also used them to monitor protests. According to records obtained by nonprofit advocacy group the Electronic Frontier Foundation, agencies across the country searched Flock’s network hundreds of times in connection with protests over a single year.

Potential benefits

The potential benefits of surveillance for crime prevention appear to be significant. A 2026 study of 216 law enforcement agencies found that after they installed fixed plate-reader networks, car thefts fell relative to other property crimes, and more theft cases were solved by arrest. In Atlantic City, New Jersey, a major expansion of plate readers didn’t reduce violent crime overall, but it was associated with fewer shootings, car thefts and property crimes.

Other law enforcement areas that could benefit from the technology include drug running and human trafficking.

In Pittsburgh, plate-reader data feeds into the police bureau’s real-time crime center. The data collected could be matched in real time with law enforcement and other databases to track the movement of offenders.

That could be used to prevent a wide range of crimes, from thefts and robberies to drug running and human trafficking, or to help solve cold cases.

A limited approach

Limited use of such technology has the benefit of curbing misuse while still using it in a controlled manner against known offenders and threats. That means using it on a person-to-person basis with prior legal or judicial approval or in high-security areas.

In this context, it would be most appropriate to take three steps to address law enforcement data collection generally:

  • Keep requiring police to get court warrants backed by probable cause for cellphone location data – records showing which cell towers a phone has connected to. That includes closing the loophole that lets agencies buy the same data from commercial brokers without a warrant.
  • Put in place federal or state laws restricting the use of facial recognition, with suitable judicial oversight.
  • Have county and municipal agencies regulate the use of surveillance cameras in public areas.

Pennsylvania’s proposals span this range and beyond. State Sen. Dan Laughlin, an Erie Republican, would ban the cameras outright. U.S. Rep. Pat Harrigan proposes legislation requiring police to get a warrant before searching plate-reader data. And the bill the state House passed in October sits in the middle, allowing the cameras but limiting their uses and how long data is kept.

Guardrails

Decisions regarding the use of mass cameras should not be left to law enforcement agencies. They are interested in crime control, which could color their judgment. Those decisions are best left to elected representatives at the federal, state and local levels, with input from legal experts and relevant law enforcement agencies.

In my view, mandatory public consultation before deploying such systems in a community would improve the legitimacy of the program and of the implementing government. Regular audits are a common safeguard when government agencies use intrusive technology. Pennsylvania’s House-passed plate-reader bill, for instance, would require agencies to adopt audit policies. Such audits could happen as often as twice a year, with information and analyses available to the community or to affected individuals on request.

Transparency of the process would go a long way toward enhancing public trust. The opposite can erode it. At Penn State, for example, the university initially declined to say how many plate-reader cameras it had installed or where, drawing criticism from students before it ended its contract with Flock.

Another precaution is to keep the data from being available in raw form to nongovernmental entities, especially corporations. Location records can be valuable to businesses. Companies already use plate-reader data for purposes such as verifying a loan applicant’s home address.

As Pennsylvania lawmakers weigh new limits, the choices they make may help determine how close any of us come to living in an Orwellian state.

item.title: Could you survive without Microsoft? Inside the costs of digital dependence
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Narmin Nahidi, Assistant Professor in Finance, University of Exeter

When I arrived at work to discover that Outlook had vanished from my computer, I wondered how I was supposed to get through my working day. No emails. No calendar. No meeting invitations.

Then another thought crossed my mind: when did we become so dependent on a single technology company that losing access to one application could disrupt our entire working routine? And what is the financial and environmental cost of that dependence?

We regularly discuss sustainability in terms of reducing plastic, cutting carbon emissions and consuming less energy. But the digital systems we rely on every day also have huge environmental consequences.

As world leaders gather at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey, perhaps it is time to ask an uncomfortable question: can our digital economy really become sustainable when so much of it depends on a handful of technology companies?

The cloud has a physical footprint

The cloud may sound weightless, but it runs on data centres, electricity, cooling systems and hardware.

The International Energy Agency estimates that data centres consumed 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, around 1.5% of global demand. It projects that consumption could reach 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, largely driven by AI and other digital services.

Microsoft’s own 2026 sustainability report illustrates the tension. The company reported a 25% year-over-year rise in total emissions in 2025, primarily because of expanding data centres and a change in renewable-energy certificate accounting. Microsoft is also investing in cleaner energy and more efficient infrastructure. Both facts matter: technological progress can reduce emissions per task, while growth pushes overall demand higher.

Asking the right questions

Turkey’s Cop31 presidency released the voluntary Antalya artificial intelligence pledge in October. This pledge aims to encourage climate-responsible AI while acknowledging the energy and water demands of the technology.

The World Resources Institute, a global research organisation, welcomed the pledge’s direction but warned that voluntary commitments need stronger accountability mechanisms. Meanwhile, the International Telecommunication Union has scheduled a Cop31 event for November 16 on financing cleaner digital infrastructure, measuring emissions, and promoting durable, repairable and reusable electronics.

The message is important: sustainability cannot stop at greener electricity. It also concerns what technology organisations purchase, how long they keep it, and who pays for its environmental effects.

When a software decision becomes a hardware bill

Consider a computer that still works but cannot support a newer operating system. Windows 10’s regular support ended in October 2025, although Microsoft offers extended security updates for eligible consumer devices through October 2027.

The transition does not make every older computer obsolete. Yet software support and compatibility can influence whether organisations replace otherwise usable equipment.

Manufacturing devices consumes energy and raw materials. It also creates electronic waste (e-waste). According to the UN’s global e-waste monitor, the world generated 62 million metric tonnes of e-waste in 2022, of which just 22.3% was documented as formally collected and recycled.

These figures cover all electronic waste, not waste attributable to Microsoft. They nevertheless show why extending equipment lifetimes deserves a place in climate policy.

Costs that are rarely counted

A software subscription has a visible price. Less visible are the costs of training employees, migrating files, replacing equipment, maintaining duplicate systems and eventually switching suppliers.

Economists call these switching costs. They can lock organisations into existing providers even when better-value alternatives emerge.

This is not merely hypothetical. In March 2026, the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority announced plans to investigate Microsoft’s business software ecosystem. It also reported steps by major cloud service providers, including Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services, to reduce data-transfer fees and improve interoperability, making it easier for businesses to switch between providers.

What might this have to do with sustainability? A buyer unable to change providers easily may also struggle to choose lower-emission computing services. That is a potential environmental consequence of lock-in, not a demonstrated claim that Microsoft users emit more carbon.

There is a wider accounting problem too. The UN estimates that global electronic waste was associated with approximately US$78 billion (£59 billion) in externalised costs in 2022, including pollution and climate-related impacts. Such costs are largely absent from the price of a software license.

A responsible procurement decision should therefore compare lifetime financial costs, equipment lifespans and credible emissions data rather than only the next annual bill.

Freedom to choose

Could workplaces use alternatives (such as Thunderbird and LibreOffice) or interoperable cloud services? Often, yes. But migration has costs and a rival provider is not necessarily greener.

The better goal is freedom to choose: portable data, open document formats, repairable devices, transparent environmental reporting and software contracts that do not penalise switching.

Digital systems that remain affordable, competitive and environmentally responsible, even when their preferred technology changes, will be the most resilient ones.

item.title: Microsoft has suffered a global outage. A tech expert explains what went wrong
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Mahmoud Elkhodr, Senior Lecturer in Information and Communication Technologies, CQUniversity Australia

Microsoft has suffered a major global outage, bringing many of its widely used tools, including email and cloud storage, to a standstill.

According to outage tracking site DownDetector, some 130,000 people reported issues accessing Microsoft Outlook as of early Thursday afternoon US Eastern time (early Friday morning in Sydney). In a statement on X, the tech giant said it was “aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact” and “restarting affected servers to return them to service”.

In an article for The Conversation last month, I explained how the whole internet is unlikely to go down but several services can become unavailable together when they rely on shared systems.

This outage shows precisely what happens when that shared infrastructure fails – and why we must prepare for digital outages in a similar way we do for natural disasters.

Beyond missed emails or workplace meetings

The list of services Microsoft says are “potentially impacted” by the outage is long. It includes services used for email, document sharing, meetings and managing tasks, such as Outlook, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Planner and Microsoft Exchange Online. It also includes Microsoft Defender, a cloud-based cybersecurity service.

With so many digital services affected, the real-world impacts of the outage have been widespread, and go far beyond missed emails or workplace meetings.

For example, family violence workers reportedly can’t access databases which contain client details. Schools can’t provide online lessons for remote students. Psychologists can’t provide telehealth consultations. Businesses are unable to process orders. Job hunters are unable to make it to planned interviews. Some government service centres have been forced to closed.

The disruption also reached services outside Microsoft. OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems with the tools that connect their artificial intelligence (AI) services to Microsoft 365.

This shows how a problem in one part of the digital world can affect tools that appear separate, and even services provided by other companies.

The outage comes after other disruptions to Microsoft services earlier this year. For example, in January, Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services were down for hours. Then in August, Microsoft Outlook and Exchange Online were disrupted by a code update which took several days to fix.

A shifting account of what went wrong

As of early Friday afternoon Sydney time, Microsoft has not yet named a root cause of the outage, and its account of the failure has shifted since it was first reported.

Initially the company said elevated load across multiple regions was reported first. It then clarified the load was not driven by an increase in traffic, but a large number of servers becoming unexpectedly unavailable.

Attention then moved to the automated “health checks” Microsoft uses to judge whether a server is fit to carry traffic, and to the component that processes them.

The company described a core process on the affected servers as becoming “overwhelmed”. Software deployments and configuration changes were paused while recent changes were reviewed, although none was found to correlate with the start of the disruption.

The evidence does not suggest a cyberattack.

A distributed denial-of-service attack works by flooding a service with requests from outside until legitimate ones can no longer be answered. Microsoft’s own statement that overall traffic had not increased is difficult to reconcile with that pattern. No evidence of malicious activity has been disclosed, and no group has claimed responsibility.

Indeed, Microsoft said: “There’s no indication this is a cyber attack.”

The more mundane explanation fits better. Health checks exist to protect a service by withdrawing servers that appear unwell. When the machinery making that judgement is itself at fault, healthy capacity can be removed, and the servers that remain are left to absorb work they were never sized for.

Outages of this scale are more often self-inflicted in this way than they are the work of attackers, as the August disruption to Microsoft email by a code update illustrates.

Until a post-incident review is published, however, that remains an inference drawn from Microsoft’s own updates rather than a settled account.

Microsoft has not yet been able to fix the outage entirely. It says that some of the affected servers are working again, but they “can become unresponsive again once they begin receiving traffic”.

Planning for outages like we do for bushfires

This outage reinforces the need for all of us to better prepare for digital outages. For individuals, this can involve storing essential information, such as contacts and medical prescriptions, offline in case of an outage.

Organisations that rely on one digital provider such as Microsoft or Google for tasks must also prepare back up plans. Crucially, they must also test these back plans to make sure they work in practice and don’t simply exist on paper – similar to how they conduct fire drills and how communities practice bushfire evacuations.

As more aspects of our lives become connected – from cars and homes to workplaces, transport and healthcare – and AI becomes more widely used, the consequences of digital disruption may grow.

Building resilience must be part of how we plan for that future.

item.title: From ancient Asia to the AI age: Has China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ found a new victim in Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Linggong Kong, Ph.D. Candidate in Political Science, Auburn University

Extramarital activities have led to the resignation of one of America’s most influential tech bosses, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The saga has also raised the specter of an age-old spying tactic: the “honey trap.”

Huang stepped down following media reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence agencies. She previously worked for Megaspeed, a cloud computing company under U.S. scrutiny for allegedly helping China obtain restricted AI chips.

Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair. And amid reports of a second with a company executive who reports to him, he tendered his resignation to the Nvidia board on Nov. 12, 2026.

The sensitivity of Huang’s work – AI is increasingly seen as central to national security – has turned a company matter into an international issue. China’s Foreign Ministry has denied the espionage allegations and accused the U.S. of “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade.” Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets have been leaked.

Yet part of what makes the accusations so believable is history is dotted with examples of men being distracted, compromised or spied on by attractive men and women deployed for that purpose.

Indeed, in China it recalls an ancient political tactic known as “meiren ji” or the “beauty stratagem.”

As a scholar specializing in U.S.-China relations, I believe that regardless of the particulars of the Huang case, the political logic behind the beauty stratagem – using personal relationships to obtain information, influence decisions and weaken opponents – remains relevant today. As such, it would be no surprise if the tactic was being used amid the growing U.S.-China competition over AI and advanced semiconductors.

The beauty stratagem of Ancient China

“Meiren ji” is one of “Thirty-Six Stratagems,” a Chinese military text of uncertain origin but generally believed to have derived from oral and written histories from the Warring States period — 475–221 BCE. Its 31st stratagem states that personal relationships can be used to influence political opponents and recommends exploiting an adversary’s personal desires and emotional vulnerabilities to weaken their judgment and undermine their leadership.

The “Thirty-Six Stratagems” is both a playbook for warfare and a reflection on past experience.

Indeed, one of China’s most famous beauty stratagem stories dates back more than 2,000 years to the Spring and Autumn period of Chinese history.

In the fifth century BCE, King Goujian of Yue, in modern-day southern China, was defeated by King Fuchai of Wu, its northern neighbor, and forced to submit. But Goujian secretly rebuilt his strength and prepared for revenge.

According to the ancient historical text “Wu Yue Chun Qiu,” Yue sent two beautiful women – Xi Shi and Zheng Dan – to Fuchai, hoping he would become distracted by pleasure and neglect state affairs.

The plan reportedly worked. Fuchai, seemingly enchanted by the beautiful women, gradually ignored Yue’s threat. Meanwhile, Goujian prepared for war and in 473 BCE Yue conquered Wu.

Xi Shi’s actual role in Wu’s downfall remains unclear. Wu’s defeat involved poor political decisions and Yue’s military recovery.

Still, the story illustrated an important idea in Chinese political strategy: exploiting an opponent’s personal weaknesses can sometimes be more effective than confronting him directly.

A similar tactic appears in the 14th-century novel “Romance of the Three Kingdoms,” considered one of the classics of Chinese literature.

It tells the story of Dong Zhuo, a powerful warlord who controlled the imperial court during the late Eastern Han Dynasty. To remove him, Wang Yun, a senior court official loyal to the Han Dynasty promised a beautiful young woman, named Diaochan, in marriage to Dong Zhuo’s military commander. He then offered the same woman to Dong Zhuo.

The scheme fueled jealousy and distrust between the two men, eventually enabling Wang Yun to persuade Dong Zhuo’s underling to kill him. Wang Yun then briefly took charge of the imperial court on behalf of the Han emperor.

The ‘honey trap’ of modern spyware

In modern intelligence operations, using romantic or sexual relationships to approach targets, obtain sensitive information or exert influence is commonly called a “honey trap.” It is, moreover, certainly not unique to China. Western and Soviet intelligence agencies used intimate relationships for espionage frequently during the Cold War.

Modern China also has documented cases. One example involves French diplomat Bernard Boursicot and the Chinese opera performer Shi Pei Pu. The pair met in Beijing in 1964 and maintained a long-term intimate relationship. Throughout, Boursicot was providing French diplomatic documents to China. The spying was eventually exposed and both involved were prosecuted for espionage in France in the 1980s.

A more recent example involves former U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell and Christine Fang, a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Swalwell acknowledged in 2015 that he had been physically intimate with Fang on several occasions. At the time, Fang helped raise funds for Swalwell’s campaign and helped place an intern in his congressional office.

Why Jensen Huang is strategically important

Jensen Huang’s position would make him a prime target for such a “honey trap” operation. His company has become central to the technological competition between the U.S and China. As AI becomes increasingly important to economic development, military capabilities and national security, moreover, Washington has repeatedly tightened restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China, hoping to slow its access to computing power.

Beijing is investing heavily in domestic semiconductor development. Yet Chinese companies still need advanced chips to train AI models and build data centers.

From Beijing’s perspective, advanced AI chips matter not only for Chinese technology companies but for future military and technological competition.

This puts Nvidia in a particularly important position and helps explain the national security concerns surrounding Huang.

However, strategic motives do not prove an intelligence operation occurred. Jensen Huang’s importance does not, in itself, establish that he was targeted by a honey trap or that Alice Huang acted for Chinese intelligence. Those are allegations that still require full investigation.

Espionage in the age of AI

Yet it is surely true that in modern politics – just as in ancient China’s rivalries – rivals seek information about opponents, try to influence important decisions and exploit weaknesses to gain strategic advantages.

What has changed is who controls important strategic resources.

In ancient China, influencing a ruler through personal relationships could affect a country’s political and military decisions. Today, approaching a major technology executive could offer access to sensitive technologies.

More than 2,000 years ago, a powerful state could lose its advantage through a ruler’s personal weaknesses. Today, political and technological power are distributed differently.

But as long as important decisions depend on individuals, personal relationships may remain a weakness that rivals can exploit.

item.title: ‘Nobody cared’: new research shows deepfakes are hurting regular people, not just celebrities
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Authors:

  • Nicola Henry, Professor of Global & Language Studies, RMIT University
  • Gemma Stevens, Research Assistant, School of Global, Urban and Social Studies, RMIT University

In 2017, a Reddit user, who went by the name “deepfakes”, shared non-consensual AI-generated videos of celebrities he’d created by “stitching” their faces onto the bodies of pornographic actors.

Nearly ten years later, AI tools can generate highly realistic sexualised “deepfake” images in seconds, sometimes using just a single photograph. Often, high-profile people are targeted.

Our recently published research – involving more than 7,000 people from Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States – reveals AI-generated image-based abuse is becoming increasingly widespread. It now affects ordinary people as well as public figures.

How are deepfakes made?

AI-generated image-based sexual abuse refers to the non-consensual creation, distribution, or threatened distribution of synthetic intimate images depicting real people. This is also known as “non-consensual sexual deepfakes”.

With little technical skill required, almost anyone can create these images and almost anyone can become a target.

These tools include “nudify” apps that digitally remove clothing from photographs, as well as AI generators that create new images or manipulate existing images from text prompts or reference images.

Read more: Australia set to ban ‘nudify’ apps. How will it work?

These tools are accessible, easy to find and sometimes free, expanding the pool of potential victims and perpetrators, including young people.

According to the Australian eSafety Commissioner, the number of reports from children involving digitally altered intimate images, including deepfakes, have more than doubled in the 18 months to June 2025 compared with the total number of reports received in the preceding seven years combined.

Four in five of those reports involve girls.

What our research found

Our team surveyed 7,230 adults in Australia, the UK and the US in July 2024. We found 7% reported being victims of non-consensual sexual deepfakes, with higher rates among:

  • people under 35
  • LGBTQIA+ people
  • Black, Indigenous, and other people of colour
  • people with disabilities
  • men.

The true prevalence is likely to be higher as many victim-survivors may never discover that images of them have been created or shared, while perpetrators may be reluctant to disclose their behaviour, even in an anonymous survey.

We also found 3.2% admitted to having created, shared or threatened to share AI-generated intimate images of someone else without their consent.

Perpetrators described a range of motivations, not all of which involved revenge or an explicit intention to cause harm. Some “thought it was funny”, while others wanted to “experiment with technology” or “show off” to friends and online peers.

These findings suggest deepfakes can occur within peer cultures where sexualised content is used for humour, social bonding or mockery, as well as humiliation and harassment.

What are the impacts?

Most victim-survivors in our study reported anger, humiliation, shame, embarrassment, fear, helplessness and distress.

While men were more likely to report victimisation, women were more likely to report a broader range of harms and negative emotional and social impacts. Men were more likely to find the experience funny, although these were a minority.

The harms do not necessarily depend on how realistic the images appear to be. Victim-survivors can experience significant distress from losing control over how they are sexually represented. They can also experience fear others will believe the images are authentic, and the possibility of further humiliation or abuse.

In our study, one participant said they felt fearful the perpetrator would “continue uploading” images and the abuse might escalate to in-person violence. Others worried sexualised material associated with their names could be discovered by prospective employers or others.

Once images circulate, victims can face an exhausting “whack-a-mole” cycle of locating and reporting images, only for copies to reappear elsewhere.

Some victim-survivors also described being disbelieved or having their experiences minimised, including by authorities, friends and family members because the images were considered to be “not real”.

As one young woman in the UK put it: “nobody cared, believed me or listened”.

A young non-binary person, also in the UK, said:

There was kind of a level of scepticism from the people I told; because it wasn’t a ‘real image’ they couldn’t really see why I was so upset and thought it was less compromising because it wasn’t actually me in the picture.

Prevention and accountability

Perpetrators must be held accountable. Prevention, however, cannot be left to individuals alone.

Technology companies must make their products and services safer and more resistant to misuse. This means building safeguards into AI tools to prevent abusive images being generated, making harmful content harder to find or circulate, and ensuring accessible reporting and rapid removal processes.

The burden should not fall on victims to continually search for and report the material.

Australia’s proposed digital duty of care, introduced into parliament last month, is an important step forwards.

This would require online services, including AI image-generation services, to take reasonable steps to keep users safe. It would also give the eSafety commissioner new powers to target nudify apps and websites.

Going further, Australia could consider following the UK in criminalising the development and supply of nudify tools.

There should also be criminal offences for non-consensual sharing and creation of AI-generated intimate images in all states and territories.

We also need consent-based and respectful relationships education which challenges the idea that creating sexualised images of others is harmless fun, and which works to address the gendered norms that normalise this behaviour.

Educational interventions need to also focus on fostering social connection and building healthy relationships.

You can also contact Lifeline crisis support on 13 11 14 or text 0477 13 11 14, Suicide Call Back Services on 1300 659 467, or Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800 (for young people aged 5-25). If you or someone you know is in immediate danger, call the police on 000.

item.title: COP31: How AI can help us adapt to climate change
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Robin Cox, Professor & Director ResilienceByDesign Research Innovation Lab, Royal Roads University

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has described COP31, being hosted in his country, as the “implementation COP,” emphasizing the need to translate climate commitments into action.

The urgency is mounting. In September, the latest United Nations Environment Programme report concluded that limiting global warming to 1.5 C, or even slightly exceeding that threshold, is no longer achievable.

Although returning below 1.5 C later this century remains possible, it would require rapid, substantial emissions reductions. Meanwhile, continued warming increases the risks of severe and irreversible climate impacts, making effective action critical.

Given this urgency, artificial intelligence (AI) is attracting attention for its potential to deepen our understanding of climate risks and inform our responses. This growing interest is reflected in COP31’s Antalya AI Pledge.

But realizing this potential raises an important question: Do the professionals working on climate adaptation have the knowledge, skills and support to use these technologies effectively and responsibly?

AI and climate monitoring

A 2023 national survey of Canadian professionals found that many do not feel adequately equipped to apply adaptation tools or make the case for adaptation measures.

This points to a gap between understanding climate risks and having the capabilities to address them. Canada’s National Adaptation Strategy sets a target for 70 per cent of relevant professionals to have these capabilities by 2027.

Canada uses AI to improve weather forecasting, and Canadian researchers use it to assess flood risks. Emerging applications include infrastructure and adaptation planning, such as flood-risk modelling in Vancouver. Yet better information does not necessarily lead to better decisions.

As AI enters climate risk assessment and adaptation planning, it adds to the challenges professionals already face as they grapple with difficult decisions about infrastructure, public safety, ecosystems and community resilience.

Read more: Adaptation policies must be built around the local communities facing climate change

AI skills for a climate workforce

The challenge goes beyond learning to use AI. Front-line climate action professionals need to understand how AI-generated information is produced, assess its reliability and limitations, and decide when and how to use it alongside other evidence and knowledge.

Consider a coastal community facing rising flood risk. AI-supported modelling might identify vulnerable roads, homes and public facilities. But deciding whether to reinforce a shoreline, restore wetlands, restrict development or consider relocation involves more than comparing projected risks.

These choices affect livelihoods, ecosystems and relationships to place. They also involve competing priorities and values, Indigenous rights and jurisdiction and questions about whose knowledge informs decisions and who has the authority to act.

Many of the competencies required to navigate these challenges are already recognized in climate adaptation practice. At the ResilienceByDesign Lab at Royal Roads University, we’ve developed a Climate Action Competency Framework that identifies systems thinking, critical assessment of information, collaboration, communication and ethical leadership as essential to effective climate action.

These capabilities remain relevant as AI enters adaptation practice, but they are insufficient on their own. Professionals also need to understand how AI systems work, recognize potential biases and gaps in the data they use, assess the reliability of AI-generated recommendations and navigate questions of transparency and accountability.

This does not mean every planner, engineer, emergency manager or public health professional needs to become an AI specialist. Instead, they need enough AI literacy to ask informed questions, recognize when additional expertise is required and exercise professional judgment rather than simply accepting what the AI produces.

From competence to professional practice

Identifying these capabilities is only part of the challenge. They must also be reflected in professional standards, education, ongoing training and the organizational conditions that shape adaptation decisions.

The Professions Advancing Adaptation Competencies initiative offers a Canadian example. By examining how the Climate Action Competency Framework aligns with the standards and practices of engineering, planning, accounting and landscape architecture, the initiative identified shared competencies and profession-specific needs.

Similar work could examine how AI is reshaping adaptation practice across professions, what existing competencies remain relevant and where additional capabilities are needed. This would strengthen workforce readiness by identifying the competencies professionals need to use emerging technologies effectively, rather than assuming that access to AI alone will automatically improve climate action.

If COP31 is to deliver on its promise to move from commitments to implementation, preparing the workforce responsible for adaptation must be a priority. Governments, professional associations and educators must ensure professionals have the competencies, resources and institutional support to use these technologies responsibly and translate climate knowledge into action.

AI can improve our understanding of climate risks, but turning that knowledge into effective, equitable action will still depend on people and the decisions they are equipped to make.

Robin Cox has previously received research funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada and Natural Resources Canada.

item.title: AI marking means uni assessments could theoretically never be read by a human. What now?
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Margaret Bearman, Professor (Assessment and Digital Learning), Deakin University

There’s a doomsday scenario where uni students hand in work generated by artificial intelligence (AI), which is then marked by AI and university assessment no longer involves any humans at all.

There’s also an alternative utopia where teachers use AI to escape the burden and time pressures of endless piles of marking. In this bright new “AI-powered” world, bias against student differences is avoided and staff use the extra free time to engage in high-quality teaching and research.

So what’s happening with AI marking in Australian universities?

AI marking isn’t new

Most people don’t realise AI marking has been commercially developed since at least 1998. The educational publisher Pearson reports its specialised trained systems have scored 39 million responses, including essays, short answers and equations.

In previous decades, the tech was an expensive specialist product that may not have been easy for unis to access. But this has changed as AI has become more readily available.

How does AI marking work?

AI models, such as ChatGPT, predict what mark should be awarded by comparing the textual patterns of a student’s work to other long-standing texts. If the AI has been trained on a lot of texts similar to the assessment task, its predictions are more likely to be closer to a human’s response.

With an openly available AI, such as ChatGPT or Claude, a teacher could upload an essay and a rubric and ask AI to grade and provide feedback on the essay.

This article is part of a series on how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education.

We take a deeper look into how AI has disrupted degrees, how universities are responding to these new challenges and what the technology means for the sector’s future. You can find more stories here.

How are unis approaching it?

Universities are generally not advertising their approaches to AI marking. But policies are guided by strong privacy regulations. Some universities state how this intersects with AI.

For example, Deakin University prohibits teachers from uploading university data and information into openly available AIs. This includes students’ assignments, as doing so might expose their private data to off-shore data storage, which is beyond Australia’s privacy regulations.

In addition, universities typically emphasise humans must take responsibility for their judgements when marking assessments assisted by a university-approved AI. For example, the University of Melbourne lets teachers use approved AIs “to support their evaluation of students’ work”, but prohibits them from relying on AI alone to determine marks or grades.

Assessment almost always involves text or video feedback, alongside a mark or grade. Universities typically appear more accepting of using AI to help provide students with feedback comments, although human oversight, again, is required.

Is AI reliable for marking?

Research suggests the answer is no, at least not at the moment.

A University of Melbourne and Cardiff University study, published in August, looked at whether later versions of AI software ChatGPT could effectively imitate human markers’ scores when marking 50 undergraduate bioscience essays.

Researchers found there was some alignment in the overall essay marks, but concluded ChatGPT could not be relied upon to assign and explain marks. It was particularly poor with respect to individual marking criterion, such as the appropriateness of essay content and sufficient supporting evidence. Researchers also found ChatGPT, on average, tended to grade students’ essays higher than humans did. This reflects how AI works – it doesn’t evaluate, it predicts.

Relationships are impacted

Another obvious risk is that AI marking can negatively impact student-teacher relationships.

My research, investigating student and teachers’ perspectives on feedback and AI, suggests AI may create distance between students and teachers. For instance, students can now turn to AI for feedback first, when they might otherwise have approached a tutor.

Other research describes how students benefit from the personal recognition that comes with comments provided by a human teacher. Feedback shows the student their learning matters.

Defaulting to AI marking could also mean teachers miss out on important opportunities to improve their classes. For example, if 40 student essays all show the same misunderstanding of a concept, the teacher marking the assignments ideally will realise there’s a problem with how they’re teaching the subject.

Grading is overlooked

In response to AI, a huge amount of effort is now being spent on assessment reform in Australian universities. However, research shows many universities are reworking assessments with little attention given to marking or the final grades that result from this marking.

But there is an opportunity to explore other grading options at the same time. Research offers longstanding critiques of numerical grading, which most universities use. These critiques highlight how they can undermine independent thinking due to focusing on “meeting the mark”. Grades also encourage unnecessary competition among students.

What next?

Removing numerical marks and grades could be one way forward – although this does not provide all the answers.

The University of New South Wales has piloted the removal of numerical marks in some subjects. Instead, teachers evaluate students on whether they are competent against defined outcomes. The university says this shifts focus towards student learning.

While these changes weren’t made in response to AI, the approach still offers clues as to how marks and grades might change in the world of AI. It shows the future is not necessarily a question of technology versus no technology.

Rather, universities can focus on systems of assessment that bring students and teachers closer together. Students want meaningful feedback, not technical tick box exercises. By worrying about the ways AI could replicate human marking, we may miss what matters in assessment.

Margaret Bearman is a member of the Australia and New Zealand Association of Health Professional Education, Australasian Society for Computers in Learning in Tertiary Education and the European Association of Learning and Instruction.

item.title: Why the doomsday prediction of 1960 matters today
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Mark Woolhouse, Professor of Infectious Disease Epidemiology, University of Edinburgh

According to the late Heinz von Foerster, Friday, November 13 2026, is doomsday. Professor von Foerster and two colleagues at the University of Illinois published that prediction in 1960 in the respected journal Science. The paper has been widely discussed ever since.

Theirs was an unconventional vision of doomsday, brought about by the world’s population growing ever faster. Eventually, there would be an infinite number of people – literally, according to the paper. As von Foerster put it, his descendants would be “squeezed to death”.

Von Foerster deliberately engineered his analysis to make this outcome inevitable. He devised a mathematical equation that was predetermined to give the desired result and fitted it to human population data over the past two millennia to come up with a precise date. November 13 2026, would have been his 115th birthday.

The paper was von Foerster’s way of making the point that the rate of human population growth in 1960 was unsustainable. That conclusion was not new – it dates back to Thomas Malthus’s 18th-century Essay on the Principle of Population. The problem was von Foerster’s proposed solution: birth control on a massive scale.

What happened next

Others reached similar conclusions. In 1968, Paul Ehrlich, an American biologist and environmentalist, wrote his bestselling book The Population Bomb. He predicted mass famine. Four years later came The Limits to Growth, a report based on a computer model predicting systemic collapse by the 2020s as the growing population exhausted the planet’s resources.

These predictions turned out to be wildly wrong, but not before egregious harm was done in the name of saving the planet. During the 1970s, international agencies aggressively promoted birth control, even making it a condition of receiving food aid. Forced sterilisation programmes were introduced in south Asia. China’s one-child policy persisted until 2015.

All of these programmes were abandoned, yet the number of people aged under 15 in the world still peaked in 2021. Many countries are now concerned about their ageing populations.

Japan, Hungary, Turkey and even China are encouraging couples to have more children. This is as far as it could be from the future that von Foerster and like-minded population pessimists were imagining in the 1960s.

Five lessons

Some regard the doomsday paper as a historical curiosity to be regarded with indulgence. I disagree. I see it as a cautionary tale that undermines confidence in scientific predictions of all kinds. It should be cause to reflect on the merits of today’s prophecies of disaster.

Last month, a high-profile report identified 17 “major catastrophic threats”, two with “extinction potential” (nuclear war and malicious use of AI), and forecast their impacts to the year 2100.

If this type of exercise is really more credible than the population growth predictions, then the difference needs to be made plain. A good place to start is to take on board five lessons from von Foerster’s paper.

First, there is an uneasy relationship between science and advocacy. Science is about informing the debate; advocacy is about winning it. A favoured tool of the advocate is the worst-case scenario, and doomsday is the ultimate worst-case scenario. It is a rhetorical device rather than a serious scientific argument.

Second, exaggerating for effect is poor science and ultimately counterproductive. As studies of public attitudes to science have shown, people lose trust in scientists when they suspect them of overreaching.

Third, the doomsday equation illustrates a general principle: the way a model is constructed predetermines the possible outcomes. Von Foerster used this to his advantage and manufactured an eye-catching result. The same is true of many other predictions, though not usually so blatantly. No model of a complex system is exempt.

Fourth, claims to be “following the science” can discourage legitimate debate and direct attention away from the subjective choices scientists make when constructing their models. Those dire predictions of accelerating population growth were seen as incontrovertible at the time, and sceptics were accused of wilfully denying the disaster that would inevitably follow. That was pure hubris.

Fifth, ignoring inconvenient evidence will backfire, eventually. Von Foerster and the others failed to take into account that people living in richer, healthier and better-educated societies would have fewer children, to the extent that the decreasing birth rate outweighed the decreasing death rate.

This “demographic transition” was already under way by 1960 and it fatally undermined the population pessimists’ argument. Development was the answer to the population explosion.

A need for reflection

The latest doomsday will pass uneventfully, but there’s always another waiting round the corner – it’s a recurring theme of human history. Scientists may have taken the mantle from prophets and mystics, but are they really any better?

The “scientific” predictions of population growth of the 1960s and 70s proved no more reliable than the doom-mongering of Nostradamus. There are too many parallels between that episode and today’s predictions for any complacency.

Many of today’s scientists are genuinely and deeply worried about global threats (my own top concern is another pandemic). There is a wealth of scientific evidence and opinion underpinning those fears. Even so, it would be irresponsible to ignore the lessons of recent history and risk making the same mistakes again.

Friday, November 13 2026, is an opportunity for scientists to reflect that, when it comes to prediction, a little humility goes a long way. Anyone who interrogates predictions of catastrophe is doing due diligence, and good scientists should welcome it.

item.title: The supermarket fridge hack exposes the cracks in tech vision of an ‘internet of things’
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Authors:

  • Vincent Charles, Professor of AI for Business and Management Science, Queen's University Belfast
  • Tatiana Gherman, Associate Professor of AI for Business and Strategy, University of Northampton

Imagine opening a supermarket in the morning to find the freezer aisle dripping, the floor wet, and thousands of euros’ worth of food ruined.

That is what happened in France overnight on 11-12 October 2026, when hackers remotely manipulated refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets. Temperatures reportedly reached 50°C, spoiling food worth millions of euros.

The attacks spread. In early November, similar incidents affected supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden. Food suppliers in the UK were also targeted. A London wholesaler narrowly avoided losing its stock by disconnecting affected equipment from the internet.

On Monday November 9, French officials accused Iran of being behind the attacks in France. Others, including cybersecurity experts, have previously suspected Russian involvement – something Moscow has denied.

Whoever is responsible, these incidents reveal an uncomfortable reality: cyberattacks are no longer confined to stolen passwords, compromised bank accounts or leaked information. They can disrupt the physical systems on which everyday life depends.

A term, the “internet of things”, is sometimes used for the increasing trend for physical objects to be embedded with sensors and communicating with other devices or systems over the internet.

But as more devices become connected to the internet, the question is not simply how hackers managed to heat supermarket freezers, but who is responsible for keeping these devices – and others like them – secure.

Modern supermarket refrigeration systems often use control panels that allow engineers to monitor temperatures, receive alerts, and adjust settings remotely.

The control panels operate electronic devices called controllers that manage the refrigeration systems and can be accessed remotely via the internet. This is useful: a failing freezer in the middle of the night can cause substantial losses and remote monitoring can help prevent it.

But the same connectivity that makes these systems convenient can also create opportunities for attackers.

From freezers to ovens

Attackers reportedly extended defrost cycles from around one hour to eight hours, delaying alarms while temperatures rose. The concern is that equipment can remain mechanically functional long after its cybersecurity protections become inadequate.

And the implications extend beyond supermarkets. Hospitals, pharmacies, and warehouses depend on refrigeration, while connected systems also manage heating, ventilation and other building functions.

Perhaps the most revealing aspect of these attacks is their potential scale. Hackers need not target supermarkets individually. They can search the internet for particular controllers for appliances, such as fridges and freezers, and attempt to exploit the same weaknesses across businesses and countries.

Since the attacks, there has been evidence that refrigeration controllers have been disappearing from the internet, consistent either with the companies taking action to protect them, or owners disconnecting the appliances. Yet more than 3,100 remained visible online on November 5 2026. Exposure does not necessarily mean vulnerability, but it illustrates the scale of the shared risk.

A refrigeration controller may accept a change to its defrost settings even when the resulting temperatures could destroy food. Businesses therefore need more than protection against unauthorised access. Critical operating limits should be protected against dangerous remote changes, with independent safeguards and local controls – allowing supermarket employees to adjust refrigeration equipment – if digital systems are compromised.

Secure connectivity is another part of the solution. In January 2026, the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre published guidance on how industrial systems connect to external networks and how those connections should be controlled.

But securing these systems also raises a question of responsibility. A supermarket may buy equipment from one company, use another for maintenance and depend on a third for software support. When vulnerabilities emerge, responsibility can become fragmented. This can leave critical security gaps unaddressed.

International cybersecurity agencies are urging organisations to consider security when purchasing industrial equipment, including manufacturers’ commitments to security updates and support throughout a product’s lifespan. This approach is known as “secure by demand”.

But what happens when an attack succeeds despite these precautions? A supermarket may suffer the immediate losses, even when the weakness lies in equipment or software supplied by someone else. Insurance may cover some of the damage, but who ultimately bears the cost depends on contracts, liability and the terms of the insurance policy. Financial risk may be transferred between organisations, but responsibility for preventing and managing cyberattacks is not necessarily transferred with it.

What about the rest of us?

The same risks increasingly extend into our homes. Smart thermostats, security cameras, doorbells and connected appliances create ongoing dependencies on their manufacturers.

Unlike traditional appliances, connected devices may rely on software updates and cloud services long after purchase. A device can become insecure before it becomes unusable. And if its manufacturer withdraws support or shuts down a cloud service, some functions may stop working altogether.

Before buying connected technology, we should ask: how long will security updates be provided? Will essential functions work without internet access? What happens when support ends?

But consumers cannot reasonably assess every vulnerability or control manufacturers’ decisions. Responsibility for security cannot rest with them alone.

We routinely ask what connected technology can do for us. Perhaps we should also ask who bears the risks when things go wrong, and who remains responsible for keeping it secure as it gets older.
