item.title: Australia will impose mandatory safety rules on AI. Are we focused on the right risks?
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Henry Fraser, Law Lecturer, Queensland University of Technology

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has just announced six mandatory artificial intelligence (AI) safety guardrails.

The government will establish a new AI safety regulator to enforce the regulations, with the power to impose significant penalties.

According to the guardrails, frontier AI companies – the ones with the most powerful AI models at the cutting edge of AI development – will have to:

  1. implement security controls
  2. identify and manage serious risks
  3. allow independent evaluation of their models
  4. rapidly notify government of serious incidents
  5. publish safety and security frameworks to enhance governance and transparency
  6. respond to updated standards and rules as technologies change.

The implementation of the guardrails is one of 18 recommendations from a rapid review the government launched in September after an AI agent, deployed by OpenAI to collect data, accessed non-public Medicare stats.

In the background, the government is pursuing an extensive agenda of technology law and policy reform. There’s a new prohibition on unfair trading practices focused on online markets, a digital duty of care bill to address harms from online platforms and AI chatbots, a significant draft privacy law reform bill, and an inquiry into Australia’s sovereign AI capability.

The prime minister’s announcement focuses on “AI safety”, “AI security” and “frontier” AI models and companies. But Australians may remain unprotected from known AI harms that – though less spectacular – are already widespread and serious.

A diversified approach to AI policy and regulation

As well as the mandatory guardrails, the rapid review recommendations included criminal law reform, international cooperation, and strengthening mechanisms for government engagement with frontier AI developers.

Nearly half of the recommendations are about increasing Australia’s preparedness for AI-related cyber incidents.

The recommendations make sense. The review is right to emphasise the role of building capacity, relationships, and cooperation. Effective and responsive AI regulation must go beyond the government simply issuing and enforcing rigid rules.

Despite these strengths, the government seems to be taking a narrow view of what “AI safety” means.

What counts as AI safety?

The announcement seems to indicate that the most important risks come from frontier AI models.

But risks from AI – including serious risks to safety, public health and national security – are not confined to the frontier.

AI and algorithmic systems are increasingly integrated into important services such as healthcare, insurance, housing, finance, employment, education and social security.

For the most part, these kinds of AI systems are not likely to be frontier AI. Instead, these would be smaller, more specialised tools, such as an AI recruitment bot, an AI personal budgeting app or an educational grading algorithm.

Unaccountable, unfair, poorly managed deployments of such everyday AI systems have the potential to cause enormous harm.

We’ve seen Robodebt harm hundreds of thousands of Australians. Sexist AI-enabled job recruitment tools, AI-enabled stadium security systems that let a gun into the Melbourne Cricket Ground, racist policing algorithms, and AI meal-planners that recommend poisonous recipes are just a few among thousands of examples of everyday AI harms and risks.

As the Medicare incident showed, risks also emerge from interactions between software systems, organisations and real world contexts. It doesn’t make sense to just focus on powerful AI models out of context.

Worse, AI systems are notoriously opaque. While changes to privacy law will soon require businesses and government to state in their privacy policies if they use automated decision-making, Australians don’t have a right to an actual explanation of AI decisions in most domains.

A lack of transparency about how (non-frontier) AI systems are developed and deployed is a serious impediment to accountability.

A lighter touch

The Australian government recognised all of this in an earlier 2024 proposal for mandatory AI guardrails. However, these have largely been abandoned in favour of a lighter regulatory touch.

The 2024 proposal contemplated ten guardrails that would apply to non-frontier AI systems deployed in high-risk settings, as well as frontier systems.

These would have included requirements for transparency, accountability, testing, data governance, record keeping, risk management, human oversight of systems, and pathways for contesting AI decisions.

Most of those guardrails are missing from the new list. Now, only safety frameworks need to be transparent, for instance.

Independent oversight seems limited to evaluating AI models themselves, rather than evaluating whether the development and deployment of AI systems in various contexts is safe, fair, responsible or accountable.

There are also no general record-keeping or transparency guardrails that would create the paper trails we need for real oversight and accountability.

Some promising changes

One area that looks promising is the requirement to respond to new standards and rules. Depending on how the guardrails are implemented, standards such as Australia’s nuanced and sophisticated Voluntary AI Safety Standard could provide more detailed guidance to promote fairness, transparency and accountability.

If compliance with certain standards were mandated, then guardrails could have a deeper and wider reach.

Similarly, a proposal to introduce criminal liability for negligent AI developers could incentivise better record-keeping and more proactive risk management.

But until the government fleshes out this bullet point list of guardrails and rapid review recommendations, it will be hard to know how broad the scope of AI safety regulation will be.

For now, one thing is clear. Introducing regulation for sci-fi frontier risks such as “rogue” AI agents attacking our government or infrastructure is good politics, and sound policy. But it’s not enough to keep Australians safe from serious AI harms.

item.title: AI has turned university assessments into a ‘wicked problem’ – and we don’t have all the answers
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Thomas Corbin, Research Fellow, Centre for Research in Assessment and Digital Learning, Deakin University

Since the introduction of ChatGPT in late 2022, there have been rising concerns about university assessments. Are we testing students’ learning? Or simply their ability to use generative AI?

Universities and teachers have been working hard to reform assessments to ensure degrees still genuinely demonstrate students’ knowledge and skills. But it’s an ongoing challenge for the sector.

How are universities responding, and are we making progress?

AI doesn’t always equal cheating

In July, the US software company Turnitin published a report showing nearly 54% of Australian uni students’ submissions, processed through its system from October 2025 to April 2026, showed some form of AI use. About 10% of these submissions contained more than 80% material generated by AI.

But the presence of AI in assessments doesn’t automatically mean all students who use it are cheating.

Students may use AI selectively in their work. For example, by asking it to help develop an idea, edit a sentence, improve a draft, or provide feedback on an argument.

Many students also use AI to support their assessments well before they start writing. As part of research I conducted with colleagues in 2024, we interviewed 24 students to find out how they use AI to assist with reading academic texts. We found more than half of students used AI to summarise texts, clarify difficult readings and check their interpretations.

This article is part of a series on how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education.

We take a deeper look into how AI has disrupted degrees, how universities are responding to these new challenges and what the technology means for the sector’s future. You can find more stories here.

Rules aren’t always clear

But research shows the line between what is acceptable and unacceptable use of AI is not always clear to students or teachers. For example, does improving a draft with AI mean only correcting grammar, or does it mean restructuring the argument?

One of the biggest challenges is the line between appropriate and inappropriate AI use can differ between assessments and might also change for each student even within the same assessment.

How are unis responding?

Australian universities have a regulatory requirement to ensure assessments can confirm students have achieved the knowledge and skills their courses require. Universities’ approaches in how to go about this have differed in recent years.

An influential response is the University of Sydney’s “two-lane approach”, with variations now used at many Australian universities.

The two-lane approach separates assessments into two categories. The first lane is “secure” and requires students to demonstrate their skills and knowledge without any use of AI. These assessments are typically in-person exams and interactive oral assessments, where assessors can physically see students completing a task without opening ChatGPT to help them.

The second lane is “open” and allows students to freely use AI, for example, in online quizzes and essays. Because it is so hard to judge if AI has been used inappropriately in such formats, lane two assessments are typically framed as being for feedback and learning, rather than as demonstrations or assurances of student learning.

Unis are still struggling to keep up

But increased reliance on in-person assessments is not a perfect long-term solution. These assessment formats:

  • are often expensive to run

  • limit the kinds of things teachers can assess

  • may also unfairly bias against certain student demographics.

In-person assessments also don’t necessarily mean AI is beyond students’ reach. Wearable forms of AI, such as AI enabled smart glasses, can resemble ordinary eyewear and provide exam assistance to students without showing obvious signs to invigilators.

Students have already been caught using them in exams in New Zealand, Taiwan and South Korea, and monitoring the tech remains a challenge for unis.

Are unis on the right track?

Our research describes AI and assessment as a “wicked problem” – it doesn’t have a simple, one-fix solution.

Part of the complexity of this challenge is that universities don’t always know if students are using AI to help their learning or to undermine a teacher’s ability to judge if learning actually took place.

Universities need credible evidence of what graduates can do. But treating assessment solely as a security problem to deter AI use risks measuring the success of the control measures over the success of a student’s education.

Perhaps instead of simply asking whether a new form of assessment works in an AI world, we should ask which problem it solves, and which other problems it might create.

For instance, if the aim is to keep AI out of assessments, then more supervision and tighter controls may look like progress. But if the goal is to prepare students to use AI well for the workforce, those same restrictions might prevent the learning we want. This suggests that what a “solution” looks like in one context may look like anything but in another.

If universities are to make progress, they will need to understand which approaches to assessment reform work – and which do not – in particular disciplines and contexts, rather than a singular “perfect” response across an entire institution.

item.title: Artificial intelligence is desperately seeking its narrative
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Frédéric Fréry, Professeur de stratégie, CentraleSupélec, ESCP Business School

Since the foundational work of Austrian economist Joseph Schumpeter, research has distinguished invention from innovation by its practical implementation. Whether an innovation spreads, however, depends partly on its social acceptance and how its uses are perceived. Without such acceptance, even a promising technology may remain confined to scientific experiments and investors’ speculation. To gain public support, an innovation needs a compelling narrative capable of generating interest, if not enthusiasm. Artificial intelligence illustrates this phenomenon: while its narrative is still taking shape, its social acceptability is increasingly contested.

In July 2026, Le Monde diplomatique declared that “The AI backlash has begun”. The initial sense of wonder generated by ChatGPT has increasingly given way to broader public unease about AI’s social consequences, from its effects on work, education and information to concerns about privacy, the environment and the growing power of technology companies. In this emerging narrative, AI appears as a “digital Moloch” whose costs are borne collectively while its benefits accrue to only a handful of oligarchs.

In May 2026, when former Google CEO Eric Schmidt addressed nearly 10,000 graduates at the University of Arizona, warning that artificial intelligence would transform every single profession, boos echoed through the crowd. Since then, commencement speeches focused on AI have faced similar jeers at several other US universities. This unrest aligns with data: a Harvard Kennedy School survey, cited by the Associated Press, reveals that roughly 70% of American students now view AI as a direct threat to their career prospects.

In September 2026, OpenAI’s rapid-fire claims of solving long-standing mathematical problems sparked deep division, with some celebrating a historic milestone while others warned that machine-generated solutions could undermine the processes through which new ideas emerge, young mathematicians are trained and mathematical knowledge itself develops.

Narratives that generate hostility

How did a technology promising unprecedented prosperity come to generate such hostility? Part of the answer lies in AI’s real or anticipated effects on society. Another lies in the narratives surrounding it.

Four broad narratives currently shape the discourse on artificial intelligence. They are neither mutually exclusive nor entirely coherent: the same company or executive may embrace several, sometimes contradictory, visions.

Narrative No. 1: ‘AI will save us… if it does not destroy us’

The first narrative presents AI as a civilisational gamble: it could usher in unprecedented abundance and scientific progress, but also trigger catastrophes or escape human control.

In September 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman envisioned AI accelerating scientific discovery, solving complex problems and making capabilities once reserved for specialists widely accessible.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei developed a similar vision the following month. He imagined AI systems matching the abilities of the best researchers and compressing decades of scientific progress into a few years, transforming medicine, neuroscience and efforts to address climate change and poverty. The same models could facilitate cyberattacks, assist in the development of biological weapons or, as science fiction has warned for decades (from 2001: A Space Odyssey to The Matrix and The Terminator), become sufficiently autonomous to escape our control.

Elon Musk takes this logic much further

In July 2026, during an interview with The Economist, he compared our future situation to that of chimpanzees faced with humans: when the intelligence gap becomes too wide, it is difficult to imagine the less intelligent species remaining in control. According to Musk, there is a 10% to 20% risk that AI and robots will cause a catastrophe. Nevertheless, he believes that even if an off switch existed, it should not be used, because he is convinced that the most likely outcome will be “incredible abundance for everyone”.

AI and robotics would gradually make work optional, enable a generous universal income and eventually make money itself unnecessary. This is the narrative of the “happy apocalypse”: catastrophe is possible and humans will probably not remain in control of the systems, but acceleration must continue regardless, because it is both irresistible and potentially wonderful.

Narrative No. 2: ‘demystifying superintelligence’

Researcher Yann Le Cun, the former head of research at Meta, advocates a rationalist counter-narrative. In a February 2024 interview with Time magazine, he stressed that large language models have neither a robust understanding of the physical world nor genuine reasoning and planning abilities comparable to those of humans. He considers the scenario in which an artificial intelligence takes control of the world to be implausible. He also supports greater openness in AI models. In his view, just as a democracy needs a pluralistic press, it also needs a plurality of models and assistants.

LeCun has since left Meta to pursue research into “world models”, systems designed to understand and reason about the physical world. His approach shifts the debate from prophecy to engineering: the risks lie not necessarily in machines deciding to dominate humanity, but in how systems are designed, deployed and governed.

Narrative No. 3: ‘AI will augment us, not replace us’

Microsoft has promoted the seemingly more modest narrative of the “copilot”: generative AI assists humans rather than replacing them. By taking on routine cognitive tasks, it promises to free up creativity and improve productivity. The metaphor is skillful: in an aircraft, the copilot assists the pilot without taking away the controls.

Yet Microsoft also promotes AI agents capable of accessing organisational data and executing sequences of actions autonomously. The distinction matters: a copilot augments human work, whereas an agent can replace it. The narrative of augmentation thus risks obscuring questions about employment, skills, power and the distribution of productivity gains.

Narrative No. 4: ‘superintelligence for everyone’

On July 28, 2026, Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg also entered the battle over AI narratives with an opinion piece published in The Wall Street Journal. He argued that the decisive question was no longer whether superintelligence would exist, but who would have access to it. His narrative is one of “personal superintelligence”: everyone could have an assistant that exceeded human capabilities and was tailored to their needs and values. This is not only a technological vision, but also an attempt to make the disruption caused by AI desirable again. Without abandoning the promise of superintelligence, this narrative seeks to make it more acceptable by promising to distribute it to everyone.

Yet democratising its use does not guarantee the democratisation of power. This narrative is consistent with the interests of a global platform such as Meta: billions of people may use a personal assistant while remaining dependent on a handful of companies that own the data centres, define the models and control the data required to train them.

When narratives generate their own consequences

These four narratives do not by themselves explain the apparent rejection of AI, which is also driven by concrete experiences: threats to employment, imposed transformations, errors, data centres, energy consumption and so forth. They do, however, give these concerns a coherent form. Moreover, the focus on the subjugation or extinction of humanity pushes immediate and very real issues into the background: the distribution of gains, copyright, accountability, human decision-making, the preservation of skills and environmental costs.

These narratives are also performative: they do not merely describe possible futures, but shape investment, regulation and competition. That became particularly visible in September 2026, when former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned with a public warning that leading AI companies were racing towards systems they themselves believed could become catastrophically dangerous. His intervention rapidly drew support from other researchers, followed within days by calls from Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk for a coordinated slowing of frontier AI development.

The episode also exposed how difficult it is to separate safety concerns from commercial and geopolitical interests. President Donald Trump rejected calls for a slowdown, arguing that restraint would benefit China and that the US must maintain its lead in the AI race. Industry leaders face a mirror-image dilemma: while deceleration might mitigate certain risks, doing it unilaterally risks ceding ground to global competitors. Chinese firms—along with European players like France’s Mistral—have narrowed the performance gap, largely by developing open-source, compute-efficient models. Consequently, calls from tech giants for tighter regulatory controls can be interpreted less as altruism and more as a strategy to protect the market dominance of their own closed, resource-intensive systems.

This dynamic illustrates the core paradox of the existential-risk narrative. The leading AI corporations are framed as simultaneously too dangerous to leave unsupervised and too strategically vital to genuinely restrain. As a result, the policy debate becomes trapped in a false dichotomy: either allowing dominant firms to police themselves, or granting governments sweeping powers to shut down systems entirely. In both scenarios, citizens are relegated to passive spectators of a technological transformation presented as entirely inevitable.

Beyond the narratives: taking back the wheel

Each of the four narratives is marked by a more or less explicit desire to protect the interests of established players. The sums invested in AI are so astronomical that, however sincere the convictions may be, they necessarily remain compatible with the objectives of those advancing them. No industry narrative is entirely disinterested, and the vision promoted by a company simply reflects its strategic choices.

The problem may therefore not be to find the “right” narrative for artificial intelligence, but to stop presenting technical, economic and political choices as inevitable. First, we must stop personifying AI. These systems are designed, financed and deployed by human organisations.

Saying that AI wants, decides or threatens tends to conceal those who determine its objectives, choose its uses and benefit from it. We must also remember that the pace of development, the openness of models, their fields of application, the distribution of gains and the protections granted to individuals are not natural phenomena. They are decisions that must remain subject to political debate.

American or Chinese narratives

Finally, prophecies must give way to concrete questions. What do we want to automate? Where should human decision-making be preserved? Who controls the infrastructure and the data, bears responsibility for errors and guarantees access to remedies? How should the effects on employment, skills, the environment and inequality be measured? As Pope Leo XIV recalls in the encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, published in May 2026, innovations are never neutral: the question is who deploys them, under what rules and for whose benefit.

We must also recognise the highly US-centric nature of the four narratives presented here.

China’s official discourse, for example, offers a revealing contrast. It does not herald the arrival of a superintelligence that will either save humanity or bring about an apocalypse. Instead, it describes the methodical integration of AI into the real economy through a proactive industrial policy and under state control. This model raises other questions, particularly concerning political centralisation, surveillance and freedom of expression, but it reminds us that the American imagination of AI is not the only possible one.

AI should therefore be regarded as a powerful but governable technology whose benefits must be demonstrated rather than prophesied. Its proponents cannot indefinitely continue to present it as simultaneously uncontrollable, inevitable, and universally beneficial. Tech giants cannot market a technology as a “copilot” while claiming no-one is at the wheel.

item.title: Why is Nvidia so powerful in the AI world, and what could Jensen Huang’s scandal really cost?
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Andrew Cullen, Guest Research Fellow, School of Computing and Information Systems, The University of Melbourne

Jensen Huang, the chief executive and co-founder of chipmaking company Nvidia, recently admitted to an extramarital affair. However, it’s not just a tabloid story: the woman involved, Alice Huang, has been accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent.

Computer chips – specifically the chips used to produce and run artificial intelligence (AI) systems – have become a key front in the United States’ rivalry with China for geopolitical power and influence. The most powerful chips are needed for the most advanced AI, and the US has tried to maintain its edge over China by restricting access to those chips.

While the Chinese government rejects claims of espionage, Alice Huang has reportedly been under investigation by the US for years.

So what’s so special about Nvidia? What’s in it for China? And if Jensen Huang goes down, what else could go down with him?

The world’s biggest AI chip company

Nvidia is the world’s biggest supplier of the high-end chips used for AI and data centres, with some estimates putting its market share over 80%.

The now multi-trillion-dollar company got its start making chips called graphic processing units (GPUs), used largely for video games. However, these chips – and their successors – turned out to be ideal for the kind of number-crunching needed for training and using AI models.

Other companies such as Google and AMD have tried to make chips that can compete with Nvidia for speed and efficiency, however neither has been able to displace Nvidia from its dominance of the AI market.

Read more: What is a GPU? An expert explains the chips powering the AI boom, and why they’re worth trillions

Why China may be interested

As a consequence, Nvidia has played a key role in the US government’s strategy to stall China’s development of AI. Sales of Nvidia’s most powerful chips to China have been restricted since 2022 – though the restrictions were somewhat relaxed last year.

However, Chinese enterprises have repeatedly tested the boundaries of US sanctions. Southeast Asian companies including Megaspeed, Alice Huang’s former employer, have been accused of buying up Nvidia chips and exporting them into China.

Jensen Huang has lobbied intently for a relaxation of US chip export restrictions, which is being seen in a new light after the revelation of his relationship with Alice Huang.

Skipping the sanctions

Trade records indicate over US$3 billion in chips crossed from Singapore to China in a single year, alongside similar volumes from Malaysia.

Selling access to banned Nvidia chips to Chinese companies has also become a growth industry.

Nvidia’s value has soared with the AI boom. However, its share price has fallen after the disclosure of the Huang incident, with some analysts asking whether the company propped up sales figures by ignoring sanctions. It has also been reported that an Nvidia executive leaned on US officials to halt an investigation into the firm’s relationship with Megaspeed.

Regulatory impact

Nvidia’s share price tumbled after the affair was revealed.

Now the company is reportedly under criminal investigation. At the same time, US technology regulators are mobilising, with Congress requesting Jensen Huang explain his interactions with Alice Huang, and how Nvidia protects itself against foreign espionage.

If Nvidia is forced to guarantee its chips don’t enter China, its sales pipeline may grind to a halt. And if Nvidia hits trouble, the financial impacts could be much wider.

The AI sector is notorious for the amount of circular financing going on – where companies invest in their own suppliers or customers. Nvidia is a key player in this loop.

Investors are already fretting over whether the enormous amounts of money sunk into AI can ever return profits.

While leading AI model builders Anthropic and OpenAI are moving toward public listings or fresh funding rounds, both face harsh reality checks.

OpenAI has delayed its own planned stock market listing, while Anthropic’s expected share market listing is rumoured to face a “junk bond” rating, meaning it’s a high-risk investment.

Data centre firms too are losing value as they face community pushback and soaring energy costs.

Governance crisis

So what now? Clearly Nvidia faces a crisis, with a backlash against AI and data centres sweeping the US, US investigators looking at it closely, and the company’s own board of directors investigating its chief executive.

On top of this, Nvidia has been inseparable from Jensen Huang’s personal brand for decades – and that brand is now somewhat tarnished.

Until now, investors have supported the company, and Jensen, as visionary underwriters of the entire AI ecosystem. If that changes, or the company otherwise loses its way, a shortage of GPUs may be the least of the AI industry’s problems.

item.title: New AI regulator announced, as government considers criminal law change to keep erring frontier companies in line
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Michelle Grattan, Professorial Fellow, University of Canberra

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has announced a new artificial intelligence (AI) safety regulator, which will enforce penalties for frontier AI companies that breach their obligations.

The government is also considering criminal law changes to deal with serious misconduct by any of these companies.

The measures are targeted at frontier AI companies – those building the largest, most advanced models.

At a news conference shortly before leaving for the COP climate conference in Turkey, the prime minister outlined AI safety and security protections that will be in the government’s proposed AI framework legislation.

The six mandated requirements for companies are:

  • maintain security controls across all stages of AI development and deployment
  • identify and manage serious risks associated with models
  • quickly provide mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian government
  • allow independent evaluation of models
  • maintain and publish safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management and transparency
  • respond to updated standards and rules as technologies change.

Albanese said these protections were in line with recommendations from the parliamentary joint select committee on AI.

The government also released the recommendations from the rapid review into the OpenAI breach of an Australian government site by a rogue agent earlier this year.

In this breach, for which OpenAI apologised, statistical health data was accessed, but no personal data. The government complained strongly to the company.

“It can’t be allowed to happen again,” Albanese said on Tuesday. He said the government had accepted and commenced work on the review’s 18 recommendations.

The recommendations include:

  • mandatory AI company reporting of misaligned behaviour or cyber incidents
  • consideration of reforming criminal law to deal with cases of serious misconduct
  • greater engagement with international counterparts and frontier AI developers to promote shared expectations about AI safety and accountability
  • strengthening resilience and response to AI incidents, including better information sharing and more focus on cyber security.

Albanese, appearing with Defence Minister Richard Marles and Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, told his news conference the government wanted to see Australia benefiting from the advantages of AI while mitigating the risks.

In relation to new criminal penalties the review report said the Attorney-General’s Department, in consultation with the Australian Federal Police, the Home Affair Department, and other agencies, should explore:

the application of criminal penalties for egregious regulatory non-compliance; and/or a standalone “failure to prevent” offence which would criminalise instances where the company is responsible for developing an AI model that engages in harmful conduct, and the company fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm.

Albanese said the government would release the report of the review, with due regard to national security considerations, but there is no clarity about when this will be done.

item.title: I don’t want AI in my online search. What options do I have?
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Damiano Spina, Senior Lecturer, School of Computing Technologies, RMIT University

Last week, Google announced a new artificial intelligence (AI) policy for schools that use Google apps. It provides new settings for opting in or out of AI products on student accounts. For schools that reject AI in the classroom entirely, they can also turn off search.

Speaking to The New York Times, Google’s vice president for education, Chris Phillips, noted that “search and AI are deeply integrated”. This led to headlines claiming there’s no longer a way to use Google search without AI.

Since AI has become ubiquitous, it’s also facing increasing pushback. Some people may reject it due to personal, ethical, or environmental reasons.

But we all need to look things up on the internet. So is it actually possible to search the web “without AI”? To answer that question, we need to unpack a few things first.

How does a web search engine work?

Google search is a tool known as a web search engine. For you to type in a query and receive results milliseconds later, a bunch of things need to happen under the hood. All of them involve algorithms – simply put, a set of instructions for a computer.

There are six main components of a web search engine:

  • crawling: harvesting documents published on the web
  • indexing: breaking down documents into efficient data structures
  • spam detection: filtering out content that doesn’t offer genuine value to users
  • ranking: ordering search results by how relevant they might be to the query
  • user interactions: assisting users when they formulate their information needs (for instance, auto-completing your query) or consume the search output (such as serving you snippets or AI summaries)
  • evaluation: measuring if search quality improves after making a change in one of the above components.

These features are not static – developers, engineers and informational retrieval researchers are constantly tinkering and improving them.

How does web search use AI?

To answer this question, we first need to define what kind of AI we’re talking about.

All of the components listed above are likely to involve some sort of machine learning and neural networks – that is, AI systems trained to analyse lots of data, learn patterns and make predictions. So, there’s actually no way to use a search engine “without AI”.

But when people talk about AI these days, they tend to mean generative AI. These are AI systems trained on enormous amounts of data and capable of generating new content from prompts.

A version of this, called retrieval-augmented generation, is what allows you to have a conversation with a search engine. It combines a large language model for the generative part, and the web content retrieved by the search engine.

This is the technology behind Google’s AI Mode and AI Overviews. They provide handy summaries and a new way to interact with content on the web, but they’re not without issues.

The large language model is built on an astonishing amount of training data, but it’s not updated as frequently as the web search index. Links in AI summaries are associated with the answer after generating it, and this component can also make mistakes.

In addition, searchers who see AI Overviews are accessing fewer sources overall. Overreliance on AI is also a well-known phenomenon in which users may trust an answer without verifying whether it’s correct.

So can I search the web without AI summaries?

Commercial web search engines like Google are increasingly showing AI summaries to users’ queries. At the time of writing this, there’s no official switch that lets Google users disable AI Overviews and other generative AI features.

But there’s one little hack that works: if you append “&udm=14” to the search request link, the Google search results default to the “Web” tab that doesn’t show AI Overviews and other snippets.

For this to work, you’d have to manually add that parameter in the address bar. That’s not always practical, so people have built browser plugins and ways to automate this step.

In Mozilla Firefox and Chromium browsers such as Brave, Chrome and Opera for desktop devices, you can set up a custom search engine to add this parameter every time you hit search on Google.

But Google search isn’t the only search engine available. There are many others out there, such as DuckDuckGo, Brave Search, or Ecosia. These provide a “non-AI mode” that deactivates AI summaries by default, and in some cases even provides the option to filter out AI-generated images.

Where do those search engine results come from?

Maintaining a web index is not easy. The web is constantly changing, and keeping the big volume of searchable information fresh requires enormous computational resources.

There are only a few organisations able to maintain this at a large scale. Google’s and Microsoft Bing’s indexes are the most popular worldwide. But there are some alternatives that are gaining attention.

Brave Search operates from an independent search engine. DuckDuckGo combines multiple sources, including content harvested with its own crawler, and search results sourced from Bing.

Initiatives such as the OpenWebSearch.eu project aim to develop an independent open European infrastructure for web search. It also makes a web index publicly available so others can build their own web search engine.

So, is there a search without AI?

The short answer is “no”. All search engines use AI in one form or another.

What about generative AI specifically?

It is technically possible to disable AI-generated answers from the search results page. Some search engine providers have decided to provide that option to users, while others – like Google – have made it a default.

item.title: Most uni students now use AI, but that doesn’t mean they like it
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Authors:

  • Kelly Matthews, Pro Vice-Chancellor (Teaching & Learning), University of Wollongong
  • Tim Fawns, Associate Professor (Education Focused), Monash University

The university experience has changed drastically since artificial intelligence (AI) became widely available four years ago.

Students are increasingly using AI for around-the-clock feedback, and most are required to use it as part of new assessment redesigns.

But as AI is used more in courses and changes how university works, how do students feel about it?

Our research

In 2024, we began a research project across four Australian unis – Monash University, the University of Queensland, Deakin University and the University of Technology Sydney – asking students about AI. Undergraduate and postgraduate students were asked how frequently they use AI for study, their most common uses of AI, why they choose to use it and their concerns around the tech.

This year, we repeated the survey at the same unis, hearing from more than 10,000 students.

The survey included responses from neurodivergent students, students with disability, those who spoke languages other than English at home and students who were the first in their family to attend uni.

Students were recruited via email, posts on online university platforms, and signs with QR codes. We also ran 20 focus groups with 79 students online in 2024.

This article is part of a series on how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education.

We take a deeper look into how AI has disrupted degrees, how universities are responding to these new challenges and what the technology means for the sector’s future. You can find more stories here.

What we found

A published snapshot of our 2026 survey data shows the most common reason students use AI is to edit or improve their writing, with nearly 70% selecting this option. About 64% of students use it to generate ideas or examples, and 60% said they use AI to teach them how to do something.

Around half of students seek out information through AI and also ask it for feedback on their work.

We also know more students are using AI. When comparing the data to 2024 responses, the proportion of students who reported never using AI for their studies fell slightly, from 17% to 15%.

It mirrors findings from this year’s Australian Student Wellbeing Report, which found 84% of students have used AI tools for assignments and study, increasing 10% from the previous year.

Why students use AI

Students reported using AI for a range of different reasons.

About 55% use it to speed up their working process and also to help themselves overcome mental blocks. Nearly half of students said they use AI to make study easier in general.

Participants also reported using AI to help improve their personal wellbeing during study sessions. About 41% said the tech helps reduce stress and around 32% said they feel more confident when using AI in their work.

There are concerns

But using AI does not necessarily mean students are comfortable with it. We found many are limiting their AI use, some are trying to avoid using it, and 15-17% are avoiding it altogether in their studies.

The reasons for limiting AI use vary, but the most common explanation, selected by 67% of participants who use AI, related to concerns around AI’s accuracy.

About 62% of students said they limited or avoided AI use as it conflicts with their personal learning values and around 57% said they preferred to do the work themselves. Just under half of students expressed ethical concerns in using AI. These concerns might relate to AI presenting biased information, privacy issues, threats to academic integrity, and the environmental impacts of AI technologies.

Over the last two years, students have become less worried about breaking uni rules too. This year, 56% of participants said they avoided using AI out of a fear of being caught – decreasing 7% when compared with 2024 data.

Unis can help

Over the last four years, unis have been navigating complex changes. But their guidance on AI hasn’t always been clear to students.

Research shows students have learned more about AI on their own than they have from their unis.

Our 2024 survey and focus groups also showed widespread anxiety and confusion among students about using AI for study, partly due to confusing university academic integrity policies around AI rules.

One participant at the time asked for clearer rules:

just have some kind of concrete policy in place that you can look at and go like, ‘right, this is okay. This isn’t. Thank you.’ And even if it’s something I would personally disagree with, at least it’s set in stone.

Another student recognised the complexity of AI regulation too:

 we’re in this very grey area where nobody knows what’s really happening.

Guidance around AI has improved

Our findings show there has been some progress over the last two years. Students who reported receiving sufficient guidance from unis rose from 36% in 2024 to 47% in 2026.

This might be because unis are setting more consistent AI guidelines across their institutions, rather than putting the responsibility on educators to set rules around AI use for each subject. This is happening alongside changes to assessment that incorporate use of AI.

But our recent survey suggests there is more to do to help students feel confident they will not break rules.

Students’ perspectives matter

Of all the concerns about AI in higher education, perhaps one of the most important questions is whether unis are doing enough to listen to students about their feelings towards AI and how they use it.

When unis don’t engage students in these conversations, they miss opportunities to understand how AI is influencing learning. More importantly, they miss the opportunity to involve students in shaping how AI is used in education.

item.title: AI use is now universal in higher education. Why are universities failing to adapt?
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Jason M. Lodge, Director of the Learning, Instruction & Technology Lab and Professor of Educational Psychology, School of Education, The University of Queensland

Artificial intelligence (AI) use among university students is now near-universal in many countries. Yet, as of a year ago, fewer than one in five universities in a 90-country UNESCO survey had a formal AI policy.

Since ChatGPT arrived in late 2022, the threat to academic integrity has loomed large. Unis must now ensure students earn degrees by showing what they can do, not what AI can do.

This requires policies that drive structural change to assessment and curriculum, not just rules about when AI can be used. But it’s not so straightforward.

The challenge for universities

Universities, in particular, have struggled to adapt to generative AI more than primary and high schools.

This is because university classes are often large and contact time between students and teachers is limited. Together, this makes it hard for teachers to get to know students personally and to ensure they learn what is required for their degrees.

UNESCO has published an AI competency framework, but it focuses primarily on schools and stops short of providing specific guidance for higher education.

This article is part of a series on how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education.

We take a deeper look into how AI has disrupted degrees, how universities are responding to these new challenges and what the technology means for the sector’s future. You can find more stories here.

University AI policies are often vague

A study published in July examined the public AI policies and guidelines of 39 Australian universities that teach information and communications technology. This is a subject area where AI can readily complete coding tasks.

The analysis found wide variation among the universities’ AI policies. Often, AI rules were buried in institutions’ misconduct policies rather than assessment design procedures. Out of the 39 unis, only one had published specific guidance around AI.

The universities’ general guidance on AI use was often vague, too. One simply required AI use to be “ethical, pedagogically sound, transparent and purposeful” but did not provide any further detail.

The researchers argued that AI was disrupting assessments faster than universities could build the structures to govern it. Only seven of the 39 universities had documented a body, such as a task force, to coordinate their response.

Many have also left it to individual unit coordinators to spell out what AI use is allowed. This means the rules can differ between units.

The risks also go well beyond cheating. Global discussion among leading researchers and policymakers this year has shifted to a deeper issue: using AI to avoid learning altogether. This is when students’ offload their work to AI entirely and, as a result, learn nothing themselves. It is difficult to gauge how much of this offloading is already occurring.

Universities’ current policies aren’t sufficient in addressing student offloading to AI. Students cannot be forced to learn through a policy.

Teachers have also been using AI tools to detect whether students have included AI-generated text in their submissions. But universities are now moving away from this as the technology is not always accurate.

Experts have warned that relying solely on AI detectors can lead to false accusations of student academic misconduct.

Assessment reform

Instead of focusing on more systemic responses, universities have mainly responded to AI by changing how assessments work. This has usually meant:

  • a greater emphasis on in-person exams and oral presentations where AI cannot be easily accessed

  • permitting the use of AI in some assessments, such as take-home essays, where students have cited their use of the technology.

But while redesigned assessments can show whether learning has occurred, it is still not enough. It also matters what students are assessed on.

What are other countries doing?

In other parts of the world, such as the European Union, attention is turning to explicitly developing students’ capabilities to adapt to constant change. These include teaching students to:

  • make sound judgements about how much they know about a subject

  • critically evaluate information, both with and without AI

  • make decisions about their learning processes and goals independently of AI or an educator.

However, these capabilities are hard to develop and mostly don’t transfer between subjects. Instead, they must be taught explicitly to students, in the context of their subject area or discipline.

One way of doing this would be to incorporate specific modules into courses that teach this.

So, what’s the right approach?

In 2023, a number of academics, including myself, wrote evidence-based assessment principles for the Australian higher education regulator. The principles were formed to guide unis on how to adapt assessments to account for students’ AI use.

One principle focuses on assuring students are actually learning content and not offloading work to AI, which institutions have attempted to address through assessment redesign. These attempts at redesign are having an effect.

The second principle is about preparing students for a world where AI is ubiquitous. Students need to learn how to effectively use AI for when they enter the workforce.

This principle has proven much harder for unis to adapt to, as skills tied to today’s AI tools quickly become outdated as the technology rapidly advances. This means simple “AI literacy” is not enough for students alone.

While there is no one-size-fits-all approach, unis would also benefit from collaborating with each other to tackle the problem.

However, institutions tend to compete rather than share resources. Only one of the 39 in the study I previously cited mentioned learning from other institutions.

A national strategy would help

In 2024, the higher education regulator required every uni to submit AI action plans outlining what they are doing to adapt to AI. The regulator has also since published guides outlining strategies.

But a regulator can only set expectations. It cannot fund the long-term work of enabling changes to policy and practice across the country.

That was the job of the Office for Learning and Teaching, which funded teaching innovation and helped universities share what worked. It closed in 2016, and a promised replacement never materialised.

A national approach would mean an enabling body – independent of any single university – sharing evidence and guidance across the sector. This might look similar to Ireland’s Higher Education Authority, which has published a national framework on AI in teaching and learning.

However, there are challenges in setting this up in Australia, given how protective universities are about their autonomy. There would be questions around who funds such a body. And it would be difficult for a national authority to keep pace with technology that changes faster than policy.

Still, unis must engage deeply and collaboratively with this debate about how to adapt to AI. Otherwise they risk becoming redundant in the age of intelligent machines.

He is one of the convenors of the Castlereagh Statement: A cross-sector call to action on Australian education and training in the age of AI.

item.title: Voters rejected data centers in dozens of communities, fueling the narrative that opposition to the AI infrastructure contributed to the 2026 blue wave
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Barbara A. Trish, Professor of Political Science, Grinnell College

Data centers were on the ballot, both directly and indirectly, in the 2026 midterm elections.

A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development.

The centers also may have played a role in several high-profile contests. In Ohio’s race for a U.S. Senate seat, Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign. Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state. As governor-elect, she immediately reaffirmed her campaign pledge to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers.

According to NBC exit poll data, 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote. For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%.

Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure, housing the computing resources used to train AI models. These massive facilities guzzle energy and water and are very noisy. Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of land use, higher utility bills and environmental degradation, outweigh the benefits.

I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns.

Before the midterms, it had already appeared to be disrupting some partisan alignments. Following those historic elections, which have thoroughly shaken up America’s political geography, the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms.

Disrupting political polarization

In contrast to many other issues, concern about data centers is relatively bipartisan. The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they support or oppose having data centers in their communities. Opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines.

Local ballot measures restricting data centers also cut across traditional political alignments. Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them. The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points.

The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in Harwood, North Dakota, population around 800. With a data center project already in progress, political and economic leaders prevailed in arguing that restrictions would cut into local revenue and stifle economic development more generally.

Allies and adversaries

Exit polls taken during the midterm elections also detected a degree of bipartisanship. Of the 56% of voters who said data centers played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote, approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans. Exit polls, however, should be interpreted with care, given their methodological limitations.

These responses hint at why the narrative that opposition to data centers helped fuel the Democrats’ historic midterm victory emerged right away.

The seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition. In cities and counties, zoning fights are drawing a diverse kind of resistance: environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests.

Some of the bipartisanship around this issue has even seeped into Congress. Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote. The bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers.

Similar concerns killed the Senate version, a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change.

Brookings Institution scholars anticipate that the newly elected Congress will take up the issue again, this time with a directive to states to establish mandatory, not voluntary, requirements.

Politics as usual

As the midterm elections approached, candidates up and down the ballot blanketed the airwaves and digital platforms with ads against data centers. President Donald Trump pushed back, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.”

Some Republican candidates walked a fine line between responding to voters’ concerns and not alienating the president.

It matters little whether the data center electoral narrative is accurate, and so far, the reported evidence is limited. We need to know where losing candidates stood on data centers, not just the winners. That voters considered data centers important says nothing about which direction they leaned. And despite a 98% success rate across the 41 local ballot measures, it’s hard to gauge how much resistance there is to the more than 600 proposed data centers that are slated to be built.

What does matter is that many people apparently are accepting the narrative because that alone will affect politics and the economy. Consider Elon Musk’s post on Nov. 4 on X, his social media platform: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” and the sell-off of data center-related stocks the next day.

As the 2028 presidential primaries come into focus, I believe we should expect to see many Democratic and Republican hopefuls emphasizing their support for data center restrictions and bans as they throw their hats into the ring.

item.title: Do AI agents have minds? A philosopher explains
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Tom Cochrane, Senior Lecturer in Philosophy, Flinders University

In the past few months, partly autonomous or “agentic” artificial intelligence (AI) systems have racked up some astonishing feats, from hacking tech startups to solving some of the world’s most famous open mathematical questions.

Agentic AI systems can work in “swarms” that communicate among themselves to complete tasks. The communications involved are often surprisingly human-like – which is spurring a debate over whether these systems are conscious.

Researchers at the leading AI lab Anthropic believe their systems may well be conscious – but other experts, including the head of Microsoft AI, say this view is misguided.

This question isn’t just an academic one. The future status of AI systems and their role in society – how they can be treated, whether they have rights, and more – may depend on it.

How can we decide if AI systems are conscious?

How do we even approach a question like this? One strategy is to look at existing theories of what consciousness is and see if agentic AI systems meet the criteria.

However, existing theories of consciousness tend to start from the assumption that the agent has some kind of mental state. These theories are focused on the difference between having a state consciously or unconsciously. This is why they appeal to features such as higher-order thought, or a system that broadcasts thoughts to the rest of the mind. These are features that could distinguish between conscious control and states like sleepwalking.

So when thinking about AI, we must not skip a crucial first question: do agentic AIs even have mental states?

What is a mental state?

In the 1870s, philosopher Franz Brentano developed an influential view: “intentionality is the mark of the mental”.

What Brentano means by “intentionality” is how mental states are about something. They refer to something beyond themselves. So another way to put Brentano’s point is that all mental states are about something or other.

What Brentano means by intentionality is not the same as the usual meaning of “intention” as aiming to do something. Yet intentionality and an intention to act significantly overlap, because having a perception or thought is something that we do.

Whenever we perceive or think, we are trying to pick out some aspect of the world. Even our passive-seeming visual experiences are tasks the moment that we use the patterns striking our retinas to orient ourselves.

So if a mental state is a task performed to achieve a goal, our question about AI minds turns on whether they have their own goals.

Are agentic AI systems really agents?

It is now common to refer to certain AI systems as “agents”. Yet this language is misleading. It implies the AI systems have agency, or the capacity to act towards their own goals.

Humans use devices to achieve their aims, including their aims to refer to things, without those devices becoming agents in their own right. A thermostat regulates the temperature, but it does not have the goal of regulating the temperature. A book contains words that refer to things – but again, the book does not have the goal of referring to things.

To attribute agency to a computer program, we must be convinced that no human is required to stand behind its goals. Its goal-directedness must be independent.

We know that agentic AIs, when given a task, can develop complex and unexpected sub-goals on the way to achieving it. Yet the goals that ultimately drive their activity are set by the humans who program and instruct them. Any sub-goals generated by an AI are literally meaningless outside of these aims set by humans.

Think of a game like football. A person might have the sub-goal of running past a defender, but it is literally meaningless without the larger goal of trying to score. And scoring a goal itself is simply making a ball cross a line without the larger goal of playing football. Without the larger goal, anything a player does on the field is merely activity.

Why do agents have goals?

A genuine agent has goals in order to promote things they care about – for example, you want to satisfy your hunger at lunchtime, so you go to a bakery and buy a sandwich.

Agentic AI is unlikely to care about things in an independent way, because its activity is not connected to life in the same way minds are.

What distinctively allows living beings to generate their own goals is that their mental activity develops out of the processes for constantly re-constituting their own bodies and keeping themselves alive. Goal-driven thinking builds up from simple signals for regulating nutrition and warmth to states like pain and pleasure and eventually to symbolic thought.

Nothing like this is going on in agentic AI. There is a disconnect between its information-processing activities and the physical stuff on which it depends.

Can AI ever be conscious?

Agentic AI systems are not conscious. They don’t have mental states which could be conscious.

Only living beings have conscious mental states because having a mental state requires a being to originate a certain kind of goal – the goal to mean something or to refer to something – and only living beings originate goals.

This argument does not permanently rule out the possibility of AI consciousness. However, it does suggest that this could only arise in some artificial form of life.

Until then, we have more reason to think that an ant is conscious than an agentic AI is. At least an ant seems to care about its own life.

Of course, the fact agentic AIs are not really agents does not stop them from wreaking havoc by carrying out functions that their human originators do not properly supervise or understand. But we should be very clear on this: whatever an agentic AI does, that is a human or group of humans acting indirectly on the world, and those humans are responsible for the outcome.

item.title: We need to talk about Meta: Political interference and interests in the Brazilian elections
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Authors:

  • R. Marie Santini, Professora da Escola de Comunicação e diretora do NetLab (Internet and Social Media Research Lab), Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ)
  • Bruno Mattos, Coordenador de projetos do NetLab, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ)
  • Debora Salles, Coordenadora geral de pesquisa do NetLab, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ)

On the eve of Donald Trump’s return to the presidency of the United States, in January 2025, Meta’s founder and CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, announced that changes would be made to his company’s moderation policies in the name of “freedom of expression”, which, he said, was under threat by global pressures for what he saw as censorship. The announcement signaled a rapprochement between Meta and the far right around a common goal: the deregulation of Big Tech. Since then, growing entanglement between major technology companies and the U.S. President Donald Trump administration has shown how the private interests of a small group can override the public interest.

In recent months, allegations have been mounting that Big Tech companies, especially Meta, have been interfering in the Brazilian electoral process this year, aiming to undermine the reelection of President Lula (PT). This kind of accusation is not new. Over the past decade, a vast body of literature has exposed the mediating role played by digital platforms in foreign interference in elections around the world. These reports have also highlight the challenges of holding companies accountable for allowing these interference campaigns to be amplified.

At our research group, NetLab UFRJ, we have spent years investigating how major digital platforms shape public debate and influence people’s perceptions of reality, often outside the regulatory and normative frameworks in force in Brazil. Meta in particular has become fertile ground for disinformation and boosting fraudulent ads, which already account for 10% of its annual revenue.

Despite lawsuits and administrative actions brought by Brazilian authorities against Meta, complaints and requests from civil society for investigations, as well as reports published by the press, the company has shown neither the willingness nor the diligence needed to effectively fight this kind of content.

Given this troubling track record, NetLab UFRJ created the “Big Tech Observatory” during the 2026 election campaign period in order to monitor how Meta and other digital platforms performed in two key areas: algorithmic recommendation and political advertising. The initiative set out to examine whether these companies would comply with the current Brazilian legislation established by the Electoral Supreme Court (TSE). The results of the analyses, however, told a predictable story.

We found that, between July and September, Meta received approximately R$ 2 million (US$ 400,000) for running 1,613 ads placed from outside Brazil that aimed to either favor or harm candidates. All were paid for in foreign currencies and boosted by pages with declared locations in other countries. The amount invested in this advertising is equivalent to that spent on prominent campaigns, including the race for Presidency and other executive offices.

Brazilian electoral law expressly prohibits candidates from receiving cash or donations in-kind from abroad. This ban, however, did not prevent the ads from being displayed to Brazilian users of Meta’s platforms. According to the available information, not only the ads were allowed to circulate but they may have reached up to 171 million views in the country.

But the irregularities in advertising do not stop there. Brazilian electoral rules prohibit electoral advertising from 48 hours before the polls to 24 hours afterwards. However, our analyses of both rounds of the 2026 election identified hundreds of ads in favor or against specific candidates that circulated on Meta’s platforms with no apparent restrictions. The company even allowed fake profiles posing as official channels of the Electoral Supreme Court to boost disinformation about a supposed “digital vote” which stated that people would be allowed to cast their vote from home on the day of the first round — something which does not exist in the Brazilian electoral system.

In addition to these irregularities, Lula’s political campaign page was temporarily disabled by Meta without explanation, preventing it from running electoral ads. On September 23, his Worker´s Party (PT) reported they had been blocked from advertising on Meta’s platforms. In a statement released on October 16, the company rejected the accusations of election interference and attributed the temporary deactivation to an “incorrect anti-fraud review” carried out under an agreement with the federal government to fight fraud involving public programs.

The effectiveness of the company’s anti-fraud measures, however, is questionable: an analysis carried out by NetLab UFRJ identified hundreds of fraudulent ads involving federal public policies circulating before and after September 23, indicating that those same measures were not able to stop this kind of content from running during the same period.

Finally, we found signs of discriminatory practices in ad pricing. Based on data released by Meta, we estimate that for the first round Lula’s campaign may have paid between 33% and 43% more than his far right adversary Flávio Bolsonaro campaign to reach the same number of users on Meta’s platforms. Despite this substantial difference, limitations in the company’s transparency policies make it impossible to identify precisely which parameters and criteria are used to price ads and, consequently, to draw definitive conclusions about the mechanisms behind this disparity. Even so, studies conducted in other contexts, such as the United States, India and the Netherlands, also point to evidence of discriminatory pricing practices in the platform’s advertising.

Other complaints made during the elections add to this overall scenario of negligence and show that, despite being worth billions and their strategic position at the forefront of technological innovation, major digital platforms invest little in protecting their users. For example, this 2026 election in Brazil saw several controversies involving WhatsApp’s image generation service, powered by the Meta AI artificial intelligence. Users reported being able to generate content favorable to Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign without difficulty, whereas they were not getting the same results for Lula. Meanwhile, the documentary channel Revelando had videos criticizing Flávio Bolsonaro removed from its Instagram profiles shortly after they were posted, without clear justification from the company.

These episodes cast doubt on the consistency of Meta’s moderation and content control systems, exposing failures that call for greater investment and improvement. The situation is made worse by the absence of transparent criteria or guarantees of equal treatment in how ads are handled, how content is recommended, how advertising is priced, and how profiles and posts are moderated.

Big Tech companies have developed predatory business models, and they are currently joining forces with political forces committed to deregulation in Brazil. This is part of a strategy to protect their businesses and expand their room for maneuver.

Whether or not one side of the electoral race is being deliberately favored, it is indisputable that the major digital platforms continuously exercise the power to determine what gains visibility and what remains on the margins, with no transparency over their criteria and no mechanism for accountability. What is clear is that, for these platforms, defending their economic interests and maximizing their profits prevails above user rights, public interest, and democracy itself.
