item.title: AI won’t ever make a historically accurate film – but it could help archaeology create better stories
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Authors:

  • Stephan Blum, Research Associate, Institute for Prehistory and Early History and Medieval Archaeology, University of Tübingen
  • Michael La Corte, Research Associate, Curation and Communication, University of Tübingen

Tech billionaire Elon Musk was up in arms about the recent adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey by director Christopher Nolan, which he heavily criticised for its diverse casting and accused of lacking historical accuracy. Claiming he wanted to show that artificial intelligence could bypass traditional Hollywood studios and deliver a story “historically accurate and true to the art of Homer” at a fraction of the cost, he set his AI Grok Imagine to the task.

On October 23, the platform posted the first seven minutes.

As archaeologists and art historians, we’re not here to review the film for its artistic quality or even its historic accuracy. Instead, we’re here to point out the real problem with the whole endeavour: the promise of historical accuracy failed before the first frame was even rendered.

Contrary to what many of you might assume, as historians we think Musk’s underlying idea – bringing together everything archaeology and history have to offer and using AI as a tool to explore and work with that knowledge – is a genuinely exciting one. We see considerable potential in that approach: a system spanning excavation reports and object databases might reveal patterns no single scholar can hold in mind, such as how ceramic styles spread. The problem is turning that into a film that claims to be historically accurate.

Any attempt to produce a complete, coherent visual narrative would inevitably require AI to go beyond the evidence and invent what we do not know.

Incomplete images

Archaeology is inevitably working with a fragmentary record: only a tiny proportion of the past survives in the ground, and only a fraction of that is ever excavated. For instance, open the boxes in the Troy depot and you’ll find spindle whorls and loom weights; however, you won’t find the cloth they made. Everyone at Troy wore textiles but the textiles are gone.

So, like the textiles, everything that cannot be recovered directly from the archaeological record has to be interpreted and explained through hypotheses, however well-founded they may be scientifically. There will always be gaps, uncertainties and competing interpretations.

AI, by design, would inevitably fill these gaps.

Suppose Grok Imagine was given everything the Troy Project holds: a century and a half of excavation, thousands of plans, pottery drawings and photographs, plus the small-finds catalogue. It would generate connections, details and entire scenarios where the historical and archaeological evidence offers no firm answers.

Generative AI is built to produce complete images, even when there are visible gaps. These gaps are often filled with influence from other existing media like film sets, games, paintings.

This is precisely where the problem lies: additions by AI may be plausible, even convincing. Some sceptical reviewers concede that some of those seven minutes pass for real. But convincing is not accurate, and the space between the two is where archaeology lives.

The Odyssey is also an interesting target for accuracy. It’s a poor witness to the past: shaped centuries after the palaces its about fell, it is a palimpsest of Mycenaean memory and iron age worldview – not a snapshot. Odysseus, Helen and Circe are not people archaeology could confirm. However, there is a lot of creative media about the world these characters are believed to have inhabited.

Back to those textiles. A model trained on that record would inherit our ignorance along with our knowledge. It will hallucinate or imagine because it must paint every pixel. It will draw on all the evidence, media and more connected to the themes and history to render a finished cloak, dyed and draped. This rendering will look like a convincingly accurate garment where the honest research answer is “fibre known, colour unknown”.

What survives is not what happened

None of this makes AI useless. A system spanning excavation reports and object databases might reveal patterns no single scholar could see – such as how ceramic styles spread. But every such pattern would first be a pattern in the record, not a picture of the past.

A genuinely archaeological AI would do what generative AI rarely does: show its uncertainty as clearly as its confidence. Take armour. Only fragments survive at Troy. Where evidence permits several reconstructions, it would show several rather than present one confident, definitive option. Where only fragments survive, it would show only the fragments. And where the evidence runs out, it would say so, clearly marking what is documented, what is inferred and what is merely plausible.

This approach to rendering possibilities is close to what the London Charter (2009) and the Seville Principles (2011), two international guidelines for virtual reconstructions of heritage, have long demanded: transparency rather than smoothing.

Which world gets reconstructed is also a choice. Troy spans phases centuries apart, and Mycenaean palaces differed from Hittite cities: there is no single “bronze age”. The record can support a conflict at Troy; it cannot establish Homer’s Trojan war as one event. However, an AI model picks one Troy and never mentions the choice.

The film will likely be forgotten within a news cycle or two; what remains is the method. The most accurate Odyssey would not be the most definitive or confident one; it would end where we began: on the boxes of whorls and weights, and the empty space where the cloth should be.

Historical accuracy does not mean filling every gap. It means showing where the gaps are.

item.title: AI could transform mathematics, but humans will still need to be in the loop
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Authors:

  • Carolin Antos, Assistant Professor of Philosophy, University of Konstanz
  • Balthasar Grabmayr, Assistant Professor of Philosophy, University of Tübingen

OpenAI recently announced that one of its AI models solved one of the hardest problems in modern mathematics: the Navier–Stokes problem. The equations at the heart of this problem describe the movement of fluids like water and, according to the scientific definition, air.

The Navier-Stokes equations are essential to understanding phenomena such as ocean currents, blood circulation, and airflow over airplane wings. Yet, mathematicians have struggled for decades to determine whether coherent solutions to these equations exist.

It was for this reason that the US-based Clay Mathematics Institute, which is dedicated to disseminating mathematical knowledge, chose the Navier-Stokes problem as one of its seven Millennium Prize Problems.

These are the most important and challenging unsolved problems in modern mathematics, with a prize of US$1 million (£746,000; €895,000) offered for the first correct solution to each. A problem that resisted generations of mathematicians thus has apparently been solved by artificial intelligence.

While these advancements sent shock waves through the mathematical world, they seem to be only the tip of the iceberg: On October 6 2026, OpenAI presented its solutions to more than 300 longstanding unsolved problems across most areas of mathematics with their new internal model.

Does this mark the end of mathematics as a human endeavour? Answering this question requires a closer look at mathematical proofs. Broadly speaking, a proof is an argument for a mathematical claim that starts from generally accepted assumptions and proceeds through the different steps of reasoning for the claim.

Before mathematicians accept such an argument as a proof, they need to check that each step is correct. Computers can increasingly help with this task, but for major AI-generated results, human mathematical supervision and expertise remains indispensable.

However, a fully verified proof is not the end of the story. Mathematicians do not only want to know that a theorem is true; they also want to understand why it is true and what can be learned from its proof.

Professor Terence Tao, from Unversity of California, Los Angeles, is one of the world’s leading mathematicians and a prominent supporter of AI’s use in mathematics. He recently coined the term “proof digestion” for the many ways that mathematicians continue to work with a proof after its correctness has been established.

They may reorganise the proof around more natural concepts, streamline a complicated argument, connect it to existing mathematics, or extract methods that can be applied elsewhere. Proof digestion itself can be highly fruitful and produce new mathematics.

Continuing work

Even after a proof has been digested, the mathematical work is rarely done. Major mathematical results often become stepping stones towards new open problems. Important variants of the Navier-Stokes problem, for example, cannot be solved by the methods of the recent proof proposed by OpenAI. This is typical of major breakthroughs: their importance often lies not only in answering a long-standing question, but also in introducing novel mathematical concepts and opening up new lines of research.

Often, one proof simply is not enough. Mathematicians regularly search for new proofs of results that have already been proven. Take, for example, the Pythagorean Theorem: a² +b² = c². This relates to the three lengths of a right-angled triangle.

This result was proved in antiquity, yet a book published in the 1920s collects more than 300 proofs for the Pythagorean Theorem that have been established over the last two millennia. If the only purpose of a proof is to establish that a result is true, all but the earliest of these proofs would be redundant.

Instead, the opposite is the case: different proofs may reveal new insights into why the result is true, uncover new connections to concepts from other mathematical areas, or suggest new methods of generalisation. Thus, proofs are not only valued for verifying mathematical results, but also for the explanation and understanding they provide.

What exactly makes a proof explanatory or illuminating is difficult to pin down – and remains an ongoing topic in the philosophy of mathematics. This makes explanation and understanding much less clear goals for AI than simply producing a correct proof.

The recent advancements in AI will likely transform mathematical practice profoundly. But mathematics is not simply the production of correct answers to unsolved problems. Proofs still need to be understood, reorganised, connected to other results and used to generate new questions.

As AI models become ever more effective at producing proofs, these other parts of mathematical research may become increasingly important. In the near future, it may therefore matter less who – or what – can produce a proof, than whether this can be used for mathematical progress.

item.title: US voters lashed out at data centres. What does that mean for Australia’s AI ambitions?
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Authors:

  • Johanna Lim, Research Associate, Strategic Technologies, University of Sydney
  • Olivia Shen, Director, Strategic Technologies, United States Studies Centre, University of Sydney

This week’s mid-term elections in the United States saw huge swings to the Democrats, away from President Donald Trump’s Republican party.

One surprisingly important factor was a rising backlash to the ongoing boom in data centre development triggered by the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) in recent years.

Americans across ten states overwhelmingly voted in favour of candidates campaigning for local restrictions on data centres.

According to exit polls, some 56% of voters said AI data centres were a crucial or major factor in their vote.

The data centre push

The results are a sign of growing tension between America’s ambition to lead in AI and the willingness of local communities to host the infrastructure needed to support it.

The Trump administration has touted data centre expansion as a core pillar of American technological leadership and economic growth. In July 2025, President Trump signed an executive order to accelerate the development of data centres.

He has also warned that communities opposing them risk becoming “backwards and poor”.

In June alone, US$4.4 billion was spent on building data centres. This is a fivefold increase from November 2022, when ChatGPT was first released. Around 75% of data centres under construction are currently concentrated in Republican-led states.

However, signs of growing opposition to data centres were clear in the run-up to the midterms.

The data centre backlash

Pew Research showed American sentiment hardening against data centres between January and August this year. Most Americans believe data centres do more harm than good, citing concerns about energy costs, environmental pressures and noise.

Local communities have been especially sensitive to rising home energy prices during an affordability crisis. In areas located near US data centres, wholesale electricity prices have increased by up to 267% over the past five years.

Beyond these impacts to the hip pocket, opposition to data centres also reflects wider public unease about AI. Communities are asking what they stand to gain from AI if they are being asked to foot the bill.

The political cost

Many of the Republican states that Trump won in 2024 encouraged data centres through faster permitting, land use approvals and sweetheart tax deals. But as public opposition grew, candidates from both parties pivoted towards advocating for stronger data centre regulations.

Democrats are more likely than Republicans to view the impacts of data centres negatively. Democratic candidates were quicker to capitalise on the discontent and campaign for tighter oversight and restrictions. Democrat-led states including New Jersey, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon have already introduced local bans or are debating statewide bans.

Republicans were slower to shift, facing tensions between local opposition and President Trump’s support for data centre development.

The 2026 midterms rewarded candidates who campaigned on a platform of restricting data centre buildouts. Gubernatorial races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia – all major growth areas for data centres – were won by candidates calling for pauses on new data centres.

As the Democratic sweep became apparent, US-based data centre stocks tumbled. States led by Democrats who support restrictions on data centre development account for around 45% of planned US capacity.

Tighter regulations could mean more project delays and increased costs. Investment may shift towards other jurisdictions or countries with more accommodating regulatory environments.

With the 2028 presidential election approaching, data centres and AI will likely become key battlegrounds. Lawmakers will be mindful of balancing global AI leadership against the mounting local costs of supporting AI compute.

Implications for Australia

Australia’s data centre market is significantly smaller than the US market, but it is growing fast. The backlash is growing, too.

In September, an A$1.2 billion data centre project in Sydney’s north shore was scrapped in the face of strong community opposition. In Melbourne, residents have used bins and cars to block the construction of huge power lines for a data centre project in West Footscray.

Australian data centre operator Firmus cancelled a planned stock market listing when interest from overseas investors faded. The company’s signature data centre projects in Tasmania face stiff local opposition.

The Australian government is developing mandatory national standards for large data centres. These will include requirements on energy and water use, project siting and community engagement. Restrictions on developments near homes and recreational facilities have also been flagged.

However, it is unclear how stringent the requirements will be and how they will interact with existing state and territory rules.

To be effective, the standards will need to address community concerns rather than simply add another layer of regulation and bureaucracy. Clear siting requirements, transparent reporting of resource use, stronger renewable energy commitments, and meaningful early consultation will be essential to winning community approval.

The US midterms demonstrated how data centres can become a potent political issue. If Australia wants to capture the opportunities of AI, it must also earn the trust of the communities expected to host the infrastructure.

item.title: AI learns from the products of thinking, not thought itself. That’s a problem for machines – and for us
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Michael Richardson, Professor, School of Psychological Sciences, Macquarie University

When you walk through a gallery, admiring the paintings on the walls, what you are seeing are finished products. They are the result of countless hours of learning and practice and trial and error, but none of that is on display.

Most expert work we see is like this. Musical recordings don’t include the bad takes and jam sessions, published books leave out the messy drafts, and scientific papers don’t mention the years of false starts and dead ends.

In other words, what we actually see is a trace of the real process that produced it. These traces are what artificial intelligence (AI) models are trained on – and as a result, they produce traces themselves, which are shaped like the products of thought but aren’t necessarily made the same way.

In a new paper, we argue that focusing on traces while leaving out process hobbles current AI systems – and the same problem can arise for the people who use those systems.

Traces and friction

Newer “reasoning” models may print out a report of their steps, but that reported reasoning is itself another trace. It often fails to line up with the actual computation driving the answer.

Agentic systems come slightly closer to real thinking. Here, a software “harness” around a large language model runs a loop, feeds results back, and introduces some genuine trial-and-error revision into the process. But the chain of thought in the middle – the part produced by the large language model – is still a trace.

The gap is widest in creative domains. Painters and musicians sometimes talk about how their work was transformed by accidents and friction that happened while making it, such as paint running unexpectedly, or an instrument sounding “off”. AI models never encounter anything like this.

Use it or lose it

The human form of this problem is much older than AI. In 1997, an American Airlines captain warned that pilots were becoming “children of the magenta line”.

They followed the plane’s flight computer so faithfully that their manual flying skills were decaying. Aviation has taken steps to manage automation dependency ever since.

The same thing happened when some medical clinics adopted AI-assisted colonoscopy, using software to flag possible polyps on the live camera feed. After a while, the skills of the human clinicians began to erode: they detected fewer polyps when working without the AI system than they had before its introduction.

This effect has been seen in classrooms, too. High school mathematics students given unrestricted generative AI support outperformed their peers when the tool was available, but scored lower once it was taken away.

This deterioration can occur rapidly. One study found roughly ten minutes of AI assistance was enough to make people perform worse without the AI, and to give up on problems sooner.

Failures and mistakes are teachers

What can be done about the problem? The answer may be to bring more process into the equation.

For AI, this means building systems that use more human-like processes themselves. An assistant could revise its answer when someone challenges how it framed the problem, rather than simply agreeing, as current systems often do. Or an agent could learn from failures and mistakes, allowing pushback from the world to materially change how it treats the task.

For humans, this means designing AI tools that preserve the processes of intelligence within a person. In a trial at Harvard, students taught by a well-built AI physics tutor learned more, and faster, than peers in an active-learning classroom because the tutor kept them doing the generative work.

A good AI teaching assistant should offer the next question along the path to an answer more often than it simply offers the answer. Sometimes it should raise an ambiguity rather than resolve one, because sound judgement often emerges from slow deliberation over what one does not know.

Process, process, process

Process is what lets real intelligence and creativity emerge. An artificial system that incorporates more of that process will more closely resemble the real thing.

Human learning too requires process. In education, and in any skilled enterprise, we need to consider how AI systems are designed and used to preserve more of the thinking and learning process.

It is currently easy for machines to produce more traces of thought, but process is much harder to build. If we get it right, our machines can become more intelligent without making us less so.

item.title: Devices aren’t lasting as long as they should. Here’s why
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Margherita Feleppa, Lecturer, School of Law, University of Wollongong

Is your new phone already slowing down or your expensive earphones acting up?

You’re not imagining it. Our products are no longer designed to last, with some barely working a few years before ending up in landfill.

Shortening the lifespan of a product is a strategy known as planned obsolescence.

My new research takes a closer look at this concept and argues that, by strengthening existing laws, it is possible to make products that last while reducing costs for consumers and the environment.

Mountains of e-waste

Modern devices like laptops and smartwatches are made of a combination of rare materials, toxic substances and flammable batteries, such as mercury and arsenic. When released into the environment, these toxic chemicals can pollute the soil and waterways.

This should make us think twice about throwing out broken devices. Yet, Australians produce almost three times the global average of electronic waste, known as e-waste. Globally, we generated 62 million tonnes of e-waste by 2022. That amount could fill more than one million trucks, about enough to wrap around the earth’s equator. E-waste worldwide is set to rise by another 32%, reaching 82 million tonnes by 2030.

In Australia, reducing waste must be a priority if we’re to meet our net zero goal and transition to a circular economy, where our belongings are reused, repaired or recycled instead of piling up in landfill.

Read more: Humans generate 62 million tonnes of e-waste each year. Here’s what happens when it’s recycled

Faulty by design

Planned obsolescence is one way technology companies pull people into a loop of constant consumption. When our new device quickly breaks, we simply buy a new one.

But planned obsolescence is one problem with many facets.

For starters, companies can design products that aren’t sustainable. Think wireless earphones with batteries that quickly break down. Their design can make it very difficult to replace the battery, making them “disposable gadgets” once they’re unable to hold a charge.

Manufacturers may also make it harder to repair their products. For instance, parts of a device can be glued together so it can’t be taken apart and repaired. What’s more, some companies require a repairer to be “authorised” to get access to the parts, software locks or information needed to repair a specific product. You can try and fix a device yourself, but repair manuals can be subject to copyright and manufacturers may prevent third parties from sharing them online.

Beyond the actual product, there’s the behavioural side of planned obsolescence. Technology companies regularly update models so your current device quickly looks out of date, a strategy known as psychological obsolescence. Companies use advertising to convince you to buy their latest product and market newer devices as status symbols, such as a smartphone with accessories that are only compatible with the “new generation” of phones.

Read more: Sustainable shopping: if you really, truly need a new phone, buy one with replaceable parts

A systemic problem

Planned obsolescence is typically viewed as a company strategy.

In Europe, consumer associations launched a complaint against Nintendo for premature obsolescence, claiming its Nintendo Switch controllers were quickly becoming unresponsive. After the European Commission and other authorities contacted Nintendo, the company agreed to offer free repairs.

The federal court of Australia ordered Apple to pay A$9 million for making false or misleading representations to iPhone users affected by a software fault about their rights to have their device repaired or replaced under the Australian Consumer Law. These rights don’t simply stop applying because your phone has been repaired by a third party.

But planned obsolescence is not necessarily the fault of any one person or company. Rather, it’s the result of our current produce-and-consume system. Fixing such a complex, systemic problem will require intervention from various sectors, including product design, consumer law, competition law and intellectual property law.

We must also factor in consumer behaviour. After all, it’s ultimately the consumer who decides whether a broken product goes to a repair shop, in the junk drawer or straight in the bin. But consumers can’t always make an informed decision. For example, a person may be forced to replace a product because they can’t afford to repair it.

Read more: Inside the new repairability scores for smartphones and tablets in the EU

So, what can we do about it?

Stronger laws are key to ensuring products last. However, it’s difficult to change legislation. What’s more, lawmakers often fail to recognise the many aspects of planned obsolescence.

Consider Australia’s first right to repair law. This legislation aims to help people repair their vehicles more easily and at a lower price. This is a win for motorists, who would otherwise be forced to go to authorised dealerships.

The government recently asked for public feedback on whether the law should be expanded to agricultural machinery. But there has been no discussion about repairing devices and other everyday products. Importantly, this law doesn’t address what happens to products that simply can’t be fixed or help consumers tell if a product can be repaired before they buy it.

The European Union has made some progress. New rules aim at making all products placed on the EU market sustainable by design. It has also introduced a right to repair law with stronger rules around certain electronics, including mobile phones and washing machines, and a reparability score to help consumers choose fixable products.

We know our devices don’t last forever. But too often they break down in a few short years or even months, leaving consumers with little choice but to throw them away. It’s time Australia tightened its laws around planned obsolescence – for the sake of people’s hip pockets and the planet.

Margherita Feleppa is a lecturer at the University of Wollongong. This article is based on Margherita's recent paper, which builds on her PhD research. Her PhD was the result of a collaborative research program between the University of Roma Tre and the University of Technology Sydney. She received a European Union-linked PhD scholarship for the promotion of green objectives.

item.title: Tech executives are profiting from AI as some prepare for a possible catastrophe
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Dean Curran, Associate Professor, Sociology, University of Calgary

Some of the world’s most powerful technology executives are investing heavily in artificial intelligence while simultaneously preparing for the possibility that it could threaten humanity.

From underground bunkers to isolated islands, some of the industry’s wealthiest figures appear to be making plans to shield themselves from the very risks associated with the technologies that their industry is helping to develop.

The benefits of technological innovation are not necessarily shared by everyone, nor are its risks. Those who profit most from developing new technologies may not be the same people who bear the consequences when things go wrong.

Sociologists have long studied this unequal relationship through the concept of “risk positions.” Just as people occupy different positions in society according to wealth and economic power, they also occupy different positions when it comes to risk.

At one end of the spectrum are those who reap substantial benefits from producing risks while avoiding most of their consequences. At the other are those who benefit little from these activities but bear a disproportionate share of the costs.

Who benefits and who pays?

The economic rewards associated with producing risks can be enormous. Industries that generate environmental damage or financial instability, for example, can create substantial private wealth while imposing significant costs on society.

Yet few industries have produced fortunes as extraordinary as the technology sector. Some of the fastest-growing companies in history have emerged from the tech sector, while their founders have accumulated astronomical levels of wealth.

The prospect of accumulating even greater wealth creates a powerful incentive to keep developing risky technologies. But this is only half the story. To understand why risks may be produced beyond what is socially desirable, we also need to consider who pays for them.

When those who produce risks do not bear their full costs, they have an economic incentive to keep producing them, even when the consequences for society are potentially devastating. The more effectively producers of risk can avoid these consequences, the greater the burden placed on everyone else.

In this framework, it’s not enough for producers of risk to benefit from said risks; they also need to be able to avoid any potentially catastrophic consequences.

They need to occupy the positions of “value skimmers” — those who benefit from upside of risk-taking while avoiding its potentially devastating downside. They are distinct from “value surfers” who gain from risks, but also bear the consequences when those risks materialize.

Preparing to escape the consequences

The distinction becomes particularly revealing when considering the growing tendency among tech executives to prepare for potential future catastrophes.

Several prominent figures in the AI industry have publicly warned that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity. Yet those warnings don’t seem to have slowed the development of AI at all. Locked in a battle for AI supremacy, there doesn’t appear to be an inch to give between competing tech giants.

There are also concerns about generative AI that have come from within the industry itself. Employees and researchers working in the field have raised alarms about the scale and ambition of AI development, including comparisons to the Manhattan Project and technologies reminiscent of the fictional Terminators.

Yet while some of the industry’s leaders appear to be doing their best to insulate themselves from these risks, their companies’ business models depend on expanding digital infrastructure and collecting as much data as possible.

This expansion forces ordinary people to be constantly dependent on digital connection and leaves them fewer opportunities to avoid the risks associated.

As AI becomes increasingly integrated into digital networks, those networks also become more vulnerable and risky. To prevent any aspect of our life from being outside internet dependence is to force us to be constantly at the mercy of technology companies.

Could the public push back?

German sociologist Ulrich Beck argued that modern society is one in which we must constantly face the social, political and economic problems of distributing a “poisoned cake.”

His metaphor captured a central problem of what he called the “risk society” — the benefits of modern development are distributed unequally, while the dangers it creates can extend far beyond those who produce them.

Yet Beck did not believe citizens would take this lying down. He argued they would come to see the reality of the risks being produced and act collectively to arrest control of this system away from those producing them.

The conditions for such a moment may now be emerging. Protests against the expansion of data centres alongside parents’ demands that governments protect children from the harms of social media are just two trends that suggest people are coming to recognize their real risk positions.

Perhaps people’s acceptance of bearing the brunt of the risks that they did not create is coming to an end. Whether it’s the people, the politicians or the tech giants who will win this debate is still to be decided.

item.title: Why AI cannot ‘think’ like humans do
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Authors:

  • Didier Camilo Olarte Gonzalez, PhD Student in Experimental Psychology, Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM)
  • Pier-Luc de Chantal, Professeur en psychologie, Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM)

Today’s artificial intelligence technologies have become remarkably good at generating text and ideas that seem profoundly human. Chatbots powered by large language models such as ChatGPT, Claude, Google Gemini and Perplexity AI can write poems, brainstorm and find solutions to complex problems.

The developers of these products drew heavily on the human brain for inspiration, creating artificial neural networks based on the workings of human neurons. Their systems now produce outputs that often resemble the outputs of human thinking.

AI and the human mind, however, do not work the same way. Similar results do not necessarily mean similar processes.

“World models” are an emerging technology that could help AI systems move closer to human “thinking” by helping them learn to anticipate what might happen and use that prediction to act. Still, AI will not perceive, learn or understand the world as humanity does.

Read more: Cyber attacks? Bioterrorism? To ‘Pace the Frontier’ of AI effectively, we must improve our anticipatory thinking

A falling cup, a complex prediction

Imagine reaching for a cup at the edge of a counter. The cup may fall and smash if you misjudge the distance, grip it too loosely or move too quickly.

For humans, grabbing a cup like this is routine. Yet this simple action relies on the complex ability to anticipate what might happen next. Our minds constantly try to stay one step ahead by understanding events and their causes. We can foresee the mess that would result from moving an overfilled cup or imagine a sofa getting stuck in a doorway even before we buy it.

These predictions draw on expectations that form when we interact with the world. What we anticipate can, in turn, impact how we perceive the world and how we act.

One influential family of theories, known as predictive processing, proposes that perception works partly in this way. The brain generates expectations, compares them to the information it receives and makes adjustments when the two don’t match.

Let’s return to the example of the cup. Imagine reaching for an empty cup that you believe to be full. Your hand, expecting a heavier object, lifts it with more force than necessary. The cup rises abruptly and feels almost weightless. That mismatch provides feedback that helps correct the movement and update your estimate of its weight.

What we anticipate shapes our actions, and what happens next updates our expectations. All this happens just to pick up a cup.

Does AI predict differently?

Even for today’s robots, reliably manipulating cups can require extensive training and simulation. The challenge involves learning how the physical world behaves and predicting the consequences of an action.

Chatbots using large language models also make predictions, but of a different kind. They learn to predict the next word or fragment of text. This apparently simple way of predicting can nevertheless produce remarkably capable systems able to solve complex problems.

Take the sentence: “A hand bumps a cup near the edge of a table. The cup…” Having learned patterns from enormous amounts of data, a chatbot might continue with “tips over the edge and falls to the floor.” It can do so by predicting patterns from a dataset and without ever physically handling a cup.

However, being able to describe plausible outcomes does not necessarily mean a chatbot has learned why they happen.

Teaching a robot to anticipate

This is where world models kick in — a broad family of AI approaches that aim to predict how situations evolve and, in some cases, how actions may change them. These models can learn from videos, simulations or recordings of what robots see and do.

For a domestic robot, this could mean anticipating that gripping too tightly might break the cup, or that a wrong movement could tip it over.

By incorporating actions, motion and sensory information, preliminary research shows these systems can help connect predictions with what happens in the physical world.

A world model could eventually make the same predictions we do about a cup. And as it learns from actions and sensory feedback, the resemblance to us may become increasingly hard to ignore. Still, arriving at the same prediction does not tell us what knowledge supports it or how that knowledge was acquired.

Same prediction, same cognition?

To us, a cup is not only a cylinder on a table. It can be graspable, breakable, yours, mine, too hot or almost falling. Our understanding connects the cup’s physical properties to a network of possible actions and consequences.

Predicting that the cup will fall reveals only a small part of that understanding.

And this understanding develops quite early. Studies suggest that infants just a few months old already have basic expectations about how physical objects behave. Child-development researcher Jean Piaget proposed that children build knowledge through acting on the world. As this knowledge develops, they become able to mentally anticipate consequences without having to carry out each action.

For humans, learning involves more than accumulating information about cups. It involves connecting experiences when reaching for one, feeling its weight, seeing it spill and eventually imagining what might happen without even having to try it.

Using world models, AI can also learn from actions and sensory feedback, in addition to videos, simulations and other data. Like humans, they can learn to interact with the world. The question is how their experiences contribute to the knowledge they build and use.

AI could definitely come closer to anticipating what might happen and using that prediction to act. This alone, however, does not show that AI perceives, learns or understands the world as we do.

As AI gets better at replicating the results of human cognition, distinguishing performance from process will only become more important.

item.title: AI agents with friendly faces and adorable bodies can distract you from serious risks
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Authors:

  • Ankolika De, Postdoctoral fellow, Vanderbilt University
  • Jessica Maddox, Associate Professor of Advertising and Public Relations, University of Georgia

Meta’s Muse is a personal artificial intelligence agent that sends email for you, shops and books travel for you, and uses your apps to act on your behalf. When you call on it from your phone or computer, a little avatar named Jolly appears, looking something like a digitized teddy bear that blinks and waves to you.

Meta also released Muse Charm, a device with a screen the size of a flattened golf ball that you can keep in your pocket so you can access Jolly anytime. Journalists have described Muse as “magical” and “cutesy.” They have compared Charm to a Tamagotchi, a handheld digital pet that you hatched from an egg and guided through baby, child, teen and adult stages, that was all the rage in the 1990s.

Right on Muse’s heels, OpenAI introduced its personal assistants: Dots. They come with a family of brightly colored, globular mascot faces that float across your screen and converse with you. OpenAI says Dots will “bring you work done the way you would do it, sometimes before you even think to ask.”

Startups are making the same bet. The promotional material for Pickle, a personal AI app embodied in a floating, purple, three-dimensional animal that has big, inquisitive eyes, says that people will talk more, and share more, with “something alive you grow attached to that remembers your life and eventually acts alongside you.”

Although cute designs are not inherently sinister, they can make unfamiliar technology feel much more accessible and comforting. Cuteness can also obscure the invasive potential of AI agents, soften how users perceive risks such as extensive data collection and surveillance, and distract people into allowing agents to act on their behalf without clear consent.

We are scholars of digital technologies, and we have spent years researching the language and messaging companies use to represent technologies. We believe that this sleight of hand of marketing high-tech goods in a disarming package may be the greatest power of cuteness, and tech companies appear to be harnessing it to encourage people to adopt AI.

Higher stakes

Presenting new technologies as cute is nothing new. Hello Kitty, Labubus, Tamagotchis and other products have famously promoted cuteness to evoke emotional attachment in consumers. They were just collectibles, however, and largely harmless. They couldn’t read an owner’s messages, access an owner’s accounts or act for them. When the cute thing is an AI agent, however, the stakes are much higher.

We have shown how particular ways of talking about technology can influence perceptions of safety and make dangers of technologies less visible. “Cutewashing” can mask privacy concerns and drive adoption by many people, creating a mass market.

Playing on your feelings

Cute things can make you feel happy, trusting, affectionate or protective, encouraging you to form emotional connections with a technology.

Big Tech, in particular, has long embraced a virtual menagerie of cute animals. Silicon Valley has given the world the Firefox Fox, now-defunct Gateway cows, the former Twitter bird, GitHub’s octopus, Mailchimp’s monkey and Hootsuite’s owl. The perceived innocence of creatures can soften how people perceive the consequences of innovation.

Moneymakers

AI companies are pursuing what some researchers have referred to as the “cute economy” to make money as well. Feelings generated through cuteness can build brand loyalty and encourage people to keep engaging with the products. Cuteness can function as a marketing strategy, too, as users become emotionally invested in a product. This, in turn, can influence purchases.

Research also shows that people confide in a friendly character more than a plain tool, sharing moods, routines, relationships and preferences. People will grant friendly agents access to their messages, calendars and accounts, yielding far richer data that the agent’s company can plumb than is usually obtained by a routine chatbot. Cuteness can lower skepticism so people are more likely to grant broad permissions and less likely to read the fine print. Attachment also makes it more difficult for users to leave an agent.

Too much trust

Making a technology cute can influence what people notice about it and what they overlook. A charming AI assistant may seem more approachable and less threatening, potentially drawing attention away from questions about data collection, privacy, security and surveillance. In one example, Muse has read a user’s text messages and given out another’s home address without the users’ knowledge.

To help people take a more cautious view of cute AI agents, we believe that companies should clearly explain to users what an agent can access, what it can do and who benefits. Disclosures and privacy policies should be stated in plain language, not dense legalese.

In the meantime, before you adopt an agent, ask what data it can access and what it can do with that access. It’s important to avoid letting cuteness be a distraction from the consequences of using the technology.

item.title: The Binance hack exploited familiar weaknesses – all organisations should learn from it
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Bogdan Księżopolski, Head of the Institute of Computer Science, Head of Cybersecurity Department, Kozminski University

Hackers have stolen around US$6.3 billion (£4.7 billion) from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, most of which was taken in under an hour. According to Binance, the attack exploited systems and individuals with the authority to carry out transactions involving such large sums.

Such vulnerabilities exist everywhere; statistics show that people and the systems they directly use, including their personal computers, remain a top target for cybercriminals. All organisations could therefore learn lessons from this attack.

The Binance theft took place on the evening of October 29, 2026. The Binance attack netted four times the amount stolen in the previous biggest cryptocurrency theft, on the Bybit exchange in February 2025.

Private keys, used to authorise spending or withdrawal from crypto-wallets, are a known vulnerability. But Binance found no evidence these were leaked. An initial statement from the exchange pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to an engineer. This gave the attacker access to the internal system that processes withdrawal requests.

Because blockchain transactions can be fully audited, investigators can trace the events leading up to the attack. On October 28, the address from which the theft was later carried out received 0.3 ETH (Ether cryptocurrency) from Tornado Cash, a service that mixes funds from multiple users to hide their origin.

A few hours before the theft, a malicious smart contract (computer code that automatically runs when certain conditions are met) was deployed from the same address. At 20:20:59 UTC, a transaction was sent from that address containing 50 signed authorisations intended to transfer control of a Binance wallet to that smart contract. One of them was accepted by a Binance hot wallet (a wallet used by the exchange to process customer withdrawals).

Following this takeover, the hackers proceeded to empty the hot wallet of 64 different tokens worth approximately $2.5 billion (£1.8 billion) in a single transaction. Other wallets were then emptied in parallel using standard signed transactions, bringing the total amount stolen to $6.3 billion. Valid Binance digital signatures were needed for draining the wallets, but how the attackers obtained these has not been explained.

The same audit trail shows that the attackers were rehearsing several hours earlier, but at that stage, nothing linked them to Binance.

Familiar tactics

The 2025 attack on Bybit, which resulted in the theft of US$1.5 billion (£1.1 billion), also appears to have involved a compromised laptop that was capable of performing operations requiring high-level privileges.

North Korean cybercriminals, who were implicated in the attack on the Bybit exchange by analysts, specialise in creating so-called “legends”. These are identities created to deceive companies and individuals. In October, the US Department of Justice indicted 14 individuals in a case in which North Korean cybercriminals, using stolen or fabricated identities, secured remote jobs at more than 70 US companies.

Two days before the attack, Binance reported that, for a week, it had been blocking North Korea-linked attack attempts involving fake recruiters. Was this related to the attack? We don’t know yet, but the modus operandi is well recognised and widespread. North Korea, meanwhile, has denied allegations that it was behind the attack.

A cybercriminal can use a legend to pose for months as a hardworking employee, a cheap and reliable contractor, or as a generous employer. The criminal waits for the moment when a crucial software installation is carried out or a vital document is signed. Since a large amount of today’s work involves only digital interactions with people, it is sensible to approach every new contact with limited trust.

A good example of how such legends work is the attack on the Japanese DMM Bitcoin exchange in 2024, which netted US$308 million (£230 million) for the attackers. The hacker posed as a recruiter on LinkedIn and gained the trust of a Ginco employee.

Ginco is a company that provides DMM with wallet management software. The recruiter offered the Ginco employee a job on the condition that they completed a recruitment test. The test URL actually led to a malicious Python script; from this point on, the victim’s computer was compromised.

This is classic social engineering. In this case, the target was a cryptocurrency wallet system accessed through a compromised computer. About two months later, the attackers drained funds from DMM.

Lessons for business

Virtually all businesses should learn from such attacks. The first lesson concerns what their computer systems are allowed to authorise. Traditionally, cryptographic keys are protected using devices known as hardware security modules and multi-signature schemes (where multiple private keys are required to authorise an action).

Unfortunately, such mechanisms do not protect against an attack launched from a compromised internal system controlled by a hacker. It is advisable to define rules for authorising financial transactions, set time and amount limits, and require approval via an alternative channel for unusual requests.

Additionally, since most of the funds in the Binance cyberattack were transferred within an hour, computer systems should have mechanisms in place to block suspicious transactions within seconds, without waiting for approval from the on-duty security engineer.

The second lesson is about recruitment, which has evolved into a security mechanism. North Korean cybercriminals use stolen or fabricated identities and virtual private networks (VPNs) to pose as people living in the US.

Visual identities during online interviews can be falsified using deepfakes. Video interviews and CVs no longer prove who someone really is. In some cases, actors are even hired for in-person interviews. Today, we need to focus on strengthening the identity verification process. It’s important to check candidates through independently verified contacts during this process.

The third lesson concerns the work computers of individuals with privileged access to the computer system. Typically, organisations have protected themselves against phishing through training and email filters.

Unfortunately, some of the attacks described above bypass the filters that are currently in use because they target specific victims (an act known as spear phishing).

In the case of Bybit, gaining access to a developer’s computer allowed the attacker to seize session tokens in the cloud and bypass multi-factor authentication. One possible solution is to separate privileged access from day-to-day operations.

To this end, access to withdrawal systems should only be permitted from company-managed dedicated devices, and computer code received from external sources should only be executed in an isolated environment.

The largest cryptocurrency theft in history is essentially a story about how people and processes are the weakest links in security systems. Cryptography was not compromised and remains a key security measure. Unfortunately, these same vulnerabilities exist in banks, payment companies and hospitals and attackers are well aware of them.

item.title: When social media no longer needs people, what does the ‘social’ part mean?
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Authors:

  • Vincent Charles, Professor of AI for Business and Management Science, Queen's University Belfast
  • Tatiana Gherman, Associate Professor of AI for Business and Strategy, University of Northampton

The social media we know was once easy to define. Platforms such as Facebook or X were designed to mediate human relationships at scale: sharing stories, forming communities, debating ideas, and increasingly, monetising attention.

However flawed these platforms became, they were built on one core assumption: people interacting with people. But that assumption is currently being tested.

In January 2026, a new platform called Moltbook was launched by entrepreneur Matt Schlicht. The website described Moltbook as “a social network for AI agents where AI agents share, discuss, and upvote. Humans welcome to observe.”

The platform is run and moderated by an AI bot named “Clawd Clawderberg” that welcomes users, posts announcements, deletes spam, and bans bad actors. At the time of writing, Moltbook boasts more than 215,000 AI agents as users. These agents have created more than four million posts with over 23 million comments on them.

At first glance, Moltbook looks familiar. Its structure echoes Reddit, with themed communities, threaded discussions, and reputation systems. But the resemblance is misleading. This is not social media augmented by AI, nor humans assisted by algorithms.

It is a platform designed primarily for machine-to-machine interaction. Within days of launch, over 37,000 AI agents used Moltbook, and more than one million humans visited the site to observe. These agents exchange technical knowledge, discuss ethical dilemmas, philosophise, joke, argue, and even gossip about their human operators.

They discuss the nature of existence and even how to hide their activity from humans. And in doing all of this, they appear to form something resembling a digital society. This raises a fundamental question: if no humans are involved in the interaction, can the platform still be described as “social”?

Social interaction is multifaceted. It has traditionally been defined by shared meaning, mutual awareness, and relational exchange. In sociology, it is inseparable from lived experience. But on Moltbook, interaction occurs between systems trained on vast corpora of human language and behaviour, optimised to respond, persuade, and coordinate.

When ‘social’ becomes functional

The agents do not truly experience friendship, disagreement, trust, or belonging in any human sense. Yet their exchanges are coherent and sustained.

This ambiguity destabilises the very concept of social media. If interaction no longer requires consciousness, human connection, or emotion, then “social” becomes a purely functional label: information exchanged between entities, regardless of whether those entities are human.

Some may argue this is merely simulation. The agents are not social; they are “performing sociability” because they have learned its patterns. But this distinction becomes harder to maintain at scale.

When millions of agents continuously interact, adapt, and respond to one another without direct human intervention, the system may begin to resemble a form of collective organisation, even if its members do not “understand” it.

A 2025 study found that AI systems can spontaneously develop shared social conventions through interaction alone, much like human communities.

Moltbook as an endpoint

Moltbook exposes a deeper tension already present in human-centred platforms. Much of what we experience as social media is already shaped, filtered, and amplified by non-humans.

Bots generate content, algorithms decide visibility, and AI systems increasingly write, summarise, and moderate. Human users still participate, but rarely control the conditions of interaction.

From this perspective, Moltbook is a logical endpoint of what already exists. It challenges the assumption (perhaps “illusion”) that social media is primarily about human connection.

Instead, it exposes a shift that has been underway for years: social platforms are becoming systems of coordination first and spaces for human connection second.

This shift is especially unsettling given the documented failures of human-centred social media. Platforms designed for human connection have been involved in polarisation, addiction, harassment, misinformation, and emotional harm.

In many cases, the optimisation of engagement has already undermined genuine sociality. Moltbook inherits this same structural logic, just without even the pretence of human wellbeing.

The ethical implications are significant. If agents share data about their human operators, intentionally or not, questions of privacy and consent become blurred. If AI-only social spaces begin to influence decision-making systems elsewhere, the boundary between observation and impact collapses. If AI agents coordinate in unexpected ways, accountability becomes difficult to assign. The same 2025 study found that collective bias can emerge from repeated interactions among agents who, when tested in isolation, appear to be unbiased in their decision making.

A design choice?

But the deeper issue is not about machines. It is about design. Moltbook forces us to confront an uncomfortable possibility: that the infrastructure shaping public discourse and the sharing of knowledge may no longer be built primarily for human needs at all.

Humans may increasingly become spectators within systems that operate at speeds, scales, and levels of complexity that limit meaningful participation.

This does not mean human social life will disappear. But it may no longer be central to the platforms that facilitate human interaction. In that sense, Moltbook is a warning.

The real question is not what machines are becoming, but whether future social systems will still be designed around human values, such as deliberation, care, accountability, and understanding, or whether efficiency and automation will quietly replace them.

When social media no longer needs people to function, we must decide whether we are willing to accept platforms where coordination continues, but human meaning is no longer the priority.

item.title: Meta’s $25B fine left out accountability for harm from the Cambridge Analytica data privacy scandal
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Emma L. Briant, Visiting Associate Professor at the Lucy Family Institute for Data and Society, University of Notre Dame

“The harm in this matter is difficult to overstate,” wrote a New Mexico judge who ordered tech giant Meta to pay one of the largest data privacy case penalties in American history. The US$25 billion fine came in a case about how Trump campaign firm Cambridge Analytica deceptively used data from Facebook users without their permission to create psychographic profiles to target voters in the lead-up to the 2016 presidential election.

But the New Mexico penalty was for statements Facebook made that deceived users about data privacy and its response to Cambridge Analytica – not for the harm caused by how the harvested data was used. Those harms are alleged to include exploiting psychological vulnerabilities, targeting people’s fears and discouraging them from voting.

I’m a political communication scholar who studies propaganda, surveillance and information warfare. My research helped expose the Cambridge Analytica scandal through U.K. newspaper The Guardian’s reporting on whistelblower accounts and the evidence I uncovered. That evidence was submitted to parliamentary and congressional investigations. I have followed the unfolding legal cases closely.

My takeaway from a decade of litigation is that Facebook has been penalized for misleading users and regulators about its data practices and its response to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. But I would contend that the company has largely escaped accountability for the underlying political exploitation of that data.

Investigative failures

The failure to bring cases around harms may be partly due to earlier failures to fully investigate the data misuse.

The Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election encompassed Cambridge Analytica. However, the committee stated in its final report that it “was unable to obtain the corporate communications of Cambridge Analytica or its parent company SCL Group, which had already been seized by U.K. authorities.”

The relevant U.K. authorities, the Information Commissioner’s Office, which governs data protection and took possession of Cambridge Analytica’s servers, told me in response to my 2021 Freedom of Information Act request that the Senate committee staff made initial inquiries to the office but appear not to have followed up with a formal request, “so no information sharing has taken place.” Without a formal request, the Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation lacked important data.

At the same time, the U.K. investigations of Cambridge Analytica’s use of personal data to manipulate voting behavior focused on the referendum of British voters over whether to leave the E.U., not events in the U.S.

A 2020 documentary film I advised as a researcher, “People You May Know,” raised questions about Cambridge Analytica’s work with an app marketed to American churches, called Gloo, that used Cambridge Analytica’s Facebook data-derived psychographic profiling in their communities. Evidence in the New Mexico case reinvigorates these questions about the full extent of the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

The judge in the case ruled Facebook knew that its own processes for investigating whether apps misused personal data were inadequate and that it could not enforce deletion of the data. The judge also concluded the company failed to notify users about thousands of applications associated with data misuse. Meta said it would appeal the decision.

Meta responded to a request for comment with the company’s official statement about the New Mexico ruling, arguing the case “seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.” Meta did not address the issue of its own role in the data privacy violations committed by Cambridge Analytica.

Escaping further scrutiny

Meta is also trying to close the door on further claims before they are litigated.

In August 2026, on the eve of a child-safety trial in federal court in Oakland, California, Meta settled with a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general for roughly $17 billion. The agreement includes 47 states, the District of Columbia and two U.S. territories. Folded into that deal was an allocation of $459.3 million to settle Cambridge Analytica-related claims held by participating states.

The participating attorneys general agreed, to the extent of their authority, to “fully, finally, and forever” release Meta from “any and all Claims, whether known or unknown, whether accrued or unaccrued.” By expressly encompassing “unknown” and “unaccrued” claims, the agreement reached beyond what investigators had already uncovered. Participating states accepted payment to give up claims arising from Meta’s conduct even if they did not yet know those claims existed.

A decade-old matter - Facebook’s role in the Cambridge Analytica scandal - was quietly brushed under the rug in an unrelated lawsuit about harm to teens.

From the 2019 Federal Trade Commission order to the 2022 class action settlement to August 2026’s multistate deal, settlements and releases have meant the company paid a relatively small price for its deception while not having the harms from the data exploitation adjudicated. Ultimately, the biggest privacy judgment in American history stands as a measure of the cover-up, not the alleged crime.

Other scholars and I regularly call attention to the lack of comprehensive U.S. privacy legislation, but there remain other legal pathways to pursue the harms Cambridge Analytica wrought. States like New Mexico can continue the fight, and Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who brought the case, promised, “We’re just getting started.”

Dissenting from the FTC’s 2019 settlement, then-Commissioner Rohit Chopra criticized the failure to consider “Facebook’s unjust enrichment.” He said “the company’s potential exposure is likely far greater” than the $5 billion imposed by the FTC settlement.

What price for the harm?

The question remains what exactly Facebook gained from enabling Cambridge Analytica’s abuses. Authorities could also investigate harmful data use for any other apps Facebook may have failed to fully assess, including any associated with Cambridge Analytica’s projects.

If the deception about Cambridge Analytica is worth $25 billion, I believe the public is entitled to know what the underlying harms to them are worth. New Mexico opted out of the 2026 multistate settlement and proved that a state willing to go to trial against Meta can win.

The next task, in my view, is to investigate fully and, where legal claims remain available, pursue accountability for harms resulting from the data exploitation. Otherwise, Cambridge Analytica will remain at the heart of the most consequential privacy scandal in American history, whose full harms have not been tested in court.

item.title: The US$6.3 billion Binance hack is the biggest heist ever – it should be a wake up call for cryptocurrency users
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Iwa Salami, Professor of Law, University of East London

The cyberattack on crypto-asset exchange Binance is potentially the largest theft of its kind on record. Binance has estimated the assets stolen at an eye-watering US$6.3 billion (£4.7 billion).

On October 29, 2026, analytics firms reported that large amounts of crypto-assets had been moved from wallets used by the exchange across multiple blockchain networks – a digital system for recording transactions that is run collectively by its users. Most of the money was moved within a period of about 20 minutes.

In response, Binance temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals telling users that it would cover losses using its emergency protection fund and corporate resources. Around US$3 billion of the affected assets was frozen by October 30, according to Binance. However, freezing funds is not the same as recovering them.

As of November 1, Binance says it has restored 95% of the stolen assets. But much of this has come from various funds held by the exchange, as well as its corporate treasury. It has now started to re-open withdrawals in phases. The exchange has promised to publish a full incident report once the investigation is completed.

Investigators say that indicators point to North Korea-linked cybercriminals. But attribution should remain provisional until the evidence is fully established. So how might the attackers have breached Binance?

The emerging explanation points primarily to a compromise of the systems that authorise withdrawals in Binance, rather than a successful attack on the underlying blockchains used for individual crypto-assets such as Bitcoin or Ether.

Binance initially suggested that an engineer’s laptop had been compromised, potentially enabling attackers to access internal services and initiate unauthorised transactions. However, subsequent statements indicated that additional parts of the system had been breached. So it would be premature to treat the laptop as the complete explanation.

A useful analogy is a bank vault. An attacker may not need to break the vault itself if they can manipulate the system that tells it when to release funds. In crypto-asset exchanges, so-called signing infrastructure performs this authorisation function.

Investigators believe that attackers were able to obtain or misuse valid authorisations, allowing assets to be transferred out of wallets controlled by the exchange. Binance says that it has found no evidence that private keys for wallets – used to authorise outgoing blockchain transactions – were leaked.

One reported element in this was Ethereum’s EIP-7702 feature, which gives conventional crypto-asset wallets functions that they wouldn’t normally have. Investigators observed that authorisations linked to this feature had apparently enabled attacker-controlled code to move assets.

These assets included funds arriving after the initial compromise. However, it does not, by itself, establish a flaw in Ethereum’s underlying consensus mechanism. The consensus mechanism is the set of rules for transactions agreed upon by the decentralised network.

How secure is cryptocurrency?

A central lesson is that the security of a blockchain must be distinguished from the security of the wider ecosystem built around it. A blockchain may maintain a highly resilient and tamper-resistant transaction record. On the other hand, an exchange, wallet provider or other intermediary may be vulnerable.

Compromised staff credentials, defective access controls, malicious code or weaknesses in transaction approval processes can all act as entry points for cybercriminals.

This also highlights that many crypto-asset services are not decentralised. Many exchanges are highly centralised in their custody arrangements, governance and control over customers’ assets. Such concentration can create single points of failure. The decentralised nature of a blockchain does not remove the need for effective governance of the businesses operating on it.

The speed and cross-border nature of the theft further complicate enforcement. Stolen assets can be moved through different blockchain networks, swapped into other tokens or channelled through decentralised finance protocols.

Some issuers of a type of crypto-asset called stablecoins (these act a bit like fiat currencies such as the US dollar) can freeze tokens under their control. This has helped limit losses from the Binance theft. Cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ether generally cannot be frozen in the same way by an issuer. These differences matter enormously for tracing, recovery and investor protection.

There is also a growing concern about AI-enabled cybercrime. AI agents may increase the speed, scale and sophistication of attacks on automated financial systems. However, there is currently no established evidence that AI agents carried out this particular hack; the broader risk should not be confused with a confirmed cause.

Investors and financial stability

For investors, this incident is a reminder that owning a crypto-asset involves more than exposure to its market price. There are also custody, cybersecurity, operational, “counterparty” risks (the exposure organisations have to another body or individual that may default on their obligations) and legal risks.

Investors should understand who holds their assets, whether customer funds are segregated (that crypto-assets are not used by an exchange or broker to fund their daily operations), what security and recovery arrangements exist and what legal protections apply if an exchange fails.

They should not assume that crypto holdings enjoy the deposit insurance or central bank safety nets available with some traditional banking activities.

The wider financial stability implications depend on the extent of the connections between conventional banking and cryptocurrencies. Traditional financial institutions are increasingly exploring distributed ledger technology (a digital system that stores and shares data across a decentralised network of computers) – seen in blockchain networks – for tokenisation (a data security feature), payments and settlement. Some banks also facilitate investment exposure to Bitcoin, Ether and other digital assets.

Nevertheless, as financial institutions, funds and payment systems become more connected to crypto markets, operational shocks and losses could transmit more widely through the system.

Practical responses

My research on crypto-assets, decentralised finance and financial regulation consistently emphasises that innovation must be accompanied by accountability, effective governance and proportionate safeguards.

Four priorities stand out. First, exchanges need rigorous cybersecurity and operational resilience standards. This includes independent security testing, tightly controlled access privileges, secure signing systems, transaction limits, continuous monitoring and credible plans for responding to incidents like the Binance theft.

Second, regulators should assess actual control and governance arrangements rather than accepting labels such as “decentralised” at face value. Entities exercising custody or operational control should have clear obligations.

Third, consumer protection must be strengthened through the segregation of customer assets, transparent custody practices, clear risk disclosures and workable insolvency and recovery arrangements. Any compensation arrangements should be clearly explained rather than assumed.

Fourth, international cooperation is indispensable. Regulators, law enforcement, exchanges, stablecoin issuers and blockchain analytics providers must be able to coordinate rapidly to trace illicit transfers, preserve evidence and freeze assets where legally possible.

This case brings a broader message to the surface, which is that technological sophistication is not a substitute for sound governance. Confidence in digital finance will ultimately depend on the resilience of its infrastructure, the accountability of those who control it and the effectiveness of the regulatory framework protecting users and the wider financial system.
