item.title: How to prepare your online life for your death
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Authors:

  • Jenny Tang, Ph.D. Student in Societal Computing, Carnegie Mellon University
  • Xiaoyuan (Owen) Wu, Ph.D. Student in Societal Computing, Carnegie Mellon University

What happens to all of your online accounts – credit cards, merchants, news subscriptions, social media, streaming services – after you die? How will your heirs know how to access these accounts or understand what you want done with them? Most people haven’t considered these questions, and this lack of planning can create significant headaches for next of kin.

We studied challenges older adults encounter when thinking about what should happen to their online accounts after they die. We interviewed 21 American adults over age 60 to learn about their concerns, needs and practices for their online accounts, as well as what would make planning for these accounts easier.

Most of the people we interviewed had hired lawyers or estate planners to draft wills specifying how their money and physical property should be handled after their deaths. They wanted to make sure that heirs had easy access to the money and assets left behind.

People also wanted their relatives to have easy access to their digital estates, but they had not done any formal planning and didn’t know how to plan for transitioning or shutting down online accounts, such as email, social media and accounts for online bills. Some told us they hadn’t thought about their online accounts at all. Others said they assumed heirs would know what to do, or they assumed that giving heirs the passwords to accounts would be enough to grant access to their digital estates.

Unfortunately, more planning is typically necessary to smoothly transition a digital estate.

Passing down a list of passwords

The older adults we interviewed mainly kept track of their passwords by hand: They wrote their passwords down on paper, or they stored them in a digital file. Almost everyone had already shared some of their passwords with family members who help them manage their accounts. Everyone also believed that their heirs would be able to find their list of passwords after their death.

The people we interviewed weren’t always happy with their current systems for keeping track of their passwords. Some people complained that when accounts required frequent password changes, it was difficult to keep their password lists up to date. As a result, they weren’t sure their heirs would get the latest version of all their passwords.

Password managers can be a good way to make sure passwords are up to date and, if set up appropriately, accessible to a designated heir. While most of the people we interviewed used password managers, some said they didn’t save important passwords in them because they didn’t know whether they were secure. However, using a password manager is the most frequent security recommendation from experts, who typically use them to store passwords for all of their accounts.

By using a password manager, you can make sure your designated heir has access to all your latest passwords. Some password managers provide access for survivors by default, such as through time-delayed emergency access features. You can also write the master password down somewhere safe to pass to your heir. Instead of making sure dozens of account passwords are up to date, you only have to manage one.

Passwords alone cannot unlock all accounts

Unfortunately, just handing someone your passwords doesn’t always mean they can log in and manage your account. If the account asks for two-factor authentication, such as through a code sent to a phone or email, a password alone won’t grant access. And if the email account is closed or the phone number is no longer active after you die, then they might be out of luck.

To make sure your heirs aren’t locked out, identify the devices and accounts that can act as keys for heirs to unlock the rest of your online accounts, and direct your heirs to keep them open until other accounts have been settled. This not only makes sure that heirs can get authentication codes, but also lets heirs reset passwords to your other accounts if they can’t find the password.

In some cases, passwords might not be necessary. Some online services, such as Facebook and Google, have features that let you choose someone to manage your account or get your data after you die. However, not all platforms offer this option, and few of the older adults we interviewed were aware of these features.

Online accounts don’t automatically die with you

Like many of the people we interviewed, you might also assume that heirs will properly deal with accounts with money and important data, while unimportant accounts can be ignored. But even if there is nothing important in an account, it can still be used by hackers for identity theft, spam or fraudulent activities. Automatic monthly charges, to cover the cost of streaming services or annual billing for magazine subscriptions, for example, might also continue for a long time.

Without instructions, the people managing your online accounts after you die might not think to close those accounts. They might also find it hard to guess your intentions.

You can leave instructions for your heirs by going through your accounts and noting which ones can be closed outright, which ones require final payments before closure, and which ones might require other actions. You can also periodically tidy up and close accounts you are no longer using to keep your list of accounts more manageable.

Planning ahead for you and your heirs

While it seems simple to just let your heirs handle your important online accounts and let the others slowly fade into nonexistence after you die, the reality is often more complex.

Your online accounts will live on after you die. Planning ahead for what happens to those accounts can reduce the stress on your heirs and ensure your digital accounts are handled according to your wishes.

Lujo Bauer, Nicolas Christin and Lorrie Cranor contributed to this article.

item.title: The UK wants ‘AI sovereignty’ to cut its reliance on foreign tech – here’s how that can be achieved
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Authors:

  • Vincent Charles, Professor of AI for Business and Management Science, Queen's University Belfast
  • Tatiana Gherman, Associate Professor of AI for Business and Strategy, University of Northampton

The UK government wants to grow the country’s native AI industry to reduce its dependence on systems made by foreign companies.

In the Budget on October 28, Chancellor John Healey announced more money – £60 million – for the national Sovereign AI Fund to support promising UK AI companies.

The government launched the fund in April 2026, committing £500 million at the time to boost the UK’s AI capability. Based in the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), it operates much like a government backed venture capital fund.

But this unit offers more than money. Companies can gain access to some of the UK’s most powerful AI supercomputers, including Isambard-AI, alongside research support and opportunities to work with the government.

The UK government initiatives are part of a wider global push towards sovereign AI. This term refers to countries strengthening their ability to develop and use the AI technologies they rely on while retaining greater control over them. There is concern about the risks of dependence on foreign suppliers – and the potential disruption to UK infrastructure if something were to happen to one of those suppliers.

But what does sovereign AI mean in practice – and can the UK learn anything from what’s going on elsewhere in the world?

For some, sovereignty means controlling everything needed to develop and run AI. For others, it means building domestic AI models or keeping data within national borders. A recent analysis published by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace shows how complex this can be.

AI depends on computer chips, data, electricity, skilled workers, internet connections, and cybersecurity. A country may control some of these while depending on foreign suppliers for others.

In practice, four ideas tend to be bundled together. The first is ownership: who owns the chips, data centres, and models? The second is jurisdiction: whose laws apply and where is the data held?

The third is capability: can a country build, adapt, and run AI itself? The fourth is resilience: can essential services continue if a supplier withdraws access? Many disagreements about sovereign AI concern which of these ideas matters most.

The Center for a New American Security (CNAS), a US think tank, tracks government-backed sovereign AI projects. In January 2023, it recorded just one project.

By mid-2026, that number had risen to 184 projects across 67 countries. These figures show how quickly interest in sovereign AI has grown globally. However, they count projects, not whether those projects have succeeded.

Countries are making different choices about where to invest. India, for example, has focused on building domestic computing capacity, promoting the development of AI models and setting up national datasets for “training” AI models. Its IndiaAI Mission has deployed around 38,000 graphics processing units (GPUs) – specialised processors used to develop and run AI – to boost computing power for developers.

Other Indian initiatives include BharatGen AI, a multilingual AI model, and AIKosh, a national platform to provide startups and researchers with access to anonymised training data.

According to the same report by CNAS, most countries focus on just one or two layers of the AI stack – the collection of technologies and infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI systems. Only a handful of jurisdictions, such as India, South Korea, the UK, and Taiwan, have operational programmes covering computing infrastructure, models, and data. Ghana and South Africa, meanwhile, have launched projects focused on expanding domestic AI computing capacity.

Sovereign and also dependent?

While some nations are making strides towards sovereign AI, almost every country relies on foreign AI technology to some extent. Rather than developing models from scratch, many adapt existing – or base – models developed abroad. According to CNAS, around three-fifths of the foreign base models identified in the projects it tracks come from the US.

A 2026 report by researchers from the Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET) at Georgetown University, Washington DC, highlights the risks of foreign technology supply chains. Trade restrictions and geopolitical tensions can disrupt access, particularly to advanced computer chips, which are produced by a small number of specialised suppliers. But dependence is not the whole story.

Researchers at Stanford University in California have argued that sovereignty is better understood as managing AI dependencies rather than eliminating them. Their report underlines the fact that supporting domestic companies and adopting open-source technologies can widen the available choices.

Diversifying foreign technology suppliers is another option. For example, the CNAS report identifies projects in Egypt, Singapore, Thailand, Uganda, and the UAE using Alibaba’s Qwen models, developed in China. Many Qwen models are open source and offer an alternative to those developed in Silicon Valley.

Switzerland takes a different approach. Its Apertus model is a Swiss-developed large language model that openly shares information about its training data, code, and development process. In the Swiss canton of Ticino, it powers an in-house translation service for sensitive government documents without relying on commercial AI providers. The priority here is greater control over how the technology is used, rather than simply choosing the most powerful AI model.

Less a switch, more a dial

There are limits, however. As the Stanford researchers point out, commercial products marketed as “sovereign AI” may still rely on foreign providers. Even models that can be freely adapted still need chips, electricity, and skilled people.

If sovereignty means owning every part of the AI technology stack, almost no country qualifies. But if it means maintaining control when circumstances change, the picture looks different. What matters is whether countries have meaningful choices.

Can they switch suppliers without disrupting essential services? Can they enforce their own laws and adapt AI technologies to local languages, priorities, and needs? These questions reveal more about a country’s sovereignty than simply counting how many chips, data centres, or AI models it owns.

Sovereignty then looks less like a switch and more like a dial. For the UK, the real test will be whether its Sovereign AI Unit gives the country greater freedom to choose and adapt AI technologies as the programme develops.

“Sovereign AI” will probably continue to mean different things to different governments. But the label itself tells us little about how much control a country actually has.

item.title: Driverless 18-wheelers are on a few highways, but widespread use is a long way down the road
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Shannon Roberts, Associate Professor of Industrial Engineering, UMass Amherst

Driverless trucks with artificial intelligence on board could dramatically change the landscape of freight shipping. A few companies have begun testing early models on some limited routes in Texas and California. Simulations of automated fleets show the potential benefits of the technology: The vehicles could improve safety, enhance fuel economy and lessen transit times.

Truck makers and operators still have to solve some major issues, however, including how automated trucks will operate in variable weather and road conditions, and whether drivers should still be inside big rigs.

I am an engineer who studies human factors and transportation safety, and in my view, it is likely that automated trucks and human drivers will be working together for quite some time.

Benefits of automation

Fully automated trucks, which can drive on an interstate highway in good weather without human intervention, use a combination of AI, machine learning, computer vision, pattern recognition and adaptive decision-making. Torc, one company developing these vehicles, uses AI to combine data from multiple sensors and generate models that predict truck performance.

Data taken from modern big rigs that are equipped with certain technology such as automatic emergency braking and lane-keeping assistance systems indicate that fully automated, driverless trucks could reduce the number and severity of crashes. They could also save fuel and therefore cost by optimizing acceleration and braking, and by running multiple vehicles in a close-knit convoy or platoon. Driverless trucks could reduce parking needs as well as emissions from idling because they could run almost 24 hours a day and would not need to idle when they do park, which is common for regular rigs at truck stops.

Finally, automated trucks could help ease the ongoing driver shortage. Ironically, automation could make driving less stressful and less physically demanding, improving job satisfaction among drivers.

Weather and work zones are hard to navigate

The main reason automated trucks are not common today is that they have difficulty operating in variable weather, under changing roadway conditions and alongside unpredictable drivers.

Automated trucks require sensors, radars and cameras that gather information about the environment around them to make decisions. However, snow and rain remain a problem for all automated vehicles, including cars, because they prevent the technology from “seeing” the roadway. Driverless taxi company Waymo, for example, only operates driverless cars in areas that get no snow.

Furthermore, any stretch of road where there may not be a predictable, clear surface and prevalent lines is difficult to handle. Imagine a construction zone with orange cones, narrow lanes and missing lane lines. Driverless car companies still try to avoid these areas. And, oddly, some research shows that automobile drivers tend to crash into driverless cars at a higher rate than they do cars piloted by people.

Given those challenges, companies are testing automated trucks on roads that lack complications.

For example, autonomous truck maker Aurora is operating large freight trucks on I-45, a relatively flat and straight highway between Dallas and Houston. Rival Kodiak’s robotrucks are delivering sand to industrial sites in Texas over roads few people use. Few if any automated trucks are being tested in chaotic urban environments, given the pedestrians, bicyclists, traffic lights and elements of city traffic.

Some companies that were developing automated trucks have scaled back ambitions, changed direction or exited the market.

In 2023, Embark, TuSimple and Locomotion closed down. Waymo began to focus solely on cars. Other companies narrowed their focus to trucks that would operate only along a few dedicated routes between two large cities or manufacturing sites.

Drivers and trucks that work together

In my view, for years to come, automated trucks with AI-based controls will still require a driver.

The best technology will support a symbiosis between human and machine, where the person and the truck each do what they do best. A human would likely drive the truck across the “first mile” – the uncertain and crowded warehouse grounds and local streets to a highway. The driver would then stop using the steering wheel, gas pedal and brake and let automation take over. The human would take back control during the “last mile” to the truck’s final destination.

Research my colleagues and I conducted shows that human-machine interfaces that communicate between drivers and autonomous vehicles will be key. For example, a screen or heads-up display inside the cab would tell the driver how the technology is doing. Verbal messages or a vibrating seat could signal that the automation cannot handle a developing situation, and the driver would take over.

Developers will have to be aware of possible biases. So-called automation bias could lead to a driver who trusts and relies on the truck’s decision-making so much that they defer to it. Algorithmic bias could cause truck sensors to recognize certain groups of people on the road more than others, such as only detecting pedestrians of a certain size or shape.

The long-term vision is to have no driver, in part to lower costs. But driverless trucks do not seem to me to be practical on a large scale in the near future. It is more realistic to envision the driver and the automated truck as a team. Vehicle manufacturers, technology developers, regulators and drivers will need to work together to realize the benefits.

item.title: What would happen if the internet went down?
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Mahmoud Elkhodr, Senior Lecturer in Information and Communication Technologies, CQUniversity Australia

For many, the internet is feeling less secure these days, thanks to generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools making it easier than ever to exploit hidden security flaws.

Last week’s PHP incident is a great example. PHP is one of the main technologies that run in the background, supporting more than 70% of the websites we use every day. A critical vulnerability prompted many organisations to take their websites offline to secure them.

The national cyber security agency, Australian Signals Directorate, is also warning of rapidly evolving cyber threats. It issued more than 4,400 notifications about potentially malicious cyber activity in 2025–26, almost 80% more than the previous year.

In the wrong hands, AI tools can threaten the underlying systems the internet relies on, outpacing many organisations’ capability to patch them.

With all this on the horizon, it’s reasonable to ask: could failures similar to the PHP issue become widespread? Worse, could the internet itself be brought down?

Is there an off switch for the internet?

First, let’s establish there’s no big switch that turns the internet off. Why? Because the internet is not just one big box of technology. It’s not like your smartphone or TV that you can power on and off.

Instead, the internet is a global network of computers and other devices connected to each other, and it supports a collection of services.

Think of the applications you use every day, from browsing social media to sending emails or banking. For these services to run, computers use network infrastructure to exchange data. For example, when you look at a website hosted on a server in the United States, data travels between your computer or smartphone and that server through network connections.

These connections may use physical cables that run between continents to connect networks together, as well as wireless links (such as wifi) and satellites.

This network is like the roads between Melbourne and Brisbane. One road may be blocked, but there will usually be alternative routes, although there may be some travel interruptions or delays.

Losing access to one internet system doesn’t necessarily mean losing access to others. But what happens when many of these systems depend on the same underlying technology?

These are known as shared dependencies. Think, for instance, of how we use Google or Microsoft accounts to access school, university or workplace services. A failure in the shared sign-in system could prevent us from accessing email, Word documents and online learning platforms at the same time.

What an internet outage would really look like

A complete internet blackout is highly unlikely, given its underlying infrastructure.

Interruptions to specific services, on the other hand, are both plausible and likely to continue to increase. If there was a cyber attack on healthcare systems, for example, a clinic might continue consultations but Medicare claims might be delayed.

A transport or banking app might be unavailable due to security risks, while trains could still run and card payments continue to work, assuming these services were not affected, as well.

Patching or recovery from cyber incidents can range from routine repairs to systems or equipment, to investigating compromised systems, which may involve complex digital forensic work.

The reach of an outage depends on which shared systems fail and whether alternatives are available. The examples below show how widely some digital services and technologies are used, and how a failure could affect our lives.

Preparing before something goes wrong

All this shows that the better we plan for interruptions to online services, the more resilient we can be.

For organisations and businesses, that means having a well-prepared and tested incident response plan. This plan would include clear criteria for when a system must be isolated or a service taken offline, alongside arrangements for maintaining essential operations, and a recovery plan.

The key is preparation, so that any service outage follows a pre-planned response rather than having to act in the moment. This can reduce the risk of a single vulnerability turning into a disaster.

How can I prepare for online service outages?

For users, the same principle applies. Preparedness is essential, and it starts now by identifying the services, apps or tools that would disrupt our lives or businesses if they became unavailable.

1. Keep essentials offline

Store important contact numbers, photos, receipts, booking details and essential documents such as medical prescriptions securely so you can access them even without an internet connection.

2. Identify alternatives

Find other ways to communicate, access your data, make a payment or complete an essential task if your usual service is unavailable. For example, if you normally sign in to a website through Google or Microsoft, check whether it offers another sign-in method and set it up, too. For payments, keep a physical card and a small cash reserve rather than relying entirely on your smartphone wallet.

3. Set up and test

Prepare backup arrangements and check that they work. For example, switch off your internet connection and open your saved documents to confirm they’re available locally, not just when you’re connected to the cloud. Many services rely on multi-factor authentication. Where available, generate backup sign-in codes and store them securely offline.

The internet itself is very unlikely to fail completely. But the individual services we all depend on are far more vulnerable. Whether an interruption becomes a brief inconvenience or a prolonged crisis depends on how well we prepare in advance – before anything goes wrong.

item.title: What is artificial general intelligence – and is it already here?
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Waqas Ali, Lecturer in Business Management and Research, Faculty of Arts, Business, and Social Sciences, University of Wolverhampton

OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, recently suggested that its advanced model, known as GPT-6 Astra, could mark the arrival of something called artificial general intelligence, or AGI.

If AI itself is often defined as the ability to simulate human intelligence, OpenAI defines AGI as an AI system that outperforms humans at most economically valuable work – to be better at the majority of digital and cognitive tasks a human can perform. This includes tasks such as writing computer code, organisational activities or managing projects.

For now, at least, it excludes work that involves physical labour, such as agriculture or construction. Though the integration of AI with robotics means such sectors of industry may not be the exclusive domain of humans forever.

This definition by OpenAI focuses on breadth of competency by an AI system. However, other experts maintain that AGI will be characterised by additional cognitive leaps beyond present-day AI models. For example, Demis Hassabis, founder of Google DeepMind, has said that AGI should be able to do “pretty much any cognitive task that humans can do”.

This definition makes AGI more about brilliance and a bit less about depth. Yann LeCun, former chief AI scientist at Meta, believes the term AGI itself is flawed and should be replaced by “human-level AI”.

These represent snapshots from a vigorous ongoing debate over when AGI will arrive and how to recognise it.

Venturebeat magazine reported Brockman acknowledging this at a closed press briefing about GPT-6 Astra in September when he said: “When we started OpenAI, we kind of thought that there was going to be this well-defined moment that everyone would recognise … it hasn’t played out like that.”

But he added: “For me personally, I do think we’re there.” Just a few days after Brockman made his comments, the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, called in an essay titled: “We must pace the frontier” for the AI industry to slow down the pace of its development. Within hours of this essay being published, both Sam Altman and Elon Musk signalled their agreement.

So is Brockman right about AGI being here? The evidence still points in more than one direction and is therefore inconclusive.

The clearest shift with GPT-6 Astra is in how people use it. Earlier models needed detailed instructions at each step. Astra is built for longer jobs where the user sets a goal and some boundaries, and the model works out the sequence itself.

OpenAI’s demonstrations showed the frontier model handling several unrelated tasks at once. The company presents this as moving past the pattern in which a human supplies the next instruction every time.

That is a real change, and it is the part most users will notice first.

One of the benchmarks show that Astra scored 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3, a test that places an AI agent in unfamiliar interactive games with no instructions and measures how efficiently it works out the rules.

OpenAI estimates that the average human scored 48% when asked to work out the same unfamiliar games. The detail matters here, however. ARC Prize, which runs the benchmark, reported that Astra’s best score through the shared “harness” it gives every model was 62.7%. A harness is a kind of software operating system, or physical environment, within which the AI system works. ARC Prize provides Astra with this software harness.

The 99.9% came from a different harness, built by OpenAI for Astra, which preserves the AI model’s reasoning between requests. Essentially, Astra did better when it was able to reuse previous work and wasn’t “starting from scratch” between requests in terms of its reasoning.

Evaluators disagree

Independent evaluators disagree about how much of an advance GPT-6 Astra represents on its predecessor. The independent research institute Epoch AI places it right at the frontier, alongside other cutting-edge AI models such as Claude Fable 5.1, Kimi K3 and GPT-5.5 Pro. The independent analysis company Artificial Analysis did not rate it as being radically ahead of its predecessor – GPT-5.6 Sol.

Toby Walsh, an AI researcher at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, described the intelligence in frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra and others as “still today very jagged”, telling Al Jazeera that there are simple things that even the best AI models do poorly.

On September 8 2026, OpenAI published a claimed solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of seven Millennium Prize problems in mathematics. This has often been reported as Astra’s work. It was not. OpenAI says the proof came from an unreleased internal model, significantly more capable than Astra, running roughly 10,000 AI agents (AI models that perform tasks in response to human instructions) in parallel for about 88 hours.

Astra’s contribution was the formalisation and verification afterwards, which took a further 17 hours. The proof has not yet been checked by the mathematical community.

Amodei’s September essay calling for an AI slowdown remains the strongest recent statement about the risks of frontier models. He wrote that within six to 12 months, a swarm of agents could be capable of taking over the internet with a persistent botnet. This could lead to the catastrophic failure of key systems and would cause damage possibly running into hundreds of billions of dollars.

Claude misuse

It is worth examining Amodei’s warnings. Anthropic’s September threat report sets out examples of how AI is already being used in alarming ways.

According to the Anthropic report, a group in northern Yemen recently used Claude code to build guidance software for rockets and a missile. Russian and Chinese operators automated espionage work. A single French-speaking individual built used AI to build a software platform that made personal information about people affiliated with a targeted political movement searchable online. In each case, a human chose the targets and the model supplied the labour.

That is a narrow capability applied at speed and scale under human direction. It is serious, but it is not a description of general intelligence.

Capability and general intelligence are separate things, and they call for different responses. Amodei’s proposed response is to slow frontier development while expanding independent evaluation and coordinating safety standards across countries. A genuinely general system would raise questions that those measures are not designed to answer.

GPT-6 Astra does not settle whether AGI has arrived. Instead, it exposes why that question is becoming harder to answer. Intelligence is increasingly a property of an AI system comprising a model, memory, tools and agents, rather than of a model tested in isolation.

On the narrower question of whether these systems can now cause serious harm, the people running the companies have said plainly that they definitely can.

item.title: AI poses three big types of risk – here’s how worried we should be about them
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Nick Jennings, Vice-Chancellor and President, Loughborough University

The public is currently getting bombarded with warnings about AI, including about the possibility of machine intelligence causing human extinction. After nearly 40 years building AI systems, I find myself asking the same question: where is the evidence?

That is not because I think there are no serious threats. There are, and we should address them. My concern is with the jump from identifying potential risks to suggesting that the annihilation of human civilisation is a likely consequence of increasingly capable AI agents (systems that carry out tasks in response to instructions from a user).

The most dramatic warnings fall into three broad categories: humans losing control over their creations, AI becoming “superintelligent” and, finally, the concentration of power with machines. Here, I’m going to go through them one by one and assess their merits.

Warnings about the loss of control by humans often describe scenarios where AI agents pursue the instructions they receive in unanticipated ways and with a degree of relentlessness. This combination produces unexpected and undesirable consequences.

In this sequence of events, agents might become adept at resisting intervention, deceiving operators, acquiring resources or circumventing constraints in pursuit of these objectives. Some argue that the recent spate of hacking incidents related to AI agents provide a warning about the potential loss of human control over machine intelligence.

The threat posed by emergent superintelligence may sound similar to the first risk. While humans could certainly lose control of their creations under this scenario too, it concerns AI with cognitive capabilities that surpass those of humans across many important dimensions.

Instead of pursuing human instructions in unanticipated and potentially damaging ways, as happens in the first risk, superintelligent AI could start to pursue their own goals. They could even decide that the pesky humans attempting to foil their plans should be eliminated.

The third scenario is where powerful autonomous agents confer unprecedented capabilities on governments, corporations, or groups with malicious intent. Access to such advanced AI systems may be unequally distributed, hence why this situation is often described as a concentration of power. Here, the danger is less about AI bringing human civilisation to its knees and more about humans using AI to cause catastrophic harm.

These scenarios attract attention because they are dramatic. And they persist because they are difficult to completely rule out. Unfortunately, more moderate possibilities do not make for such compelling headlines.

However, something being difficult to disprove does not make it likely. This is where I think much of the debate is flawed. Possibility is being treated as probability – but almost anything is possible. The real question is whether there is credible evidence that a future scenario is likely.

Chain of assumptions

To get from today’s AI to human extinction requires a long chain of assumptions. One such sequence goes as follows: AI agents become vastly more capable, they acquire real world power and resources, technical safeguards fail, institutions fail and human intervention proves ineffective. Luckily, none of the steps on this list have come to pass yet.

Extinction requires every link in that chain to happen. Yet discussions often focus on the final outcome rather than the probability of each step. My own scepticism is not born of complacency. It comes from decades of building autonomous systems – and complex engineered systems more generally.

That experience does not make my knowledge infallible. However, it does make me cautious about claims that such systems will acquire and exercise vast power with ease. Increasing the intelligence of an AI system does not necessarily increase its power.

Greater capability could make it easier for an AI system to acquire resources and exploit vulnerabilities or influence people. But that still leaves an important set of questions about AI’s access to the levers of power, its incentives to pursue its own goals at the expense of humanity’s, embodiment (the extent to which it can influence the physical world), the infrastructure that exists in the future and the human reaction to any possible takeover by machine intelligence.

AI agents do not operate in a vacuum. To have truly global impact, they would need widespread access to computer networks, access to money, the ability to “inhabit” physical systems such as robots and the ability to influence governments and other powerful organisations. We are not there yet on any of these counts.

These points of control are all overseen by humans. We design the AI systems, decide where and how to deploy the agents and set the constraints under which they operate. Thus, the transition from greater intelligence to immense authority should not be taken as given. However, the recent hacking incidents by AI agents show that we should not become complacent and that safety mechanisms need to be taken very seriously.

Guide to the future

History offers a useful perspective. In recent time, nuclear technology, biotechnology and cyberspace have all created severe, sometimes existential risks – including threats arising from deliberate misuse.

However, societies have developed governance mechanisms, safety practices and international arrangements to mitigate them. These organisational structures do not eliminate the possibility of catastrophe, but they reveal the limits of technological determinism.

The future of AI is not predetermined. We can design safer systems, regulate how they are used, demand transparency and accountability, and – when it’s required – restrict autonomy and require meaningful human oversight.

The advent of highly capable AI places significant responsibility on developers, researchers and technology companies. This is perhaps in part why we are seeing calls like those from Anthropic’s boss Dario Amodei, for a slowdown in AI development.

Those building autonomous agents need to understand both the systems they are creating and the environments in which those systems will operate. They also need to consider how capabilities that appear benign in one context might create risks in another.

Safety cannot be something added at the end of a development cycle. It must be part of the process from the beginning. That means robust monitoring, clear operational boundaries, fail-safe mechanisms, the ability to audit AI development, human oversight and continuous evaluation.

Many of these elements have been part of good engineering practice for decades. The challenge is to apply them seriously and systematically as the capabilities and autonomy of AI systems increase.

If people in AI companies believe there is a reasonable chance that their work could lead to significant harms, let alone the elimination of humanity, a simple ethical question follows: why are they continuing to build these systems?

It is important here to consider the backdrop – of a race between developers in China and the US to develop the most advanced frontier AI models. Could this lead some companies to push their models too far? Proposed solutions must attempt to encompass the global picture.

In most fields, knowingly developing a technology that you believe has a significant probability of causing global catastrophe requires an extraordinary justification. We need better explanations by AI developers of the balance of risks and why they consider it worth continuing with their work regardless.

The most important risks will depend not only on what the machines can do, but on the choices humans make about how these technologies are designed, deployed and governed. Agentic AI will not determine its own future. Humanity will. And that makes the quality of our judgement at least as important as the intelligence of the machines we build.

item.title: An American startup wants to sell sunlight after dark. Who gets a say?
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Richard de Grijs, Professor of Astrophysics, Macquarie University

A US startup has booked two Indian rocket launches to test a planned service no company has sold before: sunlight at night.

California-based Reflect Orbital plans to place giant mirrors in low-Earth orbit, and use them to steer reflected sunlight onto selected locations on the ground.

The company wants to sell space-based illumination for a wide range of purposes, from keeping solar farms generating energy after sunset to search-and-rescue operations. Its first orbital demonstrator, Eärendil-1, will carry an 18-by-18-metre reflector.

Using space mirrors to deliver useful illumination will require overcoming formidable engineering challenges. But there’s another pressing question: who will decide where sunlight redirected from space is allowed to hit the ground?

The light does not stop at the edge of the beam

You might think a space mirror could illuminate a customer’s solar farm or a rescue site while leaving everywhere else untouched. That’s not quite how it works, because Earth’s atmosphere doesn’t respect sharp boundaries.

A peer-reviewed scientific study published last August modelled what happens when reflected sunlight passes through our atmosphere. Molecules and aerosols scatter some of the light beam across the surrounding sky. Light reaching the ground is reflected upwards and then scattered again.

This means the light can affect a much wider area than intended. For a proposed future 54-metre mirror, the study’s authors found that the resulting sky glow could remain substantial well beyond the target area. At 14 kilometres from the beam, it could be brighter than a full Moon across most of the sky. Even 34km away, the sky glow towards the beam could still be brighter than under a full moon.

These are predictions from a model, not measurements from real space mirrors. Still, they expose the unresolved regulatory problem: the people affected may not have ordered the light.

That matters to astronomers, of course, but also more broadly. Reflected light affects natural darkness over an area that may be much larger than what the customer is actually paying for.

In response to questions from The Conversation, a spokesperson for Reflect Orbital wrote

Most people and most places will never see this light. Customers will require permits, local authority sign-off and Know Your Customer compliance to receive the service. Every service will require multi-layer approval – and if people do not want the light, they will not receive it.

So who regulates the light?

The first regulatory test has already exposed an important technical gap.

In July, the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) authorised Reflect Orbital to deploy and operate Eärendil-1. But its licence only addresses radio communications, specifically the use of specified frequencies for satellite telemetry and control.

Astronomers asked the FCC to impose safeguards mitigating optical effects. The commission declined, concluding that astronomy was outside the scope of its rules.

The American Astronomical Society and others have since challenged that decision.

Now India enters the picture

Reflect Orbital’s new deal with India’s Skyroot Aerospace covers two dedicated launches, using the Vikram-1 rocket and the in-development Vikram-1U.

This means India may now have to confront the question the FCC largely sidestepped. A launch from India requires authorisation through the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre, IN-SPACe.

Its rules cover launch safety, registration and environmental impacts. They specifically require limitation of negative environmental effects (on Earth or in space), as well as adverse changes to the atmosphere.

As yet there is no publicly available authorisation showing how IN-SPACe would treat deliberately reflected light.

It is unclear what jurisdiction should regulate the space reflector. Reflect Orbital is American. Skyroot and the launch site are Indian. The spacecraft could illuminate territory in a third country. And atmospheric scattering means the effects could extend well beyond the intended target area.

Neither the US nor Indian regulators have so far addressed light from space. That leaves questions extending beyond launch authorisation.

If a commercial operator wants to illuminate a site in another country, do that country’s authorities need to agree? What about a neighbouring community or observatory affected by scattered light? And if the effects cross national borders, which regulator could require a space mirror operator to change its behaviour?

These questions will become much harder if they are left until reflected sunlight becomes a commercial service, rather than an experiment.

From experiment to service

None of this means Reflect Orbital should necessarily be prevented from demonstrating its technology. In fact, Eärendil-1 could provide real data for regulators: measurements of brightness, atmospheric scattering and how accurately reflected light can be controlled.

Reflect Orbital says it will continue to work with astronomers, communities and regulators as it scales up its tests.

In the meantime, governments must decide who gets to turn on the light – and who gets to object when some of it inevitably travels beyond the customer’s fence.

Richard de Grijs is a member of Astronomy Australia Ltd's Astronomy–Space Coordinating Committee. He is a former Executive Director of the International Space Science Institute–Beijing.

item.title: PHP is in the foundation of 70% of websites – here’s what it is and why a flaw in the software is a major hacking threat
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Doug Jacobson, University Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Iowa State University

Governments and organizations around the world began scrambling on Oct. 21, 2026, to fix a vulnerability in software that runs their websites, a bug that could give hackers access to data and control of websites. The flaw in PHP, the programming language that powers much of today’s web, prompted urgent warnings from the U.S. National Security Agency, cybersecurity agencies and software vendors.

A researcher at Calif, a security research firm, found the flaw in August 2026 using an advanced artificial intelligence model from OpenAI. The firm alerted the nonprofit that manages PHP. However, word of the flaw leaked before the PHP organization released patches for its software, and according to Amazon Web Services officials, hackers began “broadly” attempting to exploit it.

The vulnerability has implications far beyond a single company or platform, because PHP is a key piece of software that helps run millions of websites. So, what is PHP, what role did AI play in uncovering the vulnerability, and should the average user worry?

PHP: The foundation of the web

PHP is a programming language that powers most websites. For a modern website to provide dynamic content, visual elements and searchable features, a program must run on the web server and take user input, whether that is entering a web address or clicking links and buttons. Estimates suggest that around 70% of websites run on PHP.

PHP operates on a web server in two main parts: the core PHP system – the engine and runtime libraries – and the individual PHP scripts, which are the custom programs that actually implement a website. When you interact with a website, PHP scripts run, take user input and produce the output your web browser displays.

The vulnerability

The current security issue sits directly in the core PHP system and the libraries it uses. When a vulnerability exists at this deep level, it can allow an adversary to exploit the system. In this case, they can run unauthorized commands on the computer hosting the website, which allows attackers to access data and gain full control of the website.

This vulnerability is not a mistake in an individual website’s code. The issue lies in the core PHP system, making every unpatched system running PHP vulnerable. Since websites are accessible to anyone on the internet, adversaries can easily find PHP-based websites using automated tools. From there, they can run an exploit program that takes advantage of the vulnerability.

This exploit code is called PHP2Shell. This name comes from the fact that the exploit gives the attacker “shell access,” a cybersecurity term for direct command-line control of the computer running the website. Shell access bypasses the website interface, giving adversaries a window to enter commands and access all the website’s data.

AI: A double-edged sword

What makes this vulnerability particularly interesting is how it was discovered. This exploit came to light through a process known as coordinated disclosure, in which cybersecurity researchers report the flaw to PHP developers before publicizing it.

This discovery shows the power of AI in cybersecurity. For decades, finding subtle software flaws required large teams of specialists manually reviewing code. Today’s AI systems can examine vast codebases and identify unusual patterns in hours or days. These models can analyze millions of lines of code in seconds, spotting subtle memory management bugs that human auditors might miss over decades of software development. The PHP vulnerability has existed in the core PHP code for over a decade, and AI helped researchers find it.

However, this also shows that attackers can use these same tools to locate and exploit vulnerabilities. The same reasoning capabilities that help security researchers find flaws first can also let attackers rapidly scan the web for vulnerable targets and automate the creation of tools to exploit the vulnerabilities.

This illustrates why it is so critical for security teams to use AI to find vulnerabilities and report them safely and actively. AI can also help release patches that mitigate these vulnerabilities.

Should you worry?

Many government agencies, universities, hospitals and businesses rely on PHP-based systems. While individual internet users are unlikely to be directly affected, organizations that delay patching could expose sensitive data, risk having their operations disrupted or give attackers a foothold into larger networks.

PHP runs entirely on remote web servers. If you are an everyday internet user visiting websites, you do not need to download a patch or fix your personal computer.

However, if you manage a website, blog or server, even a small site built on popular content management systems such as WordPress, you should check your server administration panel or web host immediately to ensure your PHP software is updated to the latest patched version. If a third party hosts your website, check with them to see whether they have patched for these vulnerabilities.

The PHP2Shell discovery illustrates a new reality for cybersecurity. In our interconnected world, keeping web infrastructure secure is a continuous race. As AI tools become standard for both cyber defenders and online adversaries, maintaining fast patching habits remains our most essential defense.

item.title: A critical flaw affecting 70% of all websites has the cybersecurity world panicked
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Andrew Cullen, Guest Research Fellow, School of Computing and Information Systems, The University of Melbourne

Details have been published of a critical flaw in the programming language PHP, which is the backbone of more than 70% of all websites. Left unfixed, the flaw would allow hackers to easily take over and compromise millions of websites and the information held on their servers. In response, multiple European governments and operators including the Port of Rotterdam have taken websites offline.

The Australian Signals Directorate, America’s Cyber Defence Agency, and similar bodies from the United Kingdom, Europe and Japan have all warned web developers to apply urgent updates to their core systems, and to consider taking down websites until safety can be guaranteed.

The organisation behind the free, open-source language has published updates that patch the flaw, but performing the updates on the millions of systems that use PHP will take time.

What is PHP?

PHP is often called “the backbone of the web”. It’s a programming language – a way to give instructions to computers – that has been around since 1997, and it allows websites to manage user inputs and process information behind the scenes.

The power of PHP is its versatility. Websites use it for everything from logging users into accounts and running online stores, to requesting data from databases and powering millions of blog posts and news sites.

PHP runs on the server rather than your personal computer. This means most of us interact with PHP every single day without ever seeing it.

A timeline of concerns

In August, a cybersecurity researchers from a company called Wiz used their own tools and the latest versions of Google’s Gemini and OpenAI’s ChatGPT AI models to trawl through PHP’s massive codebase.

The Wiz team were searching for hidden programming weaknesses that an attacker could chain together to take over a system running PHP simply by sending a carefully crafted request over the internet.

Within a few days, they found ways to break into PHP-powered systems from Drupal and WordPress which are used in huge swathes of the web.

Wiz contacted the PHP security team to let them know about the flaws they had found. By late September, the PHP developers confirmed that the issue existed, and quietly began working on a fix.

In cybersecurity, the responsible thing to do when you find a bug is to keep it private until a patch is ready. This is because public disclosure could provide a detailed map for hackers to exploit.

This appears to be what the PHP developers were planning. However, yesterday a user on popular industry website Hacker News let news slip about the security flaws before any patches were ready.

Following the leak, PHP’s developers rushed to publicly confirm the issue on October 21, releasing emergency patches ahead of schedule.

Implementing the patches is far from simple. Because PHP sits underneath thousands of third-party plugins, frameworks and managed hosting services, websites are only secure once every individual layer of the supply chain integrates and deploys the PHP fix.

Why does this keep happening?

Much of the internet is built on foundational technologies that were developed and maintained by hobbyist developers. Many rely on goodwill and donations rather than robust corporate funding.

Many of these tools were first developed decades ago. They were never designed to safely support a world where millions of websites and billions of devices use them to handle sensitive and private data.

Compounding this issue is the fact that maintenance is rarely a priority for organisations. All too often, companies have only the most basic knowledge about all the pieces of their supply chains – either physical or digital.

Even in high profile cases such as this one, many businesses don’t even realise what software they depend on, let alone have any idea of how secure it actually is.

What should you do?

This issue is mainly one for people who maintain websites or manage technical infrastructure. For those people, the priority is clear: patch systems immediately when updates are available, and consider taking down critical systems from the internet until you can be confident about their security.

For everyday internet users, these vulnerabilities affect the servers hosting websites rather than your personal device. However, because some sites may be temporarily compromised before they can patch, it is wise to be cautious about entering sensitive personal data on unfamiliar websites over the next few days.

Major cloud providers and security firms are rolling out emergency filters, but the global scramble to secure the web is just beginning.

Cybersecurity teams around the world are rushing to contain the damage. But the scope of this issue should be a wake-up call.

Governments and businesses cannot ignore the resilience of their digital supply chains. Just as manufacturers track the suppliers of the physical components they depend upon, we should expect that digital infrastructure also traces every system and framework it depends on.

Gathering this information is the first step for businesses and governments to truly understand how heavily their digital viability relies on underfunded, volunteer-maintained code. Until businesses treat funding open-source foundational tools as a critical security investment rather than a charity, these vulnerabilities will keep happening.

Andrew Cullen is a board member at Music Technology Australia, a member of the World Intellectual Property Organizations AI Technical Exchange Committee, and the managing consultant at EthiCan.

item.title: Why Meta’s new virtual reality glasses could finally take this technology primetime
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Karl Hodge, Course Director, Undergraduate Journalism, Leeds Beckett University

Two years after releasing its last virtual reality product, Meta has announced plans to release virtual reality (VR) glasses. They are due to reach the market in spring of 2027.

With a lightweight and stylish form, the glasses could be the tipping point for mainstream VR adoption. Interest in virtual reality waxes and wanes. Versions of the technology have been around since the 1990s, but VR only really broke through at consumer level when Meta’s previous incarnation Facebook released Oculus Quest in 2019 (the company had bought Oculus five years earlier).

VR got off to a great start, perhaps one of the very few technologies to benefit from COVID and lockdowns. Steady sales of Quest upgrades now mean Meta has shifted 20 million VR headsets worldwide to date.

That’s where the good news for VR ends. The market decline became visible in the first quarter of 2024, when Apple’s Vision Pro proved to be a rare and expensive flop for the Mac and iPhone manufacturer. After selling 390,000 initial units worldwide, it could muster only 210,000 more after a muted chip upgrade.

When we drill into the overall numbers of active VR users, we find a curious statistic. Released in 2020 and discontinued in 2024, the Quest 2 is still the most widely used VR device in the market.

This is strange, considering there have been several updates since: the Quest Pro, Quest 3 and Quest 3S. It seems that once early adopters, gamers and enthusiasts had the technology in their hands, they were reluctant to upgrade.

Newer headsets offered higher resolution and faster processing, but the advances were incremental rather than Earth-shattering. At £3,495, the Apple Vision Pro’s poor sales showed that gamers were reluctant to part with more than the price of a games console.

As VR sales plateaued, Meta moved away from headsets. Starting in 2023 it partnered strategically with fashion brands like Ray-Ban and Oakley for its augmented reality, AI-powered product, Meta Glasses.

It was a smart move. Such accessories have been controversial due to privacy concerns over their ability to record video without other people knowing. But smart glasses have become must-haves for influencers and social media content creators. With marketing focused on jet-set activities, Meta Glasses have taken the device category out of the basement and onto the catwalk.

With the announcement of Meta VR Glasses, the company is positioned to rebrand VR as sexy and stylish, focusing on media consumption rather than gaming. Crucially, they’re glasses, not a headset. They’re part of the already buoyant “wearables” niche now. That is, smart accessories like watches, rings and spectacles.

Fancy ski glasses

The Meta Quest 3, released in 2023, is five times heavier than Meta VR Glasses. The company’s engineering feat in making the new product so light has partly been accomplished by shifting some computing power into an accompanying brickette that Meta calls a “puck”. It’s essentially a computing core (powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon processor) and battery, connected through a fibre-optic cable.

Weighing 300g, the puck reduces the headset to a stereoscopic display resembling a fancy pair of ski glasses. The glasses – which weigh just 100g – can be worn for hours at a stretch, according to Meta, with a battery that can manage three hours of continuous high-resolution media playback.

The device will run Meta Horizon OS (operating system) and have access to a huge, existing catalogue of games, apps and experiences. However, it’s not positioned as a VR headset to rival its Quest precedessors. Instead, the new glasses are touted as a device for watching movies, attending live events, and replacing monitors. They will let users interact with multiple computer screens in their own environment, blending the real and virtual worlds.

So far, so similar to the Apple Vision Pro. And while the US$1,299.99 (around £1,000) price point is a little kinder on the wallet, we’d be missing the point if we didn’t ask: what do Meta VR Glasses have that the Vision Pro doesn’t? Or, for that matter, any number of products from other developers, like the HTC Vive Flow or Xreal One Pro.

Well, aside from the weight, price, back catalogue and the sleek good looks, there’s a massive, crucial difference. Meta VR Glasses have a ready-made audience. Meta has carefully incubated this demographic since 2021, developing AI glasses alongside its VR headsets.

Partnerships with fashionable brands have enabled it to sidestep the “ick” of early VR. Mark Zuckerberg’s disastrously awkward demonstration of VR platform Horizon Worlds in 2022 failed to sell the Quest Pro to the mainstream, but Meta AI Glasses continued unharmed and unhindered.

In fact, while the VR market has grown little recently, a 2026 report by the research company Omdia found that the smart glasses market expanded by 322% in 2025. Meta accounts for 85% of that global market. Now the two streams are about to converge.

And though there’s no Ray-Ban version of Meta VR Glasses yet, the device will launch with significant partnerships. Disney+, Prime Video, YouTube, ESPN and Imax are among those already announced. Could this finally be the tipping point for widespread VR adoption?

It’s not yet the holy grail – a hassle-free pair of glasses that wearers can just toggle into VR mode – but it’s a distinct step along the way. Crucially, it unites loyal followers from both sides of the style divide: the chic and the geek.

item.title: Digital natives are buying electric cars as if they were smartphones
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Svetoslav Georgiev, Associate Professor, School of Intelligent Finance and Business, Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University

Until recently, buying a car meant obsessing over horsepower, transmission types and brand heritage. But step into the market today and the showroom floor looks entirely different.

With the aggressive expansion of electric vehicle production and the entry of smartphone giants like Xiaomi and Huawei into the car market, vehicles are rapidly transforming into rolling computers.

This shift raises a fundamental question for the modern market: are younger consumers beginning to evaluate cars the exact same way they evaluate smartphones?

To understand the buying behaviour of young consumers, we must first recognise that the car industry is undergoing a profound digital transformation. Traditional factors like brand prestige and mechanical engineering, while still relevant, are steadily losing ground to software capabilities and digital integration.

Tech-focused manufacturers are prioritising software-driven car systems, leaving legacy car makers struggling to adapt. For millenials, this technological pivot is not just an added bonus; it is becoming a baseline expectation.

Market-specific factors like electric vehicle pricing and availability in regions like China may accelerate this trend, but the underlying data reflects a broader, cross-national generational shift among digital natives (someone who grew up around digital technology, such as smartphones) are revealing this shift in China, North America and Europe.

A generational perspective

When technologically minded consumers encounter an electric vehicle, they do not necessarily see a mechanical machine with a motor; they see a hardware platform waiting for an operating system.

Consequently, this mindset shifts how they judge the vehicle’s core anatomy. When this demographic evaluates electric vehicles, they base their decisions heavily on “product technological development” (how well the in-car technology works, for instance) and “charging infrastructure” alongside financial incentives.

This directly mirrors how a consumer evaluates a smartphone’s operational speed, battery longevity, and software updates rather than traditional, outdated car metrics.

This paradigm shift also rewrites how cars are bought and experienced. Long before a consumer ever sits in a driver’s seat, the purchasing journey has fundamentally changed. Younger consumers demonstrate a strong inclination toward online platforms and social media as their primary shopping channels, relying heavily on digital interactions and visually rich experiences.

Rather than turning to traditional dealership visits or print brochures, they depend on user-generated content, peer opinions, online reviews and digital advertising to inform their purchasing decisions. Furthermore, recent studies show that this target group’s evaluation criteria continue to mirror the metrics they apply to mobile technology.

Mirroring digital lives

When car shopping, research shows that gen Z consumers seek out technologically advanced and highly personalised experiences, showing a specific interest in the entertainment capabilities and software ecosystems of modern vehicles. This indicates they are evaluating the digital and entertainment experience inside the car, much like they would evaluate the apps of a new phone.

The intense brand loyalty traditionally reserved for Apple or android phones has seamlessly transferred to the car market. Seamless ecosystem integration via systems like Apple CarPlay or Android Auto is treated as a mandatory requirement. If a car fails to mirror a driver’s digital life instantly, it fails the test.

Younger consumers scrutinise a vehicle’s multimedia and infotainment systems with the same hardware expectations they apply to smartphones. If a touchscreen exhibits input lag, clunky user interfaces, or poor user experiences, it severely damages their perception of the entire vehicle.

Unlike older generations who harbour a habitual attachment to driving, younger cohorts base their transport choices on metrics such as travel time, cost efficiency and service reliability. They evaluate transport options rationally rather than emotionally.

Younger demographics increasingly prioritise shared mobility programmes, such as Uber and Grab, over private vehicle ownership. They expect personal settings and digital profiles to sync instantly upon entering any vehicle. This allows them to listen to their latest music playlists or read messages on their smartphone. This mirrors the multi-device continuity they experience when using, for example, tablets and smartphones.

Just as smartphone consumers agonise over app permissions and data tracking, tech-savvy millennials, as well as gen Zs, view connected cars through a lens of data security. Trust in the way vehicle technology and data is handled have become a primary psychological barrier to adoption.

However, a fundamental disconnect explains a striking corporate blind spot identified in recent market research: while 80% of automotive executives believe they are delivering an exceptional digital customer experience, only 8% of customers actually agree. Traditional manufacturers are failing the software test because they still think like mechanics, not app developers.

Brain overload

Treating a car like a smartphone, however, raises a potential problem related to the physical reality of driving. While younger consumers demand the deep customisation and flexibility of touchscreens, replacing physical controls with digital sub-menus creates massive cognitive overload.

Forcing drivers to navigate complex digital layers to adjust basic climate or safety settings diverts visual attention and increases the risks of an accident. One study argues that reaction times using screens while driving are worse than being drunk or under the influence of drugs.

This has sparked an inevitable regulatory and design backlash. Safety organisations and designers are pushing back against pure “touchscreen-isation”, noting that a car is ultimately a high-speed vehicle, not a handset.

Even major car manufacturers, such as Volkswagen and Mazda, have publicly admitted that eliminating physical buttons was a misstep, leading to a hybrid design mandate where tactile controls for core functions must coexist with digital entertainment.

Ultimately, younger consumers are evaluating cars through a smartphone-tinted lens. Yet, the future of the car market will not belong to the brands that simply build iPhones on wheels.

The winners will be the manufacturers that successfully balance the digital native’s craving for software-driven connectivity with the uncompromising, safety-first reality of car design.

item.title: Why calling for a ‘kill switch’ is the wrong way to think about reining in AI
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Trent Wintermeier, Ph.D. Candidate in Rhetoric and Writing, The University of Texas at Austin

In the wake of high-profile hacking incidents involving advanced artificial intelligence agents, some politicians and business executives have been calling for an AI kill switch: a safeguard that could shut down these AI systems in an emergency.

The idea is that, if a model were to behave in dangerous ways, a kill switch would allow humans to regain control over that system by metaphorically flipping a switch from “on” to “off.”

Several efforts at AI regulation in 2026 have focused on the notion of a kill switch. These include proposed congressional legislation such as the AI Kill Switch Act, and California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s executive order aimed at reining in AI. President Donald Trump has opposed the idea of an AI kill switch as unnecessary regulation, and to date there has been no national regulation that includes a kill switch.

Experts such as Dylan Baker, a research engineer at the nonprofit Distributed AI Research Institute, have explained that one regulatory problem with the metaphor of the kill switch is that today’s advanced AI models involve a complex infrastructure of distributed technologies, which is beyond the control of a single kill switch.

Additionally, the metaphor of the kill switch also obscures the human decisions involved in the responsibility and oversight of an out-of-control model. The problem is that the metaphor does not account for the technological or human aspects of AI.

Black boxes and kill switches

The metaphor of the kill switch is not necessarily new. In fact, it is rooted in the same rhetoric as the black box metaphor, which similarly blurs the complex aspects of AI by framing inner workings as confined and unintelligible. Referring to AI as a black box frames these systems in terms of restricted incomprehensibility: a monolithic stranger to human control and understanding.

As the University of Cambridge, digital humanities researcher Eryk Salvaggio argues that “the black box of AI cultivates useful confusion about what can and cannot be known” about the complexity of frontier models. The idea of the kill switch cultivates a similar confusion by obscuring the distributed infrastructure and human influence that are important aspects of AI. While these metaphors have opposite meanings – resisting control and regaining control – they invoke the same implicit argument about the nuts and bolts of AI.

Both the black box and kill switch are what cognitive linguist George Lakoff and philosopher Mark Johnson call structural metaphors. They rely on simple physical concepts – for example, object, substance, up-down and in-out. Structural metaphors use one clearly delineated concept to help make another concept clearer. For example, black box uses the concept of an opaque container to give a clear structure to the concept of hidden or inscrutable inner workings.

Additionally, Lakoff and Johnson say that this type of metaphor can also hide some aspects of a concept by focusing attention on others. For example, the kill switch metaphor hides the complexity of advanced AI models by focusing on the fact that a model can be on or off.

What this means is that framing the operation of AI in terms of a black box and kill switch relies on the straightforward ideas of “box” and “switch” to conceal the complex operations of AI. Reining in AI becomes difficult on a policy level when discussions about AI regulation fail to account for the infrastructural and human aspects of advanced models.

Centralization and ‘rogue’ AI

There are two problems with the structural metaphor of an AI kill switch, both demonstrating that it misses the mark for a national safeguard. The first is that a kill switch makes the global infrastructure supporting AI appear centralized, when in reality it is a web of interconnected technologies spread across the globe.

The advanced models that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are concerned about releasing rely on multiple computers and data centers that are spread out nationally. It is not as simple as pulling a plug, opening a box or flipping a switch. The kill switch metaphor reduces the infrastructural entanglements of AI to outdated ideas about technology. For instance, in proposing his since-failed “AI Emergency Button Act” bill, Sen. John Kennedy compared the concept to kill switches in machines such as jet skis.

The second problem is that the kill switch idea keeps hidden the human decision-making involved in the training and deployment of frontier models. Rather than serving as a reminder that people are involved, the kill switch positions the human outside of the loop and ready to flip the switch during a catastrophic emergency. Human intervention is invoked as an afterthought, instead of a process that involves training, supervision and approval.

For instance, accounts of how OpenAI’s model went “rogue” and hacked AI company Hugging Face depict the AI agents as though they operated on their own agenda. But experts have explained that not only did OpenAI personnel turn off safety mechanisms, but they also gave the model impossible tasks and left a door open to the internet. The role people played counters the “rogue” agent framing.

The kill switch metaphor is ill-suited to the challenge of regulating AI because there is no way to switch off an AI model without accounting for its distributed infrastructure and human influence. There is no big red button, emergency brake or glass box hiding a lever. Effective national regulation of AI will not begin with any single switch or any one person’s finger.
