item.title: As AI takes on more tasks, what happens when people have to jump in to clean up after it?
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Author:

  • Murugan Anandarajan, Professor of Decision Sciences and Management Information Systems, Drexel University

Imagine an artificial intelligence system that has performed reliably for months. Its recommendations are almost always right, and the employee reviewing them has learned that close scrutiny rarely changes the outcome. Then something unusual happens. The AI makes an error or can’t proceed and needs human intervention. The employee is expected to step in and remains responsible for the outcome.

But does the employee know how to do the task?

I’m a professor of management information systems and the academic director of Drexel University’s Center for Applied AI & Business Analytics. In my research on human-AI relationships, I call this latent risk: the possibility that people may lose capabilities their organizations still depend on them to exercise.

AI can continue to perform well while the people overseeing it become less practiced at exercising independent judgment and less prepared to intervene. The risk becomes latent when the organization still depends on that human capability to step in but has little cause to notice that that capability may be weakening.

The concern is not entirely new. The idea of latent risk builds on decades of research into how people respond to automation. For example, studies of automation bias have shown that people can miss problems or follow automated recommendations even when other evidence suggests they should not.

What is different today is the role AI is beginning to play in organizations. It is beginning to assume larger parts of the analysis and decision-making that people previously performed.

The success paradox

The better AI becomes, the more the nature of human work changes. Work that once required an employee to analyze a problem and reach a decision may instead be performed by AI, leaving the employee to review its recommendation. The employee is no longer doing the same work with AI assistance – rather, their job has shifted from doing the work to overseeing what the AI does.

This shift is already beginning to change how some companies train employees. Accounting giant Deloitte, for example, is redesigning its graduate audit training as AI takes over some of the manual work traditionally done by junior auditors. The firm is introducing simulations so trainees can still develop the judgment they will need as they move into more complex work.

More than four decades ago, cognitive psychologist Lisanne Bainbridge described one of the “ironies of automation”: As systems take over more of the work, instead of simply having their work loads lightened, people can be left facing new challenges in monitoring the systems and handling the unusual situations the systems cannot. Later studies found another problem: As people become less involved in a task, they can become less prepared to step in when needed. Researchers have called this the out-of-the-loop performance problem.

This reduced involvement may affect more than a person’s readiness to intervene. It can change the capabilities available to the organization.

What work remains for people does not necessarily become easier. It may become harder. These are the situations where experience and independent judgment matter most. The result is a paradox: People may be called upon to exercise independent judgment less often, even as the judgments left to them become more difficult.

The accountability problem

Accountability may not change as quickly as the work does when organizations deploy AI systems. An employee may now oversee far more decisions than they make themselves, while remaining responsible for the outcomes. The organization’s expectations may still reflect how the work was divided before AI took on a larger role. The organization can therefore end up holding people accountable for decisions over which they have less control.

This creates a mismatch. Research on meaningful human control suggests that responsibility should match a person’s authority and ability to act. An employee may retain the authority to override an AI recommendation and remain responsible for the outcome, yet lose the capability to do so. Authority, responsibility and capability can begin to separate.

Latent risk becomes an organizational design problem, not simply a human performance problem.

The measurement problem

Organizations typically judge AI-enabled processes by measures such as accuracy and productivity. Those numbers may look good even as the human role is changing. Suppose employees override AI recommendations less frequently over time. Is that a sign of growing dependence? Perhaps.

But it could also mean that the AI has become more accurate and there is less reason to intervene. The number of overrides alone tells little about whether employees remain ready to exercise their own judgment.

The key is to understand how the division of work between people and AI is changing. Which decisions have migrated from people to AI? What responsibilities remain with people? Looking at the performance of the employee or the AI separately may miss what is changing between them.

The governance problem

Organizational governance – defining roles and responsibilities – is also under pressure from AI.

Someone may remain formally in the loop with an AI system even as their actual role changes. Defining human and AI roles when a system is introduced is only a starting point. As AI improves and people become accustomed to using it, those roles are likely to change over time. There is nothing inherently wrong with that change.

The problem arises when the relationship changes but the assumptions surrounding it do not. It’s important for organizations to periodically ask: What relationship between people and AI did we design, and what relationship do we actually have today?

In short, organizational governance needs to be dynamic.

Maintaining the human backstop

Not every human capability needs to be preserved. If AI can perform a task well, there is little reason to require people to keep doing the same work. Organizations need to decide which capabilities they still expect people to have when human judgment is required. If people may still be called upon to use a capability, it needs to be maintained.

Overseeing AI is not the same as exercising independent judgment. If people rarely make the decision themselves, the organization cannot assume they will be ready when they need to. One way to test this is to occasionally ask employees to make a decision without first seeing the AI recommendation. The organization needs to know that the human backstop it relies on will actually work when needed.

As AI takes on more work, some human capabilities will inevitably be used less often. Some may no longer matter. Others may still be essential when AI reaches its limits. The challenge is knowing the difference and making that choice deliberately.

For me, the central question is this: Which human capabilities does an organization still depend on, and will they be there when needed?

item.title: AI can predict intimate partner violence before survivors disclose. But should it?
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Authors:

  • Eden Hoffer, PhD Candidate, Health Information Science, Western University
  • Karen A. Campbell, Assistant Professor, School of Nursing, York University, Canada

Artificial intelligence (AI) can now flag people who may be at elevated risk of intimate partner violence (IPV) years before they disclose the violence or seek help for it within the health-care system.

But what happens when a health-care system appears to know something about a survivor they haven’t chosen to reveal?

In a recent study, a research team led by researchers from Harvard Medical School in Boston trained AI models using routinely collected electronic health record data to identify patients at risk of IPV. On average, the models identified risk of IPV more than three years before patients enrolled in a hospital-based domestic abuse intervention program.

At first blush, this may sound like a revolutionary breakthrough in care for people who have experienced IPV. If health-care providers can identify patients at elevated risk of IPV victimization, they might be able to offer support or resources before survivors even disclose the abuse.

The findings, however, have their limits: the models were developed using data from female patients at a single U.S. academic health centre, though the researchers did validate the models in three other patient cohorts. The researchers noted that “careful performance evaluation on the more general population of female patients should be conducted before implementing the models for clinical use.”

However, viewed through a trauma- and violence-informed lens, the promise of early detection raises a critical question: what happens to a person’s agency when the health-care system can flag their potential risk of IPV before they choose to disclose their experiences?

A trauma- and violence-informed approach

Trauma- and violence-informed care is an approach that recognizes how trauma, inequity and systemic violence shape people’s health. These experiences also shape people’s relationships with health-care providers and the systems they work in.

The approach emphasizes principles of safety, choice, collaboration, connection and capacity-building. Those principles matter in the context of IPV because disclosure is complex.

For someone experiencing IPV, deciding when, how and whether to disclose depends on a range of factors. Among them are safety concerns, financial dependence, distrust of social services, fear of not being believed and concerns their children will be taken away.

In some cases, staying silent about abuse is a survival strategy women use to keep themselves and their children safe.

Relying on AI to detect abuse risks taking control away from survivors, removing their freedom to decide when and how to discuss their trauma with a clinician.

Read more: Domestic violence disclosure schemes may not improve safety for victim-survivors of intimate partner violence

The risk of missed opportunities

While AI may create new opportunities to identify potential IPV victimization, it may also create new ways to miss it.

If health-care systems become over-reliant on AI-generated risk assessments, the absence of an “AI flag” could discourage providers from asking whether a patient is experiencing violence. This is especially concerning because a survivor’s disclosure often depends on a health-care provider creating a safe space for them to share.

Research on clinical decision-support systems has already highlighted concerns about automation bias — the tendency of clinicians to over-rely on automated recommendations, even when those are wrong.

If AI is used to detect IPV, that’s all the more reason to ensure these tools supplement — not replace — clinical judgment. They should also support meaningful conversations between health-care providers and patients.

Detecting IPV is different from responding

This points to a crucial distinction: detecting IPV is not the same as responding to it, especially in a trauma- and violence-informed way.

An assumption worth interrogating is whether using AI to identify people who may be experiencing IPV actually improves their outcomes.

One of the researchers who developed and tested the AI tool has said its goal is not to pressure patients into disclosure. Rather, the aim is to help clinicians communicate compassionately with patients and connect them with support and resources.

What exactly happens once a patient is flagged by AI systems, however, remains unclear.

Is the clinician trained to respond to a disclosure of IPV, especially in a trauma- and violence-informed way? Are appropriate services that align with the needs of the victim-survivor available and accessible?

Even if algorithms can flag a patient who is at an elevated risk of IPV, victim-survivors will likely still encounter the same gaps in services, safety planning and other resources that already exist today.

Therefore, while health systems might become better at identifying IPV, that does not inherently mean they will be better at addressing it.

Where do we go from here?

Ultimately, interacting with the health-care system and health-care providers still represents a critical window for IPV victim-survivor intervention and support.

But creating conditions in which victim-survivors can choose to disclose abuse safely is very different from having AI infer that violence may be occurring before they have chosen to share that information.

From a trauma- and violence-informed perspective, questions about AI’s predictive accuracy are only one piece of the puzzle. Any implementation of AI-based IPV risk detection must also be evaluated against principles of safety, choice, collaboration, connection and capacity-building.

Before these tools reach clinics, those who design and deploy them need to consider who gets to decide when a survivor’s story is told.

This question is particularly important because IPV is often marked by coercion and control. For someone living with IPV, the ability to decide when, how and whether to talk about it should not be taken lightly. A tool that takes that choice away from them, however well-intentioned, falls short of truly survivor-centred care.

item.title: My own security system flagged me, a Black woman, as an animal
item.dc:creator: theconversation
item.content:encoded:

Author:

  • Kanika Samuels-Wortley, Associate Professor, Faculty of Social Science and Humanities, Ontario Tech University

The first time my home security system flagged me as an animal, I was sitting at my patio table with my morning coffee a few years ago. I figured it was a glitch. A few months later, it happened again as I walked across the yard to catch the afternoon sun.

More recently, while I was on vacation, the same system logged my South Asian teenaged neighbour, whom I’d hired to cut the grass, as an animal too. This has never happened to my husband, who is white. Two racialized people appear to produce one pattern.

My son, who is in elementary school, also told me he couldn’t chat with a friend online. I had parental controls set up on the platform, and the age verification had read his friend, a Black boy the same age, as much older than him and blocked them from communicating.

This is no longer a glitch, I realized. We have a real problem.

I keep returning to these moments following Prime Minister Mark Carney’s first Canada Investment Summit, which asked the world’s largest investors to put money into Canadian advanced technology. Energy, critical minerals, defence and technology are the four things Canada is selling, yet nobody on the summit agenda appeared to ask whose faces these systems fail to recognize.

As a Canada Research Chair examining how bias shapes technologies adopted by the criminal justice system, I wonder: Can we trust these systems built to keep us from harm when they can’t reliably tell us apart from wildlife? Can we trust these systems that reinforce the adultification of Black boys?

Algorithms that cause harm

Canada recently released a national AI strategy, premised on AI for all. While this is well intended, “for all” is hard to imagine when systems read me, or anyone with darker skin, as something other than human.

The strategy recognizes that “biases built into algorithms can cause harm to vulnerable communities,” but it stops short of acknowledging how that harm erodes trust in these systems among racialized people in particular.

Some may question the focus on race. However, it’s necessary when system errors keep reproducing long-standing stereotypes that cast Black and brown bodies as animalistic, or Black children as older than they are. And this matters as AI-powered surveillance cameras become more popular in Canada.

Read more: Is someone watching you? Facial recognition tech is here and Canada offers little privacy protection

Support for AI in policing

Take policing. Canadian law enforcement agencies remain among the most trusted institutions in this country. That trust, however, has always been lower among Black and Indigenous people.

I was surprised, then, when my national study on public perceptions of AI in Canadian policing across racial groups found that 60 per cent of Black and 62 per cent of South Asian respondents supported AI in policing, even at a potentially high financial cost, compared to only 46 per cent of white respondents.

Furthermore, white respondents were more likely than Black and Indigenous respondents to rate transparency, ethical safeguards, regulation and public input as important.

Read quickly, that might look like indifference among racialized people. But perhaps white respondents expect transparency and ethical conduct by the police, whereas for Black and Indigenous respondents, those principles have historically been absent. Their support is conditional on meaningful demonstration rather than a stated promise.

Read more: As ICE’s tech-enabled dragnet and surveillance expand, activists are fighting back with data of their own

Bias is not a moral footnote

Where these racial groups did agree, in my research, was on government regulation of AI in policing. Every group rated it as important, suggesting that Canadians see AI as a viable public safety tool, but want real accountability.

Trust is the variable that decides whether these systems earn legitimacy, but whose trust does the government seek? The federal AI Strategy Task Force did not include any Black members until a prominent legal scholar pushed for one. Now there is one single Black voice advising the country on a technology whose failures may affect an entire community.

The government is right to push for more home-grown technology, since much of what enters Canadian institutions is built abroad and trained on populations that look nothing like our own. But building in Canada has to mean building with people at the table who are empowered to ask hard questions. While this does not guarantee better systems, it can create the conditions for real oversight and measured deployment instead of legal repercussions later.

So, as Ottawa goes looking for billions over the next five years with advanced technology on the pitch list, bias cannot be a moral footnote. It must be central to the agenda. We need to ask upfront who these systems are most likely to fail, how we will know and what it will take to address those failures.

If we don’t, Canada risks not only perpetuating bias but eroding its citizens’ trust. People like me would like to sit in their own backyard without being mistaken for wildlife. That’s a low bar for a country that says it’s building technology for all.
